families.name: Ab wheel rollout
families.pattern: Dynamic anti-extension: the arms roll a wheel, ball or bar forward so the body lengthens toward the floor, then the abs and lats pull it back.
setup: Kneel on a pad, hands on the wheel under your shoulders.
Tuck your tailbone slightly and brace; back flat to a little rounded.
Arms straight.

steps.text: Roll the wheel forward as the hips follow, body getting longer and lower.
Stop just before your low back starts to sag.
Pull the wheel back toward your knees with straight arms, hips last.

cues.cue: Keep the slight tuck; never let the back sag.
cues.why: The rollout is one of the highest abdominal exercises measured, because the abs must stop spine extension.

cues.cue: Only go as far as you can keep the tuck.
cues.why: The lever grows as you go out; partial range is fine.

cues.cue: Straight arms; pull back with the lats.
cues.why: Latissimus dorsi activity was high in rollouts.

cues.cue: Hips and shoulders move together.
cues.why: Leaving the hips behind turns it into a shoulder stretch.

families.breathing: Breathe in on the way out, out as you roll back.

tempo.note: Roll out in 2 s, pause, roll back in 2 s.

mistakes.name: Low back sags
mistakes.looks: At full reach the hips drop and the back arches.
mistakes.fix: Shorten the range; tuck the tailbone.
mistakes.why: Load moves from the abs to the spine.

mistakes.name: Hips stay back
mistakes.looks: Only the arms reach forward; hips stay over the knees.
mistakes.fix: Let hips travel forward with the wheel.
mistakes.why: The trunk lever never lengthens, so the abs barely work.

mistakes.name: Bending the elbows
mistakes.looks: Elbows bend and the move becomes a push-up.
mistakes.fix: Lock the elbows; move from the shoulders.
mistakes.why: It shortens the lever and shifts work to the chest and triceps.

safety: Low back pain: start on a stability ball or roll toward a wall to limit range.
Shoulder pain: shorten the range; avoid going past arms overhead.

variants.change: Forearms on a ball: easier, still among the best abdominal exercises.
Roll toward a wall to cap the range.
From standing: very hard; the whole body becomes the lever.
Forearm plank with feet on a slider or straps, rocking forward and back.
Hands in straps: unstable and adjustable by body angle.
Roll out on a diagonal: more oblique work.

subtypes.name: Body saw
subtypes.change: Forearm plank with feet on a slider or ball; push the body back and pull forward.

subtypes.name: Stability ball rollout
subtypes.change: Kneel, forearms on the ball; roll it forward until arms are near overhead.

motion.basis: Kneeling wheel rollout. All angles estimated from the technique; activation findings from escamilla2006, escamilla2010 and youdas2008.

families.name: Agility drill
families.pattern: Quick footwork and changes of direction from a low athletic stance: shuffles, ladders, cone and dot drills.
setup: Athletic stance: feet a bit wider than the hips, knees and hips bent, chest up.
Weight on the balls of the feet.
Set cones or a ladder on a non-slip floor.

steps.text: Push off the outside foot to move sideways; do not cross your feet.
Bring the trailing foot in under you, stance stays low and wide.
To change direction, sink the hips, plant the outside foot and push back.

cues.cue: Stay low: hips back, knees bent, chest up.
cues.why: Lowering the centre of mass before a cut lets you brake and push off faster.

cues.cue: Knee over the toes on every plant; never let it cave in.
cues.why: Knee valgus on landing and cutting predicts ACL injury.

cues.cue: Slow down over a few short steps before a sharp turn.
cues.why: Braking on the steps before the final plant lowers knee load in sharp cuts.

cues.cue: Quick light feet, eyes up.
cues.why: Agility combines fast footwork with reading what is around you.

families.breathing: Breathe freely; each drill is short.

tempo.note: Work 5-20 s per drill at full speed with full rest; quality over fatigue.

mistakes.name: Knee caves in on the plant
mistakes.looks: The planted knee falls inside the foot.
mistakes.fix: Push the knee out over the second toe and sink the hips.
mistakes.why: High ACL load.

mistakes.name: Standing too tall
mistakes.looks: Legs nearly straight, hips high.
mistakes.fix: Sit into an athletic stance.
mistakes.why: Slower direction changes and stiffer, harder landings.

mistakes.name: Feet cross or click
mistakes.looks: Feet clip together or cross in a shuffle.
mistakes.fix: Keep the feet at least hip width apart.
mistakes.why: Easy to trip and lose balance.

safety: Warm up first; build from slow to full speed.
Use a non-slip surface and good shoes.

variants.change: Shuttle running forward, back and sideways: about 11.0 MET (02078).
Ladder, dot and shuffle footwork: same code, lower in practice when done at walking pace.

subtypes.name: Lateral shuffle
subtypes.change: Default keyframes.

subtypes.name: Ladder and dot drills
subtypes.change: Small fast steps or two-foot hops into boxes; upright, heels off the floor.

subtypes.name: Cone, T, L and X drills
subtypes.change: Sprints between cones with a plant and turn at each; lean into the turn.

harder: high hurdle jump to sprint and cut

motion.basis: Cutting and braking principles from dossantos2018 and hewett2005; agility definition from sheppard2006. Shuffle angles are estimates.

families.name: Ankle and foot
families.pattern: Small, controlled ankle and foot movements: pointing and pulling up the foot, turning the sole in and out, circles, and toe work, often against a band.
setup: Sit on the floor or a chair with the leg straight or the heel on the floor.
For band work, loop the band around the forefoot and anchor it opposite the direction you will move.
Keep the knee and shin still; only the foot moves.

steps.text: Foot relaxed, toes pointing up.
Move the foot slowly to the end of the range against the band (up, down, in or out).
Return slowly over about 3 seconds, resisting the band.

cues.cue: Shin and knee still; only the foot turns.
cues.why: Rotating the leg hides the ankle motion you are training.

cues.cue: Train up, down, in and out.
cues.why: Four-way band strengthening improved strength, balance and hop tests in chronic ankle instability.

cues.cue: Slow on the way back.
cues.why: Eccentric control was part of the strength protocol that improved eversion strength.

cues.cue: For towel curls and foot activation, lift the arch without curling the toes hard.
cues.why: The small foot muscles support the arch and feed balance information.

cues.cue: 2-3 sets of 10-15, about 3 days a week.
cues.why: Supervised rehab exercise lowers the risk of another sprain.

families.breathing: Breathe normally.

tempo.note: About 2 s out, 1 s hold, 3 s back; 10-15 reps.

mistakes.name: Leg rolls instead of the ankle
mistakes.looks: For inversion or eversion the whole leg turns from the hip.
mistakes.fix: Hold the shin with a hand or pillow; move only the foot.
mistakes.why: The hip does the work and the ankle muscles get little load.

mistakes.name: Toes do the work
mistakes.looks: The toes claw hard while the ankle barely moves.
mistakes.fix: Relax the toes, lead with the whole foot.
mistakes.why: The long toe muscles take over from the ankle movers.

mistakes.name: Band snaps back
mistakes.looks: The foot is pulled back quickly by the band.
mistakes.fix: Lighter band, 3 s return.
mistakes.why: Loses the eccentric half of the rep.

safety: Acute sprain: early gentle movement helps; start pain-free range work within a few days and see a clinician for a bad sprain.
Sharp pain, a pop, or you cannot put weight on the foot: get it checked.
Diabetes or poor foot sensation: check the skin under bands and towels.

variants.change: Band or cable adds load; anchor it opposite the movement.
Standing: body weight on the foot; harder and more like daily life.
Towel curl: pull a towel toward you with the toes, heel down.

subtypes.name: Ankle circles and alphabet
subtypes.change: Draw slow full circles with the foot, both directions.

subtypes.name: Band inversion and eversion
subtypes.change: Seated, heel down; turn the sole in (inversion, about 30°) or out (eversion, about 15°) against the band. ankleEv is eversion, + outward.

subtypes.name: Toe and arch work
subtypes.change: Seated or standing, heel down; spread, lift, press or curl the toes, or shorten the foot to lift the arch.

subtypes.name: Heel walk
subtypes.change: Walk on your heels with the toes pulled up high.

subtypes.name: Ankle stretches and rocks
subtypes.change: Kneel or half kneel and rock the knee forward over the toes (dorsiflexion), or sit back on the tops of the feet (plantar flexion). Hold or rock slowly.

motion.basis: Default: seated band dorsiflexion. Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion ranges from soucie2011 (adults 20-44: dorsiflexion about 13°, plantar flexion 55-62°); inversion and eversion ranges are common clinical norms (estimate). ankleEv (eversion, + outward) and toeFlex are extra keys not yet in the README convention; the rig needs a subtalar and toe joint for them. Protocol cues from hall2018, kaminski2013 and mckeon2015.

families.name: Back extension and good morning
families.pattern: Trunk and hip extension: the trunk lowers forward from the hips and lifts back to a straight line, with the legs fixed.
setup: Set the pad just below the hip crease so the hips can bend freely.
Heels against the foot plate, legs straight or a little soft.
Arms crossed on the chest; harder: hands by the head or a plate on the chest.

steps.text: Bend at the hips and lower the trunk under control.
Stop when you feel the hamstrings stretch or the back starts to round.
Squeeze glutes and lift the trunk back up.
Stop in a straight line from head to heels. Do not arch past it.

cues.cue: Finish in a straight line, not an arch.
cues.why: Over-arching adds load on the lumbar joints without extra hip work.

cues.cue: Hinge at the hips; pad below the hip crease.
cues.why: The 45° back extension works glutes and hamstrings strongly as well as the back.

cues.cue: Make it harder by moving the arms up: chest, head, then overhead.
cues.why: Back muscle activity rose step by step with hand position and a more horizontal bench.

cues.cue: To target the back, bend the hips less and move the spine more.
cues.why: Limiting hip flexion cut hamstring activity and kept the load on the back extensors.

cues.cue: Smooth reps, no bouncing at the bottom.
cues.why: Momentum takes load off the muscles you are training.

families.breathing: Breathe in going down, out as you lift.

tempo.note: Two seconds down, two up.

mistakes.name: Over-arching at the top
mistakes.looks: The chest lifts above the line of the legs and the low back pinches.
mistakes.fix: Stop when your body is straight; squeeze glutes.
mistakes.why: Range at the top comes from lumbar extension only.

mistakes.name: Bouncing out of the bottom
mistakes.looks: The trunk drops fast and rebounds up.
mistakes.fix: Two seconds down, a short pause, then lift.
mistakes.why: The stretch reflex and momentum do the work.

mistakes.name: Back rounds under load (good morning)
mistakes.looks: The upper and low back curve as you bend forward with the bar.
mistakes.fix: Lighter load, soft knees, stop higher.
mistakes.why: A loaded flexed spine is the riskiest version of the hinge.

safety: Low back pain: start on the floor or with a short range; avoid loaded good mornings until pain-free.
Good morning: start light; knees bend more as the load goes up.

variants.change: 45° bench: easier than a 90° (horizontal) bench.
Load held at the chest or behind the neck; hold it close.
Rotate the trunk at the top: more oblique work.
One foot on the plate: more glute and hamstring on that side.
Spine curls down and up on purpose with the hips fixed: targets the back muscles; keep the load light.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top for upper back work.
Over a stability ball, feet against a wall: smaller range, easier.
Hold the straight-body position for time.
Seated machine: less glute and hamstring work than the 45° bench.
Standing with a bar on the back; knees almost straight; no knee flexion moment, so hamstrings carry the hip work.
Trunk fixed, legs swing up behind you; posterior chain work without spinal load from above.

subtypes.name: 90° back extension
subtypes.change: Body horizontal at the top; trunk lowers toward vertical.

subtypes.name: Good morning
subtypes.change: Standing, bar on the upper back, knees soft, hinge until the trunk is near level.

subtypes.name: Reverse hyperextension
subtypes.match: reverse hyper|reverse back extension|reverse extension|reverse hyperextension
subtypes.change: Trunk on the pad, hips at the edge; legs swing from hanging down up to straight behind you.

subtypes.name: Floor back extension
subtypes.match: floor hyperextension|lying back extension|lying floor|lower back curl|snow angel|lying hyperextension|static position lying front
subtypes.change: Lying face down, lift the chest a little off the floor.

motion.basis: 45° Roman chair default: at the top the body is a straight line tilted 45°, so trunk = 45 + hip flexion. Good morning knee about 5° from schellenberg2013, rising with load in vigotsky2015; reverse hyper hip and trunk flex about 5° more with heavy loads (lawrence2022). Other angles are estimates.

families.name: Balance training
families.pattern: Standing on one leg or on an unstable surface and keeping your centre of mass over a small base of support.
setup: Stand next to a wall, counter or sturdy chair you can touch if you wobble.
Barefoot or flat shoes, feet hip width.
Eyes on a fixed point at eye level.

steps.text: Shift your weight onto one foot, spreading the toes.
Lift the other foot a few centimetres, knee soft on the standing leg.
Hold 20-40 seconds, making small corrections at the ankle; switch legs.

cues.cue: Grip the floor lightly: big toe, little toe and heel down.
cues.why: The small foot and lower-leg muscles make most of the fine corrections.

cues.cue: Standing knee soft, not locked.
cues.why: A slight bend lets the hip and knee help absorb wobbles.

cues.cue: Hips level; don't let the free side drop.
cues.why: The gluteus medius holds the pelvis level over one leg.

cues.cue: 20-40 s per hold, about 4 drills, 2 sets, 3 times a week.
cues.why: These were the most effective training doses for steady balance in young adults.

cues.cue: Make it harder one step at a time: eyes closed, soft pad, then board.
cues.why: Wobble boards and BOSU raise lower-limb muscle activity the most.

cues.cue: Keep it in your routine for good.
cues.why: Balance work prevents falls in older adults and repeat ankle sprains in active people.

families.breathing: Breathe slowly and normally; holding your breath makes you stiff.

tempo.note: Hold 20-40 s, rest, repeat 2 sets each leg.

mistakes.name: Hip drops or hikes
mistakes.looks: The pelvis tilts down on the free-leg side, or the body leans far over the standing foot.
mistakes.fix: Hips level, squeeze the standing-side glute.
mistakes.why: The hip abductors are not holding; you balance by leaning instead.

mistakes.name: Standing knee locked
mistakes.looks: The standing leg is snapped straight and rigid.
mistakes.fix: Unlock with a slight bend.
mistakes.why: Takes the hip and knee out of balance control.

mistakes.name: Arms flail or grab
mistakes.looks: Arms swing wide and the hand keeps grabbing the support.
mistakes.fix: Make it easier until you can hold 20 s, then progress.
mistakes.why: The drill is too hard to train the ankle strategy.

safety: Always have a wall or chair within reach; clear the floor around you.
Older adults: balance and functional exercise is the best-proven way to prevent falls, but start supported.
Recent ankle sprain: start on the floor, eyes open, when standing is pain-free.

variants.change: Soft surface: more ankle and calf work, larger wobbles.
Wobble board: highest muscle activity, hardest; start on two feet.
Stand on one leg and tap the other foot forward, side and back: reaching drill, like the Star Excursion test.
On one leg, rotate the pelvis open and closed over the standing hip.

harder: single leg on a wobble board

subtypes.name: Balance board (two feet)
subtypes.change: Both feet on a wobble board, knees soft; keep the board edges off the floor.

subtypes.name: Three-point toe tap
subtypes.change: Stand on the left leg in a quarter squat, tap the right toe forward, out to the side and behind, back to centre each time.

subtypes.name: Standing hip rotation
subtypes.change: On the left leg, knee lifted, turn the pelvis and trunk open to the right and back, foot fixed.

subtypes.name: Tightrope walk
subtypes.change: Walk heel-to-toe along a line, arms out, eyes ahead.

metrics.label: Hold on one leg
metrics.good: about 40 s eyes open, under 10 s eyes closed is typical for adults under 40; drops with age

motion.basis: Default: single-leg stance on the left leg. Joint angles are estimates of a relaxed single-leg stand; hold norms from springer2007, dosing from lesinski2015, device and muscle-activity cues from sanchez2022. trunkRot (+ toward the right) is an extra key not yet in the README convention.

families.name: Battle ropes
families.pattern: Athletic half squat while the arms whip two heavy rope ends into waves, slams or circles.
setup: Rope anchored at the middle; hold one end in each hand, thumbs up.
Step back until the rope has a little slack.
Feet shoulder width, hips back, knees bent, chest up.

steps.text: Snap the right hand up to chest height as the left drives down.
Switch fast: left up, right down. Keep the waves reaching the anchor.

cues.cue: Stay in a quarter to half squat, hips back.
cues.why: The legs and trunk brace the body so the arms can drive; rope work loads the trunk muscles as well as the arms.

cues.cue: Chest up, ribs down, back flat.
cues.why: A rounded back under fast arm work strains the spine.

cues.cue: Move from the shoulders, elbows soft, hands to chest height.
cues.why: Shoulder-driven waves keep the rope moving to the anchor.

cues.cue: Short hard bouts: 15-30 s on, rest as long.
cues.why: Rope work drives oxygen uptake and heart rate very high, higher than many body-weight and lifting exercises.

families.breathing: Short sharp breaths out with the waves; do not hold your breath.

tempo.note: About 2 waves a second per arm in alternating waves.

mistakes.name: Standing up tall
mistakes.looks: Knees straight, hips forward, only the arms move.
mistakes.fix: Sit back into a half squat.
mistakes.why: Loses the brace and the legs' help; the back takes the shock.

mistakes.name: Back rounds
mistakes.looks: Shoulders hunch forward over the rope.
mistakes.fix: Chest proud, eyes ahead.
mistakes.why: Spine bends under repeated jolts.

mistakes.name: Waves die before the anchor
mistakes.looks: Rope flaps near the hands only.
mistakes.fix: Bigger, faster arm drives, or step closer.
mistakes.why: Less work per wave.

safety: Shoulder pain: use lower, smaller waves and fewer slams.

variants.change: Rope training sits in vigorous calisthenics: about 7.5 MET (02020).
Kneeling or seated: arm and trunk work only, lower energy cost.
Combined with leg moves: higher energy cost; leg keyframes from that family.

subtypes.name: Alternating waves
subtypes.change: Default keyframes. Kneeling and seated: legs still, trunk upright.

subtypes.name: Double waves and slams
subtypes.change: Both arms together; slams lift the rope overhead and drive it down with a hip hinge.

subtypes.name: Circles and side to side
subtypes.change: Arms sweep outward or across; Russian twist turns the trunk side to side while seated.

motion.basis: Energy cost from fountaine2015 and ratamess2015; muscle activity from calatayud2015. Angles are estimates of a coaching-standard half squat.

families.name: Bench press
families.pattern: Horizontal push lying on your back: the weight goes from straight arms down to the chest and back up while the shoulder blades stay pinned.
setup: Lie with your eyes under the bar, feet flat and planted.
Hands a little wider than your shoulders, bar low in the palm over the wrist.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the bench, small arch in your lower back.
Head, upper back and butt stay on the bench the whole set.

steps.text: Take the bar out with straight arms and bring it over your shoulders.
Bend your elbows and lower the bar to your lower chest, elbows about 45-70° from your sides.
Touch the chest lightly, forearms vertical, without bouncing.
Drive your feet into the floor and press the bar up and slightly back over your shoulders.

cues.cue: Squeeze them back and down, keep them there.
cues.why: A retracted scapula lowers shear across the shoulder joint and rotator cuff effort.

cues.cue: Hands about 1.5 shoulder widths apart, not ultra wide.
cues.why: Grips wider than about 1.5 shoulder widths raise load on the AC joint; wide grip is linked to shoulder pain.

cues.cue: Elbows about 45-70° from your sides, under the bar.
cues.why: Less abduction keeps the shoulder out of the end range where pain and injury are reported.

cues.cue: Touch the lower chest, press back over your shoulders.
cues.why: This keeps forearms vertical at the bottom and the bar balanced over the shoulder at the top.

cues.cue: Five points down: head, upper back, butt, both feet.
cues.why: A stable base lets you press more and keeps the lower back from over-arching.

families.breathing: Big breath in and hold as you lower, breathe out past the hardest part of the press.

tempo.note: Control the lowering about 2 s, light touch, press hard.

mistakes.name: Elbows flare out
mistakes.looks: Upper arms go straight out to the sides, like a T, with the bar near the neck.
mistakes.fix: Tuck elbows to about 45-70° and touch lower on the chest.
mistakes.why: Wide elbows load the front of the shoulder and the AC joint.

mistakes.name: Shoulders roll forward
mistakes.looks: Shoulder blades come off the bench and the shoulders rise toward the ears.
mistakes.fix: Reset: pull the blades back and down before each rep.
mistakes.why: Losing retraction raises shear on the shoulder joint and rotator cuff demand.

mistakes.name: Butt lifts off the bench
mistakes.looks: The hips rise and the lower back arches hard as you press.
mistakes.fix: Drive the feet down and back, keep your butt on the bench.
mistakes.why: It makes the lift easier by turning it into a decline and stresses the lower back.

mistakes.name: Bouncing off the chest
mistakes.looks: The bar drops fast and rebounds off the ribs.
mistakes.fix: Lower under control and touch lightly.
mistakes.why: The fast drop at the bottom is the phase linked to pec tears and AC joint pain.

safety: Use a spotter or safety pins for heavy sets, never a thumbless grip.
Shoulder pain: narrow the grip to 1.5 shoulder widths or less and shorten the range (floor or board press).
Wrist pain: stack the bar over the forearm, wrist only slightly bent back.

variants.change: Bench 30-45°: about 30° gives the most upper-chest; at 45-60° the front delts take over.
Head lower than hips: the upper chest works less; shorter range.
Hands about shoulder width, elbows close: more triceps, less load on the AC joint.
Hands about 2 shoulder widths: more chest stretch, more AC joint load.
Palms toward you, elbows tucked: often easier on the front of the shoulder.
Each arm free: a bit more stabiliser work, deeper range possible.
Hold 1-2 s on the chest before pressing.
One side at a time: brace the trunk so you do not twist.

subtypes.name: Incline press
subtypes.change: Bench raised about 30°, bar touches the upper chest, press straight up over the shoulders.

subtypes.name: Decline press
subtypes.change: Head below hips about 15-20°, legs hooked, bar touches low on the chest.

subtypes.name: Floor press
subtypes.change: Lying on the floor (or bar stopped on boards or pins): the upper arms stop at the floor, about 0° shoulder extension, so the range is shorter.

subtypes.name: Seated chest press
subtypes.change: Sitting upright against a back pad, handles at mid-chest, press forward. Same arm angles as the flat press.

subtypes.name: Standing cable or band press
subtypes.change: Standing in a split stance, trunk leaning about 10-20° into the press, same arm path as the seated press; suspension presses tilt the whole body like an incline push-up.

subtypes.name: Close-grip and JM press
subtypes.change: Hands about shoulder width, elbows 20-35° from your sides; the JM press lets the elbows drift forward so the bar comes to the chin.

motion.basis: Grip widths, elbow abduction range (45-90 tested) and the effect of scapula retraction from noteboom2024; bench angles from rodriguezridao2020 and barnett1995. Joint angles and scapular values are estimates: elbow 85-100 at chest touch and shoulder about level with the torso from the bar touching the lower chest; scapula held retracted and depressed (no study gave degrees); upward rotation scaled from mcclure2001 ratios for arm elevation; shoulder rotation about neutral because forearms stay vertical.

families.name: Biceps curl
families.pattern: Elbow flexion: the forearm curls the weight up toward the shoulder while the upper arm stays still.
setup: Stand tall, feet hip width, knees soft.
Hold the weights with palms forward, arms straight by your sides.
Elbows close to your ribs, shoulders back and down.

steps.text: Arms long, elbows just in front of your hips.
Bend your elbows and bring the weight up toward your shoulders; the upper arm stays still.
Squeeze at the top with the forearm near vertical, elbows still by your sides.
Lower slowly all the way until your arms are straight.

cues.cue: Pin your elbows to your sides.
cues.why: Fixing the shoulder position is what the curl variants rely on to keep the biceps doing the work.

cues.cue: No swing: hips and back stay still.
cues.why: Body swing adds momentum and moves load to the lower back.

cues.cue: Straighten your arms fully at the bottom.
cues.why: The standard and incline curls keep high biceps activity through the whole range; the preacher curl only over a short part.

cues.cue: Palms up for biceps, thumbs up for brachioradialis.
cues.why: Hand position changes how much the brachioradialis helps; the biceps works in every grip.

cues.cue: Wrists straight, not curled.
cues.why: Curling the wrist moves work to the forearm flexors and can irritate the wrist.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you curl, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Curl in 1 second, lower in 2 to 3.

mistakes.name: Body swing
mistakes.looks: The hips push forward and the trunk leans back to heave the weight up.
mistakes.fix: Lighter weight; stand against a wall if needed.
mistakes.why: Momentum replaces elbow-flexor work and loads the lower back.

mistakes.name: Elbows drift forward
mistakes.looks: The elbows travel forward and up as the weight rises.
mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows by your sides; stop when the forearm is vertical.
mistakes.why: The front delt takes over and the biceps loses tension at the top.

mistakes.name: Half reps
mistakes.looks: The arms never straighten at the bottom.
mistakes.fix: Lower until your elbows are straight each rep.
mistakes.why: Skipping the bottom skips the part where the biceps is longest.

safety: Elbow pain: try an EZ bar or dumbbells so the forearm can find its angle.
Preacher curls: do not drop into a fully straight elbow with a heavy load; slow the last part.

variants.change: Thumbs up (forearm 0): more brachioradialis and brachialis.
Palms down (forearm 80): brachioradialis does more; the biceps is at a disadvantage, so use less weight. Zottman: curl up palms up, lower palms down.
EZ bar: hands slightly turned in; biceps and brachioradialis activity a little higher than with dumbbells.
Drag curl: the bar slides up the body as the elbows move back behind you.
Cheat curl: a small hip drive starts the rep, then lower slowly; advanced only.
21s: 7 reps bottom half, 7 top half, 7 full.
Hold the elbow at about 90° for time.
Cable: tension stays on at the bottom and the top.
Close grip: slightly more outer (long) head.
Wide grip: slightly more inner (short) head.

subtypes.name: Preacher and spider curl
subtypes.match: preacher|spider|arm blaster|over incline bench|over exercise ball|prone
subtypes.change: Upper arm rests on a pad or hangs from a chest-down incline bench, in front of the body.

subtypes.name: Incline curl
subtypes.change: Lying back on a bench at about 45-60°, arms hanging behind the body so the biceps starts long.

subtypes.name: Concentration curl
subtypes.change: Seated, leaning forward, the back of the upper arm braced on the inner thigh; arm hangs down.

subtypes.name: Overhead cable curl
subtypes.change: Upper arms held out at shoulder height (or overhead lying under a cable); the hands curl toward the head.

subtypes.name: Hammer curl
subtypes.change: Thumbs up (forearm 0) through the whole rep; otherwise the same as the standing curl.

subtypes.name: Reverse curl
subtypes.change: Palms down (forearm 80); otherwise the same as the standing curl.

metrics.label: Elbow bend
metrics.good: 0-15 at the bottom, 120-140 at the top

motion.basis: Elbow range and shoulder fixation from oliveira2009; grip effects from kleiber2015 and marcolin2018. Shoulder blades stay still, held slightly back and down (estimate). Other angles estimated from normal standing posture.

families.name: Box jump and depth jump
families.pattern: Jump up onto a box from a quick dip and arm swing, or step off a box and rebound: the legs load and explode, then land softly.
setup: Stand an arm's length from a stable box, feet hip width.
Pick a height you can land on in a quarter squat, not a deep squat.
Arms relaxed by your sides, weight on the balls of your feet.

steps.text: Swing your arms back and dip quickly into a quarter squat.
Swing your arms up and drive through hips, knees and ankles.
Pull your knees up to clear the edge of the box.
Land quietly with both feet flat, knees bent and over your toes.
Stand tall on the box, then step down, one foot at a time.

cues.cue: Land soft and quiet, knees and hips bent.
cues.why: Bending the knees and hips on landing lowers the impact force; people land softer once taught to.

cues.cue: Knees over your toes, not caving in.
cues.why: Knees that cave in on landing are linked to a higher risk of knee ligament injury.

cues.cue: Big arm swing back then up.
cues.why: An arm swing adds height to a jump through several mechanisms working together.

cues.cue: Choose a box you land on in a quarter squat.
cues.why: Landing deep means the box is too high: you are measuring hip mobility, not the jump.

cues.cue: Step down, do not jump down (unless it is a depth jump).
cues.why: Stepping off a box loads the legs more than landing from a jump of the same height.

families.breathing: Breathe in on the dip, out as you jump.

tempo.note: One max effort jump, then step down and reset; rest a few seconds between reps.

mistakes.name: Stiff landing
mistakes.looks: The legs stay nearly straight on contact and the landing is loud.
mistakes.fix: Land on the balls of the feet rolling to flat, sink the hips back.
mistakes.why: A stiff landing raises impact forces on the knee.

mistakes.name: Knees cave in
mistakes.looks: From the front the knees fall toward each other on landing or take-off.
mistakes.fix: Push the knees out over the second toe; lower the box.
mistakes.why: Greater knee valgus on landing predicted ACL injury in young female athletes.

mistakes.name: Landing in a deep squat
mistakes.looks: Feet reach the box only with hips below the knees.
mistakes.fix: Use a lower box and jump higher.
mistakes.why: The box, not the jump, sets the height and the landing is out of balance.

safety: Use a stable box with a soft edge; start low.
Plyometrics on fresh legs, low volume: stop when landings get loud.
Knee or Achilles pain: switch to lower jumps or step-ups.

variants.change: Step off a low box (30-45 cm), land, and rebound up as fast as you can. Short ground contact; much higher knee loading than a box jump.
Stand beside the box and jump sideways onto it.
Take off and land on one leg; much lower box.
Start kneeling, swing the arms and jump to the feet, then to the box.
Turn 90-180° in the air before landing.
Depth jump into a hurdle hop or forward jump.
Upper body depth jump: drop from a raised surface to the hands and rebound.

subtypes.name: Depth or drop jump
subtypes.change: Step off the box, land on both feet, rebound up at once.

subtypes.name: Lateral box jump
subtypes.change: Side-on to the box; same dip and swing, jump sideways.

subtypes.name: Single-leg box jump
subtypes.change: One-leg take-off and landing on a low box, free knee bent.

easier: squat jump onto a low box

metrics.label: Knee cave on landing (front view)
metrics.good: under 13 and even on both sides

motion.basis: Landing targets from padua2009 (knee over 30° at contact, soft landing) and herrington2010 (normal drop-jump valgus about 7-13°); valgus risk from hewett2005 and ford2003; arm swing from lees2004. Keyframe angles are estimates, not measured values.

families.name: Breathing and pelvic floor
families.pattern: Slow belly breathing with the diaphragm, and gentle squeeze-and-relax of the pelvic floor, usually lying on your back with knees bent.
setup: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat; a pillow under your head.
One hand on your chest, one on your belly.
Let your jaw, shoulders and belly relax.

steps.text: Breathe in slowly through your nose so the belly hand rises and the chest hand stays still.
Breathe out slowly through soft lips; the belly falls.
Pelvic floor: on a breath out, gently squeeze and lift as if stopping wind and urine; hold a few seconds.
Let go fully on the breath in. Relaxing is as important as squeezing.

cues.cue: Belly rises, chest stays still.
cues.why: Diaphragmatic breathing uses the diaphragm instead of neck and chest muscles; it is linked to lower stress and better breathing efficiency.

cues.cue: Squeeze and lift, then fully let go.
cues.why: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training cures or improves stress urinary incontinence in women.

cues.cue: Squeeze on the breath out, relax on the breath in.
cues.why: Pelvic floor activity naturally rises with breathing out and falls as you breathe in.

cues.cue: Keep the belly soft; don't bear down or hold your breath.
cues.why: The pelvic floor works together with the deep abdominals; a gentle draw-in, not a hard brace or push, brings it in.

cues.cue: Rest as long as you squeeze.
cues.why: Fatigue makes the squeeze weaker and sloppier.

families.breathing: In through the nose for about 4 s, out through the mouth for about 6 s.

tempo.note: About 6 breaths a minute. Pelvic floor: hold 3-10 s, rest the same.

mistakes.name: Chest breathing
mistakes.looks: The chest and shoulders rise; the belly stays flat.
mistakes.fix: Hand on the belly; breathe into the hand.
mistakes.why: Neck and chest muscles take over from the diaphragm.

mistakes.name: Pushing down
mistakes.looks: The belly pushes out and you strain as if lifting.
mistakes.fix: Think lift and draw in, not push.
mistakes.why: Bearing down loads the pelvic floor instead of training it.

mistakes.name: Squeezing the glutes
mistakes.looks: The buttocks clench and the hips lift off the floor.
mistakes.fix: Keep the glutes and thighs soft; only the inside lifts.
mistakes.why: Bigger muscles hide a weak pelvic floor contraction.

safety: Pelvic pain, leaking or after childbirth or surgery: see a pelvic health physiotherapist for a check.
Feeling dizzy: breathe more gently and slowly; return to normal breathing.

variants.change: Lying down: easiest to feel and relax.
Upright: harder; good for daily practice.
Quick squeezes: 1 s on, 1 s off, for sudden loads like a cough.

motion.basis: The body does not move: the rig should animate belly rise (in) and fall (out) as a soft-tissue morph, not joint angles. Crook lying pose is standard; 6 breaths a minute is a common slow-breathing rate (estimate).

families.name: Broad jump and bounds
families.pattern: Horizontal jump: swing, dip and drive forward (or sideways) as far as you can, then stick a soft landing.
setup: Feet hip width behind a line, toes forward.
Clear, non-slip floor and space to land.
Arms relaxed, ready to swing.

steps.text: Swing your arms back as you hinge and bend your knees.
Throw your arms forward and up and push hips, knees and ankles straight, out and up at a low angle.
Bring your knees forward and your feet out in front of you.
Land on both feet, sink into a quarter squat, chest over your knees, and hold.

cues.cue: Big arm swing.
cues.why: Free arm motion added about 40 cm to a 1.6 m simulated standing long jump.

cues.cue: Jump out more than up.
cues.why: The best take-off angle is lower (about 20-27°) than the 31-39° people choose by instinct.

cues.cue: Stick it: soft knees, hips back, chest forward.
cues.why: Bent knees and hips at landing cut impact; falling back loses distance.

cues.cue: Knees track over your toes.
cues.why: Knees caving in on landing link to knee ligament injury risk.

families.breathing: Breathe in on the swing, out as you jump.

tempo.note: Max effort jump, stick the landing for 1-2 seconds, walk back. Bounds and frog hops link jumps without a pause.

mistakes.name: Stiff landing
mistakes.looks: Legs nearly straight on contact; a loud slap.
mistakes.fix: Reach your feet forward and sink into a quarter squat.
mistakes.why: Raises impact force on the knees.

mistakes.name: Knees cave in
mistakes.looks: Knees fall inward as you land, often more on one side.
mistakes.fix: Shorter jumps; land with knees over your toes.
mistakes.why: Knee valgus on landing predicted ACL injury.

mistakes.name: Falling back
mistakes.looks: Torso upright or behind the feet on landing; you sit or step back.
mistakes.fix: Chest over your knees as you land.
mistakes.why: Distance is measured to the rear heel; balance is lost.

safety: Land on a non-slip surface; start with short jumps.
Single-leg bounds load the landing leg far more; build up slowly.
Stop when landings become loud or uneven.

variants.change: Single-leg bound sideways: push off one leg, land on the other and hold.
Repeated deep squat jumps forward, hands touch down between.
Band around the waist from behind; the jump is shorter and the take-off harder.
Broad jump, then rebound straight into a vertical jump.
Running bounds: exaggerated long strides with flight, alternating legs. Among the highest-force horizontal plyometrics.

subtypes.name: Lateral bound
subtypes.change: Push sideways off the right leg, land on the left leg and hold.

subtypes.name: Frog hops
subtypes.change: Deep squat with hands down between the feet, jump forward, land back in the deep squat.

easier: short broad jump with a stick

metrics.label: Chest over the knees on landing

motion.basis: Take-off angle from wakai2005; arm swing effect from ashby2002 and ashby2006; landing targets from padua2009 and hewett2005. Trunk here is the trunk from vertical; whole-body forward lean at take-off is about 40-50° and joint angles are estimates.

families.name: Burpee
families.pattern: Squat down, jump the feet back to a plank, jump them back in, then jump up: a full-body conditioning loop.
setup: Stand with feet hip width, arms by your sides.
Clear space of your body length in front of you.

steps.text: Squat and place your hands flat on the floor just in front of your feet.
Jump your feet back into a straight plank, body in one line.
Jump your feet back in under your hips.
Stand and jump up, arms reaching overhead; land softly into the next rep.

cues.cue: Straight plank: hips not sagging or piked.
cues.why: The trunk muscles hold the spine straight in the plank; a sag loads the lower back.

cues.cue: Land the jump softly, knees bent.
cues.why: Soft, bent-knee landings lower impact force.

cues.cue: Hands flat, shoulder width, under your shoulders in the plank.
cues.why: Keeps the push-up and plank stable and the wrists loaded evenly.

cues.cue: Keep a steady pace you can hold.
cues.why: Burpee intervals drive oxygen uptake and heart rate to vigorous levels; form fails before fitness does.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you jump back and as you jump up; keep a steady rhythm.

tempo.note: About 2-4 s per rep; in intervals, as many good reps as you can.

mistakes.name: Hips sag in the plank
mistakes.looks: The lower back dips when the feet land behind you.
mistakes.fix: Brace before the feet land; step back instead of jumping if needed.
mistakes.why: Loads the lower back.

mistakes.name: Stiff jump landing
mistakes.looks: Straight legs and a loud landing after the jump.
mistakes.fix: Land on the balls of your feet and sink into the next squat.
mistakes.why: Raises impact on the knees.

mistakes.name: Rounded back squat
mistakes.looks: Legs stay straight and the back curls to reach the floor.
mistakes.fix: Bend the knees and sit down to the floor.
mistakes.why: Many rounded reps add up on the lower back.

safety: Low impact: step the feet back and in, skip the jump.
Wrist pain: hands on a bench or fists.
Stop and walk if you feel dizzy; burpee sets push heart rate very high.

variants.change: Add a push-up in the plank.
Jump the feet wide and back in (a jumping jack) in the plank or at the top.
No jump, step back and in: about 3.8 MET (moderate calisthenics, 02022).
Hands on the weights; often finished with a clean or press.
Finish with a jump over an object, onto a box or forward.
Turn in the air on the jump.
Max-effort intervals: about 11.0 MET (02214).

subtypes.name: Burpee with push-up
subtypes.change: Chest to the floor in a push-up at the plank, then press up.

subtypes.name: Squat thrust or silent burpee
subtypes.change: Step or jump the feet back and in, then just stand up (no jump).

motion.basis: Plank stiffness from howarth2008; landing from padua2009; intensity from gist2014 and ratamess2015 (burpee VO2 about 23 ml/kg/min in sets of 10). Keyframe angles are estimates. MET 7.5 is Compendium 02020, which names burpees; HIIT 11.0 (02214).

families.name: Calf raise
families.pattern: Ankle plantarflexion: rise onto the balls of the feet and lower the heels, knees straight or bent.
setup: Balls of your feet on a step edge, heels free, feet hip width and pointing forward.
Knees straight but soft for standing raises; bent 90° for seated ones.
Hold a rail or wall lightly for balance.

steps.text: Let your heels sink below the step for a full calf stretch.
Push through the big toe and rise as high as you can.
Pause for a moment on your toes.
Lower slowly back to the stretch.

cues.cue: Full range: deep stretch to high on your toes.
cues.why: The calf raise is often cut short; a full range with a pause at the stretch makes each rep count.

cues.cue: Push through the big toe, ankle straight, not rolling out.
cues.why: Rolling onto the little toes shifts load to the outside of the ankle.

cues.cue: Knee straight for the gastrocnemius, bent for the soleus.
cues.why: Bending the knee lowers gastrocnemius activity, so the soleus does more.

cues.cue: Toes forward by default.
cues.why: Toes in slightly favoured the outer calf, toes out the inner calf; forward is balanced.

cues.cue: No bouncing at the bottom.
cues.why: The Achilles tendon stores and returns energy; bouncing lets it do the work.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you rise, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Rise in 1 second, hold 1 at the top, lower in 2, brief pause at the stretch.

mistakes.name: Short range
mistakes.looks: The heel barely rises and never drops below the step.
mistakes.fix: Use less weight and take every rep from deep stretch to high toes.
mistakes.why: Half the movement, half the training effect.

mistakes.name: Bouncing
mistakes.looks: Quick rebounds at the bottom with no pause.
mistakes.fix: Pause 1 second in the stretch before rising.
mistakes.why: Tendon recoil replaces muscle work.

mistakes.name: Knees bend to help
mistakes.looks: In a standing raise the knees dip and drive the body up.
mistakes.fix: Lock in a soft knee and keep it still.
mistakes.why: The quads and body bounce do the lifting instead of the calf.

safety: Achilles pain: slow lowering (heel drops) is a standard rehab method; build up under guidance.
Balance: hold a rail for standing and single-leg raises.
Do not drop deep into the stretch under heavy load until your calf is used to it.

variants.change: Knees bent about 90°: more soleus, less gastrocnemius.
One leg: twice the load per calf; hold support.
Hips bent about 90° with the trunk leaning forward: the hamstrings and gastrocnemius are stretched.

variants.when: leg press|calf press|hack|lever calf|bench press machine
variants.change: Push the platform with the balls of the feet; same ankle range, lying or seated.
From the floor: no stretch below level, shorter range.
Walk on your toes, heels high; loop as steps.
Raise the heels while holding a squat: soleus focus.
Heels drop below the step: full stretch.
Weight rolls around the foot; small range, balance focus.

easier: two-leg calf raise on the floor
harder: single-leg calf raise off a step

subtypes.name: Seated calf raise
subtypes.change: Seated, knees bent 90°, weight on the knees; ankle range the same.

subtypes.name: Tibialis raise
subtypes.change: Back against a wall, heels on the floor in front of you, lift your toes toward your shins: trains the front of the shin. Muscles: shins.

subtypes.name: Donkey calf raise
subtypes.change: Hips bent, trunk leaning forward on a support, legs straight.

metrics.label: Ankle angle
metrics.good: 10-20 at the bottom, -35 to -45 at the top

motion.basis: Ankle range estimated from typical active plantarflexion (about 40°) and step-edge dorsiflexion; knee angle effects from heberlosier2012; foot-angle effects from riemann2011.

families.name: Chest fly
families.pattern: Horizontal hug: arms stay almost straight and swing out wide and back together in front of the chest.
setup: Lie on the bench, dumbbells above your chest, palms facing each other.
Soft bend in the elbows, about 15-25°, and keep it fixed.
Shoulder blades back and down, feet planted.

steps.text: Lower the weights out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch across the chest.
Stop with the elbows about level with the bench, not below it.
Bring the weights back up and together, as if hugging a tree.

cues.cue: Small fixed bend, do not turn it into a press.
cues.why: The fly loads the pecs at long lengths with the elbows almost straight; bending them shifts the work to the triceps.

cues.cue: Stop with elbows at bench level.
cues.why: Pec major tears are reported in flies; going below the torso stretches the tendon under load.

cues.cue: Keep them pinned back and down.
cues.why: It keeps the stretch in the chest instead of the front of the shoulder.

cues.cue: Use about half of your dumbbell press weight.
cues.why: Flies give similar peak pec activity to presses but for a shorter part of the rep, and need control.

families.breathing: Breathe in as the arms open, out as you bring them together.

tempo.note: Slow and even, short pause in the stretch.

mistakes.name: Turns into a press
mistakes.looks: Elbows bend a lot at the bottom and the weights come down near the chest.
mistakes.fix: Lock the slight elbow bend, use a lighter weight.
mistakes.why: The triceps take over and the chest loses its stretch.

mistakes.name: Arms drop too low
mistakes.looks: Elbows sink well below the bench and the shoulders roll forward.
mistakes.fix: Stop at bench level.
mistakes.why: Large shoulder extension under load stresses the pec tendon and front shoulder.

mistakes.name: Shoulders come off the bench
mistakes.looks: At the top the shoulders round forward and lift.
mistakes.fix: Keep the blades pinned; hands meet over the chest, not past it.
mistakes.why: The shoulder blade leaves its stable position and the front delt takes over.

safety: Shoulder pain: shorten the range and use a machine or cables.
Never go heavy to failure in the bottom stretch without a spotter.

variants.change: Bench at about 30°: more upper chest.
Head lower: more lower chest.
Machine: peak pec activity about the same as the bench press (98%); fixed path.
Cables keep tension at the end where hands meet; bent-forward crossovers give about 93% of bench press pec activity.
Low-to-high: more upper chest. High-to-low: more lower chest.
One arm: brace the trunk against twisting.
Hold the stretch position still.

subtypes.name: Pec deck / seated machine fly
subtypes.change: Seated upright, back on the pad, arms at shoulder height.

subtypes.name: Standing cable crossover
subtypes.change: Standing in a split stance between two pulleys, leaning slightly forward; hands meet low in front.

subtypes.name: Floor fly
subtypes.change: Lying on the floor: the elbows stop on the floor, so the stretch is short and safer.

subtypes.name: Svend and squeeze press
subtypes.change: Press a plate or two dumbbells together in front of the chest, squeezing the hands inward the whole time; elbows bend and straighten like a press.

subtypes.name: Suspension or ring fly
subtypes.change: Body leans like a push-up while the arms open and close; harder the lower you lean.

motion.basis: Coaching convention plus EMG (welsch2005, solstad2020, schanke2012); no kinematic study of the fly was found. All joint angles are estimates: elbows held at 15-25° and the upper arm reaching about bench level at the stretch; slight shoulder external rotation (palms up, elbows pointing down) at the stretch is estimated; scapula held retracted.

families.name: Clean
families.pattern: Explosive pull from the floor or hang: the legs and hips drive the bar up fast, then you drop under it and catch it on the front of your shoulders.
setup: Feet hip width, bar over the middle of your feet.
Hands just outside your legs, arms straight, hook grip if you know it.
Hips a bit above your knees, chest up, back flat, shoulders just over the bar.

steps.text: Brace and push the floor away; the bar leaves the floor slowly and stays close.
As the bar passes your knees, keep your back angle and shoulders over the bar.
Let the bar slide to your upper thigh as your knees move back under it.
Jump: drive hips, knees and ankles straight and shrug hard, arms still long.
Pull yourself under, whip your elbows forward and catch the bar on your shoulders in a quarter squat.
Stand tall with elbows high, then lower the bar to your thighs and the floor.

cues.cue: Long arms until your hips are straight.
cues.why: Power comes from the hips and knees; bending the arms early cuts bar speed.

cues.cue: Keep the bar close, brushing your thighs.
cues.why: A bar that swings out makes the catch harder and costs force.

cues.cue: Push the floor away; hips and shoulders rise together.
cues.why: Hips shooting up first turns the pull into a back lift and puts the bar in front of you.

cues.cue: Fast elbows: point them forward in the catch.
cues.why: High elbows make a shelf on the shoulders so the wrists do not take the load.

cues.cue: Catch soft, knees bent, heels down.
cues.why: The power clean catch absorbs energy with knee bend much like a jump landing.

cues.cue: Back flat from floor to catch.
cues.why: Rounding under load raises spinal stress and leaks force.

families.breathing: Big breath and brace before the pull, hold it through the catch, breathe out once you stand.

tempo.note: The pull and catch take under a second; lower under control and reset each rep.

mistakes.name: Arms pull early
mistakes.looks: Elbows bend before the hips and knees are straight.
mistakes.fix: Think of your arms as ropes until you have jumped.
mistakes.why: It slows the bar and drags it forward.

mistakes.name: Hips shoot up
mistakes.looks: Knees straighten off the floor while the chest stays down.
mistakes.fix: Chest and hips rise together; push with the legs.
mistakes.why: The back does the lift and the bar drifts away from you.

mistakes.name: Elbows drop in the catch
mistakes.looks: The bar lands in the hands with elbows pointing down.
mistakes.fix: Whip the elbows forward fast, fingers loose.
mistakes.why: The wrists and elbows take the bar instead of the shoulders.

mistakes.name: Back rounds
mistakes.looks: The lower back curves as the bar leaves the floor.
mistakes.fix: Lighter load, chest up, brace before you pull.
mistakes.why: It raises the load on the spine.

safety: Learn it with a coach and light weight; start from the hang before the floor.
Wrist or elbow pain in the catch: work on front rack mobility, use fingertips.
If you miss, push the bar forward and step back; use bumper plates.

variants.change: Start standing; slide the bar to above the knee (or below for 'below the knees'), then extend. Mid-thigh starts make the highest power output.
Bar starts on blocks at the knee or thigh, no lowering phase.
Catch in a full front squat, then stand.
No drop under: arms pull the bar around to the shoulders, legs straight.
Dumbbells at your sides or one hand; same hip drive, catch on the shoulders.
The bell swings between the legs, then the arm zips up close and the bell rolls onto the forearm in the rack.
Clean first, then press, jerk or thruster from the rack; see jerk-push-press.

subtypes.name: Kettlebell clean
subtypes.change: One or two bells: hike between the legs, hinge snap, arm stays close and the bell rolls onto the forearm, wrist straight.

subtypes.name: Dumbbell clean
subtypes.change: Dumbbells hang at your sides; same hinge and jump, catch the heads on your shoulders, elbows forward.

subtypes.name: Muscle clean
subtypes.change: Legs stay straight after the extension; arms turn the bar over onto the shoulders.

subtypes.name: Hang clean
subtypes.change: Starts standing, bar slides to just above the knee, then the same extension and catch.

subtypes.name: Squat clean
subtypes.change: Catch in a deep front squat (split stance for split clean), then stand.

metrics.label: Back angle as the bar passes the knee
Knee bend in a power catch

motion.basis: Phase order (first pull, transition with knee re-bend, second pull, catch) from gourgoulis2000 and kipp2011; power-catch knee bend similar to jump landing per moolyk2013. All joint angles are estimates from typical lifter photos and coaching texts, not measured values.

families.name: Climbing machine
families.pattern: Vertical climbing: arms and legs drive alternately on a near-vertical track, like climbing a ladder.
setup: VersaClimber: feet in the pedals with straps snug, hands on the handles at about shoulder height.
Jacob's ladder: step onto the lowest rung, hands on the side rails or rungs, belt on if fitted.
Start with short, steady strokes.

steps.text: One hand reaches up as the opposite knee drives up.
Press the other foot down and pull that hand down, standing tall over it.
Swap sides in one smooth rhythm.

cues.cue: Stay upright, hips close to the machine.
cues.why: Leaning back hangs on the arms and loads the lower back.

cues.cue: Push through the whole foot; legs do most of the work.
cues.why: The large leg muscles drive the stroke; climbing uses both arms and legs, which is why it raises oxygen uptake so high.

cues.cue: Long strokes for strength, short fast strokes for sprints.
cues.why: Stroke length and rate set the work; long strokes cover more vertical distance.

cues.cue: Arms pull and push in time with the opposite leg.
cues.why: A cross pattern keeps the trunk stable, as in walking.

families.breathing: Steady, in rhythm with the strokes; do not hold your breath.

tempo.note: Steady 100-130 steps a minute on a VersaClimber; Jacob's ladder is self-paced.

mistakes.name: Leaning back
mistakes.looks: Hips and shoulders drift away from the machine, arms straight.
mistakes.fix: Pull your hips in and stand tall.
mistakes.why: The arms take your weight and the lower back arches.

mistakes.name: Choppy short strokes all the time
mistakes.looks: Feet only move a few inches.
mistakes.fix: Use the full pedal travel at steady pace.
mistakes.why: Short strokes cut the work done by the hips and legs.

safety: Jacob's ladder: use the belt and step off only when the rungs stop.

variants.change: Pedals and handles on a vertical mast; logs vertical feet and stroke rate.
Rungs on a 40° incline treadmill-style belt; logs vertical feet.
The Compendium has no VersaClimber or Jacob's ladder code. 15538 (treadwall climbing, 10.5 MET) is the closest; for an easy pace use the stair machine, 02065, 9.3 MET.

subtypes.name: VersaClimber
subtypes.change: Body near vertical, short to long pedal strokes.

subtypes.name: Jacob's ladder
subtypes.change: Body leans forward about 40° with the ladder; hands climb the rungs.

motion.basis: No kinematic study found for either machine. All angles are estimates from the machine geometry; cross (opposite arm and leg) pattern is coaching convention.

families.name: Rock climbing and bouldering
families.pattern: Moving up a wall on hand and foot holds: the legs push you up, the arms mostly hold you close.
setup: Snug climbing shoes; chalk for dry hands.
Roped climbing: harness buckled, figure-eight knot tied and both partners check each other.
Bouldering: check the mats cover your landing zone; nobody under you.
Warm up on easy routes and open-hand holds for 10-15 minutes.

steps.text: Hang from your skeleton: arms long, hips close to the wall, weight on your feet.
Look at the next foothold and place your toe on it precisely.

steps.phase: Stand up on the leg, reach left
steps.text: Push up with the leg and reach with the opposite hand.

steps.phase: Hips in, bring the left foot up
steps.text: Hold the new hold, bring your hips back to the wall, then move your feet.

cues.cue: Push with your legs; pull only to stay on.
cues.why: Forearm and finger endurance limit climbing; using the legs spares them.

cues.cue: Keep your hips close to the wall.
cues.why: A centre of mass near the wall puts more weight on the feet and less on the hands.

cues.cue: Straight arms when resting; bend them only to move.
cues.why: Holding a bent arm keeps the biceps and forearms working and they pump out sooner.

cues.cue: Use open-hand grips when you can; save full crimps.
cues.why: The full crimp loads the finger pulleys most; pulley tears are the most common climbing injury.

cues.cue: Quiet feet: look at the hold and place the toe once.
cues.why: Precise footwork keeps weight on the legs and holds balance when you release a limb.

cues.cue: Bouldering: down-climb when you can; land on both feet, knees bent, then roll back.
cues.why: Lower-leg injuries in bouldering are fewer but more serious, and most come from falls and jumping off.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you make a hard move; on rests, slow deep breaths and shake out each arm.

tempo.note: One loop = one move: step, push, reach, settle. Climb steadily; rest on good holds.

mistakes.name: Climbing on bent arms
mistakes.looks: Elbows stay bent and the body hangs close by pulling.
mistakes.fix: Let the arms go long and sink the hips; push with the legs.
mistakes.why: The forearms and biceps pump out fast, and grip fails.

mistakes.name: Hips away from the wall
mistakes.looks: Bottom sticks out, body like an A-frame.
mistakes.fix: Turn a hip in or push the hips toward the wall.
mistakes.why: Weight shifts from the feet onto the hands.

mistakes.name: Stiff-legged landing
mistakes.looks: Dropping off a boulder with straight legs or onto one foot or hands.
mistakes.fix: Land on both feet, bend the knees, roll onto your back.
mistakes.why: Falls and jumping off cause most serious bouldering leg injuries.

safety: A pop in a finger with pain at its base: stop climbing that day and get it checked (pulley injury).
Roped climbing: always do partner checks of knot, harness and belay device.
Build finger load slowly; new climbers should not hangboard in the first year.
Shoulder pain on big reaches: shorten moves and train shoulder blade control.

variants.change: Ascending or traversing rock, low-to-moderate difficulty. MET 5.8 (Compendium 15537).
Ascending rock, high difficulty. MET 7.3 (Compendium 15535).
Rock climbing, free bouldering. MET 8.8 (Compendium 15534).
Speed climbing, very difficult. MET 10.5 (Compendium 15536).
Rappelling. MET 5.0 (Compendium 15540).
Treadwall, 4-10 m/min. MET 10.5 (Compendium 15538).
Climbing machines are the climber-machine family.

subtypes.name: Bouldering
subtypes.change: Short, hard problems above mats without a rope; more dynamic moves; finish by down-climbing or a controlled two-foot drop.

keyframes.phase: Stand up on the leg, reach left
Down-climb, drop and land on both feet

subtypes.name: Top rope
subtypes.change: Rope runs from above, so falls are short; steady move-by-move climbing.

keyframes.phase: Stand up on the leg, reach left
Hips in, bring the left foot up

subtypes.name: Lead climbing
subtypes.change: You clip the rope into bolts as you go; clip from a stable stance at waist to chest height, never with the rope behind your leg.

keyframes.phase: Hips in, bring the left foot up
Stand up on the leg, reach left
Hips in, bring the left foot up

motion.basis: Movement principles from quaine1999 (force on holds when a foot is released) and zampagni2011 (expert centre-of-mass control). All joint angles are our estimates for a vertical wall; hipRot shows the turned-out hips. Trunk 0 = upright facing the wall.

families.name: Crunch and sit-up
families.pattern: Trunk flexion: the ribs curl toward the pelvis. A crunch lifts only the shoulder blades; a sit-up keeps going until the trunk is upright.
setup: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat about hip width.
Hands across your chest or fingertips lightly behind your ears.
Low back in its natural curve, not pressed hard into the floor.

steps.text: Breathe out and curl your ribs toward your hips until your shoulder blades leave the floor.
Pause for a moment, chin about a fist from your chest.
Uncurl slowly, one part of the spine at a time, until your shoulders touch down.

cues.cue: Ribs to hips: curl, don't hinge.
cues.why: Curling the trunk works the abs; swinging up from the hips shifts work to the hip flexors and loads the low back more.

cues.cue: Lift just your shoulder blades for a crunch.
cues.why: The curl-up challenges the abs with much less low-back compression than a full sit-up.

cues.cue: Keep a fist between chin and chest, hands don't pull.
cues.why: Pulling on the head bends the neck instead of the trunk.

cues.cue: Feet free, not hooked under a pad, for crunches.
cues.why: Anchored feet let the hip flexors take over the lift.

cues.cue: Lower slowly, no bounce off the floor.
cues.why: Control keeps the abs working through the whole range.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you curl up, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Curl in about 1 second, hold 1, lower in 2.

mistakes.name: Pulling the head
mistakes.looks: Hands yank the head forward and the chin hits the chest.
mistakes.fix: Hands light behind the ears or across the chest; look at the ceiling.
mistakes.why: The neck bends while the trunk barely moves.

mistakes.name: Swinging up from the hips
mistakes.looks: The back stays flat or arched and the whole trunk hinges up at the hips.
mistakes.fix: Curl the ribs down first; free the feet.
mistakes.why: Hip flexors (psoas, iliacus) take the load and press on the low back.

mistakes.name: Throwing the arms
mistakes.looks: Arms fling forward to throw the body up.
mistakes.fix: Arms across the chest; move slower.
mistakes.why: Momentum, not the abs, does the lift.

safety: Low back pain: choose curl-ups over full sit-ups; they load the spine less.
Neck strain: rest your head in your hands or on a towel between reps.
Pregnancy (later stages) or abdominal separation: ask your clinician before lying-flat crunches.

variants.change: Curling on a ball raises abdominal activity compared with the floor.
Head lower than feet: harder, more hip flexor work.
Load held on the chest is easiest; held overhead or pressed up is harder.
Turning one shoulder toward the opposite knee adds oblique work.
Full sit-up: about twice the trunk range and more hip flexor and low-back load than a crunch.

easier: curl-up with hands under the low back

subtypes.name: Sit-up
subtypes.change: The trunk keeps rising to upright; hips flex a lot.

subtypes.name: Kneeling or standing cable crunch
subtypes.change: Kneel facing away from the cable, rope by your head; curl the ribs toward the hips while the hips stay still.

subtypes.name: Seated crunch machine
subtypes.change: Seated, chest or hands on the pads; curl down against the weight.

metrics.label: Trunk lift
metrics.good: -65 to -55 at the top of a crunch (shoulder blades just off the floor)

motion.basis: All angles are estimates from the described technique (shoulder blades clear the floor at about 30 degrees of trunk lift). Upper-trunk curl is shown with the trunk key; the convention has no thoracic key. Twisting variants need trunk rotation, which the convention lacks.

families.name: Dance and aerobics classes
families.pattern: Rhythmic stepping, bouncing and turning to music, with the arms adding work; impact ranges from low (one foot always down) to high (hops and jumps).
setup: Supportive trainers with some cushion and a smooth sole for turning; a sprung or wooden floor is best.
Step aerobics: set the platform low (10-15 cm) to start; it must not slide.
Space to move an arm's length in every direction.
Water nearby; the class warms up for the first 5-10 minutes.

steps.text: Step to the beat with soft knees; let the hips move with the step.
Bend both knees a little in rhythm; arms go up or out with the move.
Same on the other side; the weight moves fully onto the stepping foot.
Keep the chest lifted; add arms only when the feet are steady.

cues.cue: Knees soft and over your toes on every step and landing.
cues.why: Knees caving inward on landing predicted ACL injury in a prospective study of athletes.

cues.cue: Choose low impact (one foot down) if you are new, heavy or have sore joints.
cues.why: High-impact moves give clearly higher ground forces and joint loads than low-impact versions.

cues.cue: Step: start with a low platform; your knee should not bend past about 90° on top.
cues.why: Ground reaction force rises with step height and faster music.

cues.cue: Step: whole foot on the platform, step down close to it, toe-ball-heel.
cues.why: Heels hanging off or stepping down far behind adds ankle and Achilles strain.

cues.cue: Work at a level where you can still sing a line.
cues.why: A Zumba class runs at about 79% of max heart rate on average, already vigorous for most people.

families.breathing: Breathe freely to the rhythm; never hold your breath on jumps.

tempo.note: Classes run at about 120-160 beats per minute; step aerobics usually 118-128 bpm. One loop = one 4-count move.

mistakes.name: Knees cave in
mistakes.looks: On landings, lunges and squats the knee drops inside the foot.
mistakes.fix: Push the knees out over the second toe; land softly.
mistakes.why: Inward knee collapse raises load on the knee ligaments.

mistakes.name: Stiff landings
mistakes.looks: Hops land flat on straight legs with a loud slap.
mistakes.fix: Land ball of foot to heel with bent knees, quietly.
mistakes.why: Stiff landings pass more force up to the knees, hips and back.

mistakes.name: Heel off the step
mistakes.looks: Only the front of the foot is on the platform, or you step down far behind it.
mistakes.fix: Whole foot on top; step down close to the platform.
mistakes.why: It strains the Achilles and calf and risks a fall.

mistakes.name: Platform too high
mistakes.looks: The knee bends past 90° and you lean forward to get up.
mistakes.fix: Lower the platform or skip the risers.
mistakes.why: Higher steps and faster tempo raise impact forces.

safety: Twisting on a planted foot is the classic knee injury in dance; turn on the ball of the foot with the knee soft.
Shin or foot pain: switch to low impact and check your shoes and floor.
Feel dizzy after spins: spot a point with your eyes and slow down.

variants.change: Zumba, group class (home video 5.5, code 02315). MET 6.5 (Compendium 02310).
Aerobic dance, low impact, moderate. MET 4.8 (Compendium 02005).
Aerobic dance, high impact, vigorous. MET 8.0 (Compendium 02006).
Aerobic, general. MET 7.3 (Compendium 02000).
Step aerobics with a 4-inch (10 cm) step. MET 5.5 (Compendium 02001).
Step aerobics with a 6-8 inch (15-20 cm) step (bench step class general 7.8, code 02004). MET 7.3 (Compendium 02002).
Step aerobics with a 10-12 inch (25-30 cm) step. MET 9.0 (Compendium 02003).
Jazzercise / slimnastics. MET 6.0 (Compendium 02090).
Ballroom, slow. MET 3.0 (Compendium 03040).
Ballroom dance, recreational. MET 6.0 (Compendium 03042).
Salsa with a partner (to a video 6.3, code 03091). MET 4.8 (Compendium 03090).
Ballet, modern or jazz class. MET 5.0 (Compendium 03010).
Nightclub or folk dancing, vigorous. MET 9.8 (Compendium 03031).
Closest Compendium entry: aerobic dance, high impact. MET 8.0 (Compendium 02006).

subtypes.name: Zumba / cardio dance
subtypes.change: Latin-style steps (merengue, salsa, cumbia) with hip sway and arm patterns; keep the feet under you on fast moves.

subtypes.name: Step aerobics
subtypes.change: Basic step: right up, left up, right down, left down on a platform; whole foot on top, step down close.

subtypes.name: Dance (social)
subtypes.change: Box step shown: forward, side, back, close, upright posture with a partner frame. Other styles change the steps but keep soft knees and a lifted chest.

subtypes.name: High-impact aerobics
subtypes.change: Hops, jogs and jumps between low-impact steps; land softly on bent knees.

motion.basis: Joint angles are our estimates for a 4-count move at about 128 bpm. Step heights and impact effects from maybury1997, scharffolson1997, michaud1993 and wu2012; valgus risk from hewett2005.

families.name: Dead bug and bird dog
families.pattern: Opposite arm and leg reach out while the trunk holds still: face up (dead bug) or on hands and knees (bird dog).
setup: Dead bug: lie on your back, arms pointing at the ceiling, hips and knees bent 90 degrees.
Bird dog: hands under shoulders, knees under hips, back flat.
Brace lightly so the low back does not move.

steps.text: Slowly reach one arm and the opposite leg away from you.
Pause for a breath with the trunk perfectly still.
Bring them back and switch sides.

cues.cue: Move the limbs, not the spine.
cues.why: These drills train the trunk to stay stiff while the limbs load it, with modest spine compression.

cues.cue: Dead bug: low back stays in contact with the floor.
cues.why: Dynamic stabilization drills aim to keep the lumbar spine still while the limbs move.

cues.cue: Bird dog: hips level, like a glass of water on your back.
cues.why: Hip rotation is the most common way to cheat the reach.

cues.cue: Reach long; don't lift the leg higher than the hip.
cues.why: Lifting higher arches the low back and raises spine load.

cues.cue: Slow: hold each reach for a breath or up to 10 s.
cues.why: Slow reaches with short holds are the standard progression for this drill.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you reach, in as you return; keep breathing during holds.

tempo.note: Reach in 2 s, hold 2-10 s, return in 2 s.

mistakes.name: Low back arches
mistakes.looks: Dead bug: the low back lifts off the floor as the leg lowers. Bird dog: the belly sags.
mistakes.fix: Shorten the reach or keep the knee bent.
mistakes.why: The trunk has lost control of the pelvis.

mistakes.name: Hips tip or rotate
mistakes.looks: Bird dog: the lifted-leg hip opens toward the ceiling.
mistakes.fix: Point the lifted toes at the floor; keep both hips level.
mistakes.why: Rotation lets you reach without stabilizing.

mistakes.name: Rushing
mistakes.looks: Limbs swing out and back without a pause.
mistakes.fix: Pause for a full breath at full reach.
mistakes.why: Speed hides loss of control.

safety: Low back pain: these are often well tolerated; start with arm-only or leg-only reaches.
Wrist or knee pain in bird dog: use a cushion under the knees and fists or forearms.

variants.change: Holding a load or pressing a ball between hands and knees raises the abdominal demand.
Straight leg: longer lever, harder.
Different support, same rule: limbs move, trunk stays still.

harder: bird dog from a plank (bird dog plank)

subtypes.name: Bird dog
subtypes.change: On hands and knees; reach the right arm forward and left leg back.

motion.basis: Default is the dead bug (right arm and left leg reach). Starting 90/90 positions are the standard setup; reach angles estimated. Bird dog spine-load findings from callaghan1998 and kavcic2004.

families.name: Deadlift
families.pattern: Hip hinge: a weight is lifted from the floor (or from a hang) by driving the hips forward while the spine stays still.
setup: Feet hip width, the bar over the middle of your feet, close to your shins.
Push your hips back and bend your knees until your hands reach the bar just outside your legs.
Chest up, back flat, shoulders over or just in front of the bar.
Pull the slack out of the bar: arms long, armpits squeezed, brace your belly.

steps.text: Brace, flat back, bar against your shins.
Push the floor away. Hips and shoulders rise together, the bar slides up your legs.
Stand tall: squeeze your glutes until your hips are straight. Do not lean back.
Hips back first, then bend the knees once the bar passes them. Keep the bar close.

cues.cue: Flat back from setup to lockout.
cues.why: Spine loads in a heavy pull are very high; a neutral spine keeps them on the strongest posture.

cues.cue: Bar over midfoot and touching your legs the whole way.
cues.why: Where the bar starts changes knee, hip and torso angles and which muscles work.

cues.cue: Hips and shoulders rise at the same speed.
cues.why: Hips that shoot up first turn the lift into a stiff-leg pull and put the load on the back.

cues.cue: Push the floor away, then drive the hips through.
cues.why: The quads work most early in the lift; glutes and back extensors finish it.

cues.cue: Finish with glutes, ribs down. Stand straight, not backwards.
cues.why: Leaning back at the top adds spine extension load without more hip work.

families.breathing: Big breath and brace before each pull; breathe out at the top or after the bar is back down.

tempo.note: Lift with intent, lower under control, reset your brace on the floor.

mistakes.name: Rounded back
mistakes.looks: The lower back curves like a cat as the bar leaves the floor.
mistakes.fix: Lower the weight, chest up, brace harder, start with the bar closer.
mistakes.why: A flexed spine under a heavy load is a weaker and riskier posture.

mistakes.name: Hips shoot up
mistakes.looks: The hips rise before the bar moves; the legs straighten and the chest drops.
mistakes.fix: Push with the legs first; keep the chest angle until the bar passes the knees.
mistakes.why: The back ends up doing the lift the legs should start.

mistakes.name: Bar drifts forward
mistakes.looks: The bar swings away from the legs in front of the toes.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze your armpits and drag the bar up your legs.
mistakes.why: A bar farther forward lengthens the lever on the hips and lower back.

mistakes.name: Leaning back at lockout
mistakes.looks: At the top the hips push forward and the shoulders fall behind the heels.
mistakes.fix: Stop when you are standing straight; squeeze glutes, ribs down.
mistakes.why: Extra arch at the top loads the lumbar joints without adding hip work.

safety: Low back pain: start with trap bar or blocks to shorten the range; stop if pain travels down the leg.
Keep the load where you can hold a flat back; form breaks first near failure.
Use chalk or straps before a mixed grip for heavy sets; a mixed grip twists the shoulders.

variants.change: Wide stance (about twice hip width), toes out about 40°, hands inside the knees: trunk 5-10° more upright, less bar travel, more quads.
Handles at your sides: more knee bend, more knee work, lower hip and back moments; most people lift more.
Starts standing, knees soft and fixed; lower only as far as the hips go back with a flat back.
Knees almost straight from the floor: most hamstring stretch; use lighter loads.
Standing on a plate: more range at the bottom, more knee and hip bend at setup.
Bar starts at or below the knee: shorter range, heavier loads, less leg drive.
Stop 1-2 s just off the floor or below the knee while holding position.
Load grows toward the top; the lockout gets harder.
Weight in one hand at your side: the trunk must resist leaning to that side.
Back foot on its toes for balance; most of the load on the front leg.
Weights hang between or beside the legs; same hinge, lighter load.

subtypes.name: Sumo deadlift
subtypes.change: Wide stance, toes out, more upright trunk, hands inside knees. Jefferson is an asymmetric straddle version.

subtypes.name: Romanian / stiff-leg deadlift
subtypes.change: Starts at the top, knees soft and fixed, hips travel back until the bar is near mid-shin.

subtypes.name: Trap bar deadlift
subtypes.change: Handles at the sides: more knee bend, more upright trunk.

subtypes.name: Rack pull / block pull
subtypes.change: Bar starts at the knee; only the top half of the lift.

subtypes.name: Cable pull-through
subtypes.change: Facing away from a low cable, rope between the legs; hinge back, then drive the hips forward. Load pulls backward, not down.

metrics.label: Trunk angle change before the bar passes the knee

motion.basis: Relative angles from escamilla2000 (sumo trunk 5-10° more upright, thigh 11-16° more horizontal, conventional knees and hips about 12° more extended at lift-off, stance 70 vs 32 cm, toes out 42 vs 14°) and swinton2011 (trap bar more knee, less hip and back moment). Absolute joint angles are estimates built from those differences and the bar-over-midfoot geometry; trunk = hipFlex - thigh angle from vertical. Arms hang vertically, so shoulderFlex is about the trunk angle minus 5.

families.name: Dip
families.pattern: Vertical push down: you hold your body up on straight arms, then bend the elbows and let the shoulders go into extension, and push back up.
setup: Grip the bars about shoulder width, jump or step up to straight arms.
Shoulders down away from your ears, chest proud.
Knees bent or legs straight, ankles together; brace your trunk.

steps.text: Start on straight arms, body still, shoulders pushed down.
Bend your elbows and lean slightly forward, elbows pointing back, not out.
Stop when your upper arms are about level with the bars or a bit below, shoulders still down.
Push the bars down until your arms are straight again.

cues.cue: Lower until upper arms are about parallel to the bars, not deeper.
cues.why: The dip takes the shoulder to about 65-70° of extension; deeper loads the front of the shoulder and the pec tendon.

cues.cue: Keep shoulders down, away from your ears.
cues.why: The serratus anterior and lower trapezius work hard to control the shoulder blade, more so when tired.

cues.cue: Elbows point back, close to your sides.
cues.why: Typical bar-dip abduction is only about 30°; wide elbows move the load onto the shoulder.

cues.cue: Lean forward about 20-40° for chest, stay upright for triceps.
cues.why: Bar dips show about 37° of forward lean at the bottom; the lean shifts work to the chest.

cues.cue: Lower in 2 seconds, no drop and bounce.
cues.why: Pec major ruptures are reported during dips; the fast stretch at the bottom is the risky part.

families.breathing: Breathe in on the way down, out as you push up.

tempo.note: Slow down, press up in about 1 s.

mistakes.name: Going too deep
mistakes.looks: Shoulders sink far below the elbows and roll forward.
mistakes.fix: Stop with upper arms about level with the bars.
