mistakes.why: Misses the range where the quads work hardest.

mistakes.name: Weight drops
mistakes.looks: The stack crashes down and the knee jerks into deep bend.
mistakes.fix: Take about 2 seconds to lower.
mistakes.why: Skipping the lowering half wastes the eccentric work and jolts the knee.

safety: After ACL surgery, early leg extensions are usually limited to about 90-45° of knee bend; follow your therapist.
Knee-cap pain: try a shorter range, or squats and leg presses instead, which load the knee cap less near straight.
Never lock the knee hard against a heavy load.

variants.change: One leg at a time: same angles, half the load.
Band or ankle weight while seated on a chair: same keyframes, lighter.
Standing with a band: hip and knee start bent, then straighten the knee.
Isometric: hold the knee straight for 5-10 seconds.
Toes turned in a little; small shifts in quad activation only.

easier: seated knee extension with no weight

subtypes.name: Kneeling sissy squat
subtypes.change: Kneel upright, lean your straight body back from the knees, then pull back up with the quads.

subtypes.name: Sissy squat
subtypes.change: Standing on your toes, lean back from the knees with hips straight, knees travel forward and down, then rise. Kneeling version: lean back from the knees.

metrics.label: Knee bend
metrics.good: 90 at the start, 0-10 at the top

metrics.label: Hips off the seat (degrees of hip change)

motion.basis: Range (90° to straight) from escamilla1998 and wilk1996; seat back assumed reclined about 10° (estimate). Sissy squat angles estimated from the movement; no lab data found.

families.name: Leg press
families.pattern: Machine squat: the back is supported while the legs bend and press a sled or platform away.
setup: Sit with your back and hips flat on the pad.
Feet hip to shoulder width in the middle of the platform, toes slightly out.
Hold the handles, brace, and release the safety catches.

steps.text: Legs almost straight, knees soft, not locked.
Bend your knees and let the platform come toward you, knees in line with your toes.
Stop at about a 90° knee bend, or just before your hips start to lift off the pad.
Push through your whole foot back to the top.

cues.cue: Hips and lower back stay glued to the pad.
cues.why: Going so deep that the pelvis tucks rounds the lower back under load.

cues.cue: Knees follow your toes, never inward.
cues.why: Keeps the load even across the knee.

cues.cue: About 90° at the knee for most people.
cues.why: Quad activity peaks around 90° knee bend; going deeper mostly adds knee-cap pressure.

cues.cue: Higher feet for more glutes, lower feet for more quads.
cues.why: High foot placement raised glute activity; low placement raised quad activity in most studies.

cues.cue: Stop just short of locking your knees.
cues.why: Keeps tension on the muscles and avoids snapping the knee straight under a heavy sled.

families.breathing: Breathe in as the platform comes down, out as you press.

tempo.note: Lower in about 2 seconds; never let the sled drop.

mistakes.name: Hips curl off the pad
mistakes.looks: At the bottom the tailbone lifts and the lower back rounds.
mistakes.fix: Shorten the depth or move your feet higher on the platform.
mistakes.why: Hip flexion has run out, so the spine bends instead.

mistakes.name: Knees cave in
mistakes.looks: The knees drift toward each other as you press.
mistakes.fix: Push your knees out over your toes; use less weight.
mistakes.why: Weak hip abductors let the thighs roll in.

mistakes.name: Knees snap locked
mistakes.looks: The knees straighten hard or bend slightly backward at the top.
mistakes.fix: Stop with a soft bend in the knee.
mistakes.why: A locked knee carries the whole sled on the joint.

mistakes.name: Heels lift off the platform
mistakes.looks: Only the balls of the feet stay on the platform at the bottom.
mistakes.fix: Move your feet higher and press through your heels.
mistakes.why: Feet too low for your ankle range; load shifts onto the knee and toes.

safety: Set the safety catches and never push the sled with your hands on your knees.
Lower-back pain: keep the range shallow so your hips never leave the pad.
Knee pain: work from about 90° to nearly straight; deeper knee bend raises knee-cap pressure.

variants.change: Hack squat: standing with your back on an angled pad; shins travel further forward, more knee bend and more quads.
Belt squat: load hangs from a hip belt, trunk upright, spine unloaded; squat keyframes.
Pendulum squat: the pad swings on an arc; deep knee bend with an upright trunk.
One leg at a time: half the load, the other foot rests on the frame.
Seated horizontal press: trunk nearly upright, same leg angles.
Band leg press lying on the floor: pull the knee to the chest and push the foot out against the band.
Smith leg press: lying under the bar, feet press it up; same leg keyframes, trunk flat.

subtypes.name: Hack squat
subtypes.change: You stand on the platform with your back and shoulders under pads that slide on rails tilted back; it moves like a squat.

subtypes.name: Belt squat
subtypes.change: Standing on a platform with the weight hung from a belt at the hips; upright squat.

metrics.label: Knee bend
metrics.good: 85-100 at the bottom, 5-15 at the top

metrics.label: Knee inside the foot line (front view)

motion.basis: Knee range (about 90° to near straight) and foot-height effects from martinfuentes2020 and escamilla2001b; seat back assumed at 45° (trunk -45) for a 45° sled. Hip angles estimated from the seat and knee angles. Hack and belt squat keyframes estimated from the squat pattern.

families.name: Lever and static hold
families.pattern: Gymnastics static: straight arms hold the whole body still in a hard lever position (front lever, back lever, planche, L-sit, flag, cross), the trunk locked as one piece.
setup: Front lever: hang from a bar, hands shoulder width, palms away.
Pull your shoulders down and squeeze the bar; arms stay straight the whole time.
Start from the tuck version and only extend the legs when you can hold the tuck 10-15 seconds.

steps.text: Press the bar down toward your hips with straight arms until your body is level, face up, then hold still.

cues.cue: Elbows locked straight.
cues.why: These skills are judged and loaded as straight-arm holds; bent arms change the muscles and the skill.

cues.cue: Front lever: shoulders pulled down and back. Planche: shoulders pushed forward and down.
cues.why: The scapula sets each skill: depression and retraction for pulling holds, protraction with serratus for pushing holds; training drills that drop serratus work miss this.

cues.cue: Ribs down, glutes and legs squeezed, one straight line.
cues.why: A long, rigid body is needed for the lever; any sag adds a bending load the trunk cannot hold.

cues.cue: Move from tuck to advanced tuck to straddle to full.
cues.why: Body length and leg position set the lever arm; shorter shapes are much easier to hold.

cues.cue: Short holds, 5-15 seconds, several sets, fully rested.
cues.why: Static strength is trained near maximal effort; long fatigued holds break form.

families.breathing: Short, shallow breaths behind a braced trunk; do not hold your breath for long holds.

tempo.note: Hold 5-15 seconds per set.

mistakes.name: Elbows bend
mistakes.looks: The elbows soften and the body sinks toward the bar or floor.
mistakes.fix: Lock the elbows and shorten the lever (tuck the knees) instead.
mistakes.why: Bending the arms turns the hold into a different, easier skill and loads the elbow.

mistakes.name: Hips drop or pike
mistakes.looks: In a front lever the hips sag below the line or bend up into a pike.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes, ribs down; go back to a tuck or straddle.
mistakes.why: Breaking at the hips shortens the lever to make it easier and hides weak spots.

mistakes.name: Shoulders collapse
mistakes.looks: The shoulders ride up to the ears in a lever, or sink and pinch back in a planche.
mistakes.fix: Lever: press the bar toward your hips. Planche: push the floor away and round the upper back slightly.
mistakes.why: Losing the scapular position moves the load from the muscles onto the shoulder joint.

safety: These are advanced skills: build pull-ups, dips and hollow holds first.
Straight-arm work loads the elbow and biceps tendon; add volume slowly over weeks.
Planche and lean holds load the wrists: warm them up and use parallettes if they hurt.
Iron cross and maltese place very high stress on the shoulder and elbow; do not attempt them without coaching.

variants.change: Knees pulled to the chest: much shorter lever.
Back flat, knees at about 90° to the trunk.
Legs straight and wide: shorter lever than the full version.
One leg straight, one tucked.
Moving version: lower slowly into the hold or raise up into it.
Lean planche: feet on the floor, shoulders far in front of the hands.
Frog or elbow planche: knees or hips rest on the bent elbows; a balance drill.
Hanging L-sit: hang from a bar with legs straight out at 90°.

subtypes.name: Front lever
subtypes.change: Hanging, body horizontal and face up, arms straight to the bar.

subtypes.name: Planche
subtypes.change: Hands on the floor or parallettes, body horizontal and face down, shoulders far ahead of the hands, feet off the floor.

subtypes.name: Back lever
subtypes.change: Hanging from a bar or rings, body horizontal and face down, arms straight behind the body.

subtypes.name: L-sit
subtypes.change: Hands on the floor or parallettes beside the hips, arms straight, hips lifted, legs straight out in front at about 90°.

subtypes.name: Dragon flag
subtypes.change: Lying face up on a bench, hands gripping behind the head; the body rises straight from the shoulders and lowers slowly as one plank, head lower than the feet.

subtypes.name: Human flag
subtypes.change: Gripping a vertical pole, top arm pulls and bottom arm pushes; the body sticks out sideways, level with the floor. The rig rolls the body 90° onto its side.

subtypes.name: Iron cross and maltese
subtypes.change: On rings, arms straight out to the sides. Cross: body upright, hands level with the shoulders. Maltese: body horizontal face down, hands at hip level.

motion.basis: Muscle roles (serratus, pectoralis, latissimus) from the ring-strength EMG studies bernasconi2004 and bernasconi2009, lever-arm and body-shape effects from wang2023 (planche model). Joint angles and scapular positions are our estimates from coaching texts (low2016); no kinematic study of these holds was found. The dragon flag trunk value (-135) means face up with the head lower than the feet.

families.name: Loaded carry
families.pattern: Walking under load: a weight is held in the hands, at the chest, on the shoulder or overhead while the trunk stays tall and still.
setup: Deadlift the weights up with a flat back; never pick them up rounded.
Stand tall: shoulders down and back, ribs over hips, eyes forward.
Squeeze the handles hard and brace before the first step.

steps.text: Step out with short, quick, controlled steps.
Stay tall as one leg passes the other; no swaying.
Keep walking heel to toe; set the weights down with a hinge at the end.

cues.cue: Walk tall; do not lean or twist.
cues.why: Carries make the trunk muscles stiffen the spine against bending in every direction.

cues.cue: Shoulders down and back, not shrugged or rounded.
cues.why: A packed shoulder holds the load close and keeps the neck relaxed.

cues.cue: Short quick steps.
cues.why: Better carriers in the farmer's walk use a quick stride rate and short ground contacts.

cues.cue: With one weight, stay level: do not lean away from it.
cues.why: The suitcase carry adds work for the side muscles of the trunk.

cues.cue: Keep the hips level at each step.
cues.why: The gluteus medius works hard to hold the pelvis during a farmer's walk.

families.breathing: Short breaths behind a braced belly; do not hold your breath for the whole walk.

tempo.note: Carry for 20-40 m or 20-60 s, rest, repeat.

mistakes.name: Leaning to one side
mistakes.looks: With one weight, the trunk bends toward or away from it; with two, the body sways side to side.
mistakes.fix: Lighter weight; ribs stacked over the hips.
mistakes.why: The trunk muscles are losing the fight; spine load rises.

mistakes.name: Shoulders round or shrug
mistakes.looks: The weights pull the shoulders forward and up to the ears; the head pokes forward.
mistakes.fix: Shoulders down and back, chest tall.
mistakes.why: Neck and upper back strain; the load drifts from the body.

mistakes.name: Low back arches (overhead)
mistakes.looks: The arms drift forward and the low back leans back to balance the weight.
mistakes.fix: Lighter weight; biceps by the ears, ribs down.
mistakes.why: Shoulder mobility or core control is short for the load.

safety: Pick up and put down the weights with a hinge, flat back.
Clear the path; drop the weight forward if you lose the grip.

variants.change: Equal weights both hands: hardest on grip and upper back. Moderate pace with 23-68 kg is about 6.5 MET (17019).
One weight in one hand: more side trunk work, about half the load.
Arms locked overhead: shoulder stability; much lighter.
Kettlebell held upside down: grip and shoulder control.
Load in front of the chest: the upper back and abs work to stay upright.
One weight overhead, the other at the side.
Load on the back: easier on grip; the Compendium lists backpacking at 7.0 MET (17010).
Load on one shoulder or across both: switch sides each set.

subtypes.name: Suitcase carry
subtypes.change: Weight in the right hand only; the trunk stays level.

subtypes.name: Overhead carry
subtypes.change: Weights locked out overhead (one or both arms).

subtypes.name: Front-loaded carry
subtypes.change: Load held against the chest or in the crook of the elbows.

subtypes.name: Shoulder / back carry
subtypes.change: Load on one shoulder, across the shoulders or in a pack.

motion.basis: Two-step walking cycle with arms fixed by the load. Leg angles are typical walking values shortened for a loaded stride (estimates; no carry study here gave joint angles). The joint convention has no side-bend key, so side lean is shown as opposite hip abduction. MET from the 2024 Compendium walking table (17019 carrying 23-68 kg at a moderate pace).

families.name: Lunge and split squat
families.pattern: Split-stance squat: one foot in front, one behind, both knees bend and the hips drop straight down.
setup: Stand tall, feet hip width, like standing on two rails, not a tightrope.
Step one foot forward (or back) about a long stride, back heel up.
Weight mostly on the front foot, trunk upright, brace.

steps.text: Start tall with feet together, or already in the split stance for a split squat.
Step out and bend both knees, dropping your hips straight down.
Back knee just above the floor, front shin about vertical to slightly forward.
Push through your front heel and midfoot back to the start.

cues.cue: Front knee over your middle toes, not falling inward.
cues.why: Inward knee drift is the main fault in single-leg work and loads the inside of the knee.

cues.cue: Front heel stays down; push through it.
cues.why: A lifted heel shifts load onto the knee and toes and costs balance.

cues.cue: Tall trunk for more quads; lean forward about 30° for more glutes.
cues.why: A forward trunk raised hip-extensor work; an upright trunk kept more on the knee.

cues.cue: A long stride for glutes, a shorter stride for quads.
cues.why: Longer steps move the work toward the hip; short steps push the front knee further forward.

cues.cue: Hips level and square to the front.
cues.why: A dropping or twisting pelvis shows the side hip muscles are not holding.

families.breathing: Breathe in on the way down, out as you drive up.

tempo.note: Lower in about 2 seconds; a split squat stays in place, a lunge steps out and back.

mistakes.name: Front knee caves in
mistakes.looks: The front knee moves inside the big toe as you go down or drive up.
mistakes.fix: Push the front knee out over your middle toes; widen your rails.
mistakes.why: Weak or late hip abductors let the thigh roll in.

mistakes.name: Front heel lifts
mistakes.looks: The front heel comes up and the knee shoots past the toes.
mistakes.fix: Take a longer step and keep your weight on the front heel.
mistakes.why: Stride too short for your ankle range; it loads the knee and costs balance.

mistakes.name: Trunk folds forward
mistakes.looks: The chest drops toward the front thigh and the back rounds.
mistakes.fix: Chest up, brace; lean from the hips only, back flat.
mistakes.why: A small hip lean is fine; rounding the back is the trunk giving way.

mistakes.name: Hip drops or twists
mistakes.looks: The pelvis tilts down toward the back leg or rotates open.
mistakes.fix: Hips level and pointing forward; slow down and use less weight.
mistakes.why: The side glutes are not stabilising the front leg.

safety: Knee pain: use a reverse lunge, which is easier on the front knee than stepping forward.
Balance: hold a wall or rack with one hand until you are steady.
Back knee: lower to just above the floor, or put a pad under it.

variants.change: Step backward: less braking on the front knee, easier to balance.
Walking lunge: step through and repeat forward; loop as a cycle.
Split squat: feet stay planted; only up and down.
Front foot (or both) raised: deeper range for the front hip.
Weight locked overhead: trunk must stay upright.
Weight in front: trunk more upright, more quads.
Weight in the hand opposite the front leg: more side-hip demand.
Faster or jumping reps make it conditioning; land softly with the knee over the toes.
Arm movement added at the bottom or top; keep the legs still while the arms work.

subtypes.name: Bulgarian split squat
subtypes.match: bulgarian|rear foot|elevated split|leg elevated split|smith elevated
subtypes.change: Back foot laces down on a bench behind you; most of the load on the front leg.

subtypes.name: Lateral lunge / Cossack squat
subtypes.change: Step wide to the side, sit into that hip with the other leg straight; toes forward or slightly out.

subtypes.name: Curtsy lunge
subtypes.change: The back leg steps behind and across the front leg, like a curtsy; more side-hip work.

metrics.label: Front knee inside the foot line (front view)
Trunk lean
metrics.good: 0-10 upright, up to about 30-40 for glute bias

motion.basis: Default keyframes are a static split squat, right leg in front (left = back leg, on the toes). Trunk lean effect from farrokhi2008; Bulgarian split squat joint emphasis from mackey2021. Joint angles are estimates for an average adult and a stride of about 1 leg length.

families.name: Lying leg raise
families.pattern: Lower-body-first flexion: lying on your back, the legs lift and the pelvis curls toward the ribs while the trunk resists arching.
setup: Lie on your back, legs straight, arms by your sides or hands holding a bench behind your head.
Brace gently and set your low back flat-ish against the floor.
Point your toes lightly, legs together.

steps.text: Lift both legs together until they point at the ceiling.
At the top, roll your hips a little off the floor, tailbone toward the ceiling.
Lower the legs slowly; stop before your low back starts to arch.

cues.cue: Keep the low back down as the legs lower.
cues.why: Leg raises strongly fire the psoas, which pulls the lumbar spine into an arch and compresses it.

cues.cue: Finish by curling the hips up, not just swinging the legs.
cues.why: Hip lift (reverse crunch) is what brings in the abdominals; reverse crunches rank high for abdominal activity.

cues.cue: Lower only as far as you can keep your back still.
cues.why: Long straight legs make a large lever on the spine; bend the knees to shorten it.

cues.cue: Slow down on the way down.
cues.why: Dropping the legs uses momentum and lets the back arch.

families.breathing: Breathe out as the legs rise and the hips curl, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Lift in 1 second, lower in about 3.

mistakes.name: Low back arches
mistakes.looks: A gap opens under the low back as the legs come down.
mistakes.fix: Bend the knees, or stop higher; press the low back toward the floor.
mistakes.why: The hip flexors pull the spine into extension when the abs cannot hold it.

mistakes.name: Legs only, no hip lift
mistakes.looks: Legs swing to vertical but the pelvis never leaves the floor.
mistakes.fix: At the top, push the feet to the ceiling and lift the tailbone.
mistakes.why: It stays a hip flexor exercise.

mistakes.name: Dropping the legs
mistakes.looks: Legs fall fast and bounce off the floor.
mistakes.fix: Count three on the way down; tap, don't bounce.
mistakes.why: Momentum replaces muscle and jars the back.

safety: Low back pain: start with bent-knee reverse crunches or dead bugs; straight-leg lowering loads the spine.
Hip flexor or groin pain: shorten the range and bend the knees.

variants.change: Bent knees shorten the lever: easier on the back.
Head higher than hips on a decline bench: harder; a 30 degree inclined reverse crunch is among the highest abdominal exercises measured.
Legs stay low and move in small fast alternating kicks; keep the low back still.
Arms and legs lift together and meet over the hips: a whole-body fold.
Seated, leaning back on the hands, knees pull in and push out.

subtypes.name: Reverse crunch
subtypes.match: reverse crunch|hip raise|tuck crunch|leg.hip raise|hip lift|bottoms|pull in|knee raise
subtypes.change: Knees bent about 90 degrees; curl the hips off the floor.

subtypes.name: Flutter and scissor kicks
subtypes.change: Legs low, about a hand off the floor, kicking up and down in small alternating beats.

subtypes.name: V-up and jackknife
subtypes.change: Arms overhead to start; arms and legs lift together and meet over the hips.

motion.basis: Hip and pelvis angles estimated from the technique; psoas-driven lumbar extension risk from juker1998. Inclined reverse crunch ranking from escamilla2006.

families.name: Medicine ball throw and slam
families.pattern: Throw a weighted ball as fast as you can: legs and hips start the push, the trunk passes it on, the arms release.
setup: Pick a ball light enough to move fast: about 2-6 kg for most throws.
Feet shoulder width, knees soft, ball held in both hands.
Clear space in front, or face a solid wall for rebounds.

steps.text: Rise onto your toes and reach the ball overhead, body long.
Fold at the hips and pull the ball down hard, throwing it at the floor just in front of your feet.
Squat with a flat back to pick it up after the bounce.
Stand and go straight into the next reach.

cues.cue: Throw with your hips, not just your arms.
cues.why: Throw distance tracks lower body power: leg drive and hip extension power the backward overhead throw.

cues.cue: Light ball, max speed every rep.
cues.why: Ball speed falls as mass rises; lighter balls train speed of release.

cues.cue: Brace your middle as you throw.
cues.why: The trunk passes force from the legs to the arms; a loose trunk leaks it.

cues.cue: Flat back when you pick it up.
cues.why: Many reps of rounded lifting add up on the lower back.

cues.cue: Arms follow through after release.
cues.why: Overhead throws ask the shoulder to slow the arm after release; a full follow-through spreads the load.

families.breathing: Breathe in on the reach or load, breathe out sharply as you throw.

tempo.note: Explosive. Rest between reps for power; go continuous for conditioning.

mistakes.name: Arms only
mistakes.looks: The torso stays upright and only the arms swing the ball.
mistakes.fix: Hinge hard at the hips; the chest follows the ball down (or the hips turn first in a rotational throw).
mistakes.why: The big leg and hip muscles do not help, so the throw is weak.

mistakes.name: Rounded back pickup
mistakes.looks: Legs straight and back curled when picking the ball up.
mistakes.fix: Bend the knees and squat down to it.
mistakes.why: Repeated rounded lifts strain the lower back.

mistakes.name: Arching overhead
mistakes.looks: Ribs flare and the lower back bends back at the top.
mistakes.fix: Ribs down, reach tall without leaning back.
mistakes.why: It loads the lower back instead of stretching the trunk muscles.

safety: Slam only a dead-bounce slam ball; a rubber medicine ball can rebound into your face.
Stand side-on to a wall for rotational throws and leave room for the bounce.
Shoulder pain: use chest passes and scoop tosses instead of overhead throws.

variants.change: Push the ball from the chest like a jump into a push; on the back, throw straight up and catch.
Side-on, turn the back hip then the trunk, release past the front hip.
Scoop between the legs and throw back over your head with a jump: a full triple extension.
Ball behind the head, step and throw forward like a soccer throw-in.
Front squat to full depth, drive up and throw to a target about 3 m high, catch into the next squat. Conditioning: about 7.5 MET (vigorous calisthenics).
Sit-up into a throw or slam: a trunk flexion exercise.
One-hand slam: same hinge, add a trunk rotation.
Circle the ball around the head before the slam.

subtypes.name: Chest pass
subtypes.change: Ball at the chest, step or jump forward and push both arms straight.

subtypes.name: Rotational throw
subtypes.change: Side-on to the wall; load into the back hip, then hips, trunk and arms turn in order.

subtypes.name: Backward overhead toss
subtypes.change: Squat with the ball between the knees, then jump and swing it straight-armed back over the head.

subtypes.name: Wall ball
subtypes.change: Ball at the chest, full front squat, drive up and throw high to the wall, catch into the next squat.

motion.basis: Lower body and trunk contribution from stockbrugger2003 and hardy2025; ball mass effects from vandentillaar2013; overhead shoulder demands from cordasco1996. Joint angles are estimates, not measured values.

families.name: Mobility drill
families.pattern: Slow, controlled movement of a joint through its full comfortable range, repeated for reps, usually as a warm-up.
setup: Warm, clear space; a mat for floor drills.
Start in the drill's base position: standing, half kneeling, on hands and feet, or lying.
Know your range: move to a firm stretch, never into pain.

steps.text: Step one foot far forward into a deep lunge, hands down inside the front foot.
Drop the inside elbow toward the front instep, back knee off the floor.
Open the chest and reach the inside arm to the ceiling, eyes follow the hand.
Hands down, shift the hips back and straighten the front leg.
Step back to standing or into the next lunge on the other side.

cues.cue: Controlled and slow; no bouncing.
cues.why: Controlled dynamic stretching improves range and later power; fast ballistic swings help less.

cues.cue: Go a little further each rep, always pain-free.
cues.why: Range gains come from lower muscle-tendon stiffness built up over repeated reps.

cues.cue: Use 5-10 reps per drill before training.
cues.why: Dynamic drills in a warm-up raise range without the short-term strength loss of long static holds.

cues.cue: Brace lightly so the joint you are training does the moving.
cues.why: If the low back moves instead, the target joint (hip, shoulder, upper back) gets less range.

cues.cue: Nerve glides: gentle, no tingling that lasts.
cues.why: Sliders move the nerve with little strain; tensioners stretch it and are harder on an irritated nerve.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you move into the end range, in as you return.

tempo.note: About 2 s into the range, a short pause, 2 s back; 5-10 reps per side.

mistakes.name: Bouncing at end range
mistakes.looks: Fast swings or jerks at the end of the movement.
mistakes.fix: Slow down and pause for a breath at the end.
mistakes.why: Ballistic swings give less benefit and more strain than controlled moves.

mistakes.name: Low back does the work
mistakes.looks: In lunges and leg swings the low back arches or rounds instead of the hip moving.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze the back glute, ribs down, smaller range.
mistakes.why: The hip stays stiff and the spine takes the range.

mistakes.name: Front knee caves in
mistakes.looks: In the lunge or squat drills the knee falls inside the foot.
mistakes.fix: Knee over the second toe, foot flat.
mistakes.why: Loads the inside of the knee.

safety: Jefferson curls (loaded spine rounding): start with bodyweight, add load very slowly, skip with disc problems or osteoporosis.
Nerve glides: stop if tingling or numbness lasts after the drill.
Recent joint injury or surgery: follow your physio's range limits.

variants.change: Light load adds a pull into the range; keep it slow.
Band, stick or wall guides the path; same joint range.
Same drill, a different step in the sequence or a different view.

easier: hands on a box or chair

subtypes.name: Nerve glides
subtypes.change: Seated; move two joints in opposite directions so the nerve slides, e.g. tip the head toward the arm as the wrist bends back, then reverse. Sciatic: knee straightens as the head lifts.

subtypes.name: Jefferson curl
subtypes.change: Standing on a step, legs straight, roll down one vertebra at a time from the head, then roll up. Light load in the hands.

subtypes.name: Pelvic tilts
subtypes.change: Lying with knees bent (or standing), tip the pelvis to flatten the low back, then arch it gently. 'Into bridge' rolls on up into a bridge.

subtypes.name: Lunge flows, world's greatest stretch
subtypes.match: greatest|in lunge|kneeling to|half kneeling(?! halo)|side lunge|knee down|butt walking
subtypes.change: Deep lunge flows that open the hip flexor, adductor and upper back in one sequence; half-kneeling and kneeling-to-stand drills train the transitions.

subtypes.name: Squat mobility
subtypes.change: Sink into a deep squat, heels down, chest up; pry the knees out with the elbows, shift side to side, stand up. Overhead version holds a stick overhead.

subtypes.name: Good morning (hinge drill)
subtypes.change: Hands behind the head or a stick on the back, soft knees; push the hips back with a flat back until the hamstrings stretch, then stand.

subtypes.name: Inchworm, plank to down dog
subtypes.change: From standing, fold and walk the hands out to a plank, then walk the feet up to the hands with straight legs.

subtypes.name: Leg swings and hip circles
subtypes.match: leg circle|figure 8|half circle|leg swing|front kick|hip circle
subtypes.change: Standing tall holding a support (or lying), swing or circle one leg through a smooth, growing range; the trunk stays still.

subtypes.name: Knee circles and patella
subtypes.change: Feet together, knees soft, hands on the knees; circle the knees. Patella: seated, leg relaxed, glide the kneecap gently with the fingers.

subtypes.name: Upper-back rotation
subtypes.match: side to side knee|windmill|archer|push through|diagonal reach|wring|headbanger
subtypes.change: Turn the rib cage while the pelvis stays put: lying knee drops side to side, standing windmill or archer reach, or a reach-through from all fours.

subtypes.name: Shoulder circles, halos, stick raises
subtypes.match: halo|around the world|front raise|overhead|phelps|warming up|military press|floor slide|ballerina|clap|shrug
subtypes.change: Move the arms through a full overhead circle: halos pass a light weight around the head; stick raises lift a dowel from the hips to overhead; floor slides keep the arms on the floor like a snow angel.

motion.basis: Default flow is the world's greatest stretch. No kinematic study of these drills was found; angles are estimates kept within adult normal ranges from soucie2011 (hip extension about 17°, shoulder flexion about 170°, ankle dorsiflexion about 13° unloaded, more when loaded in a lunge). Dosing and speed cues from opplert2018 and behm2011. Subtypes are grouped by joint and listed most specific first; the first match wins. trunkRot (+ toward the right) is an extra key not yet in the README convention.

families.name: Mountain climber
families.pattern: Running in a high plank: knees drive alternately toward the chest while the hands and trunk stay still.
setup: High plank: hands under the shoulders, arms straight.
Body in one line from head to heels, on your toes.
Brace your abs as if for a punch.

steps.text: Drive the right knee toward your chest, toes touching down under the hip.
Swap legs in one quick move: right back, left in.
Left knee in, right leg long behind you. Hips stay low.

cues.cue: Hips at plank height, not up in the air.
cues.why: The trunk muscles must hold the spine still while the legs move; high hips take that work away.

cues.cue: Shoulders stacked over the wrists, push the floor away.
cues.why: Shoulders behind the hands load the wrists and lose the plank.

cues.cue: Full knee drive: toes land under the hip.
cues.why: Short drives cut the range and the work.

cues.cue: Fast only as long as the plank holds.
cues.why: At speed in HIIT this reaches about 11 MET; form breaks first in the hips.

families.breathing: Quick, steady breaths; out with every second drive.

tempo.note: About 2 knee drives a second at a fast pace, one a second for control.

mistakes.name: Hips bounce high
mistakes.looks: Hips rise above the shoulders with each drive.
mistakes.fix: Slow down; keep the hips level with the shoulders.
mistakes.why: The core stops working and the move turns into a jog in a pike.

mistakes.name: Shoulders behind the hands
mistakes.looks: Weight shifts to the feet, shoulders drift back.
mistakes.fix: Lean forward until the shoulders are over the wrists.
mistakes.why: Wrists bend too far and the shoulders lose support.

mistakes.name: Lower back sags
mistakes.looks: The belly drops toward the floor.
mistakes.fix: Brace and squeeze the glutes.
mistakes.why: The lower back arches under load.

safety: Wrist pain: hands on a bench or on fists.
Lower-back pain: slow, controlled drives with hands raised.

variants.change: Fast in HIIT: about 11.0 MET (02214).
Steady, moderate HIIT: about 7.0 MET (02210).
Knee drives across to the opposite elbow (cross) or outside to the same elbow (spider): more obliques.
Feet in straps or on a slider: no foot contact on the drive, more core work.

subtypes.name: Mountain climber
subtypes.change: Default keyframes.

subtypes.name: Cross and spider climber
subtypes.change: Knee travels to the opposite or same elbow; hips turn a little.

subtypes.name: Standing climber
subtypes.change: Standing tall, alternate knees to hip height while the opposite arm reaches up.

subtypes.name: Bridge or lunge climber
subtypes.change: Climber steps combined with a bridge, lunge or inchworm; use those families' keyframes for the other part.

motion.basis: No kinematic study of the mountain climber found; all angles are estimates. Trunk is 75 (not 90) because the shoulders sit higher than the feet in a high plank.

families.name: Muscle setting (quad and glute sets)
families.pattern: Isometric squeeze: a muscle is tightened hard and held without the joint moving, often the first exercise after injury or surgery.
setup: Quad set: sit or lie with your leg straight, a small rolled towel under the knee if you like.
Glute set: lie on your back, or stand, legs relaxed.
Breathe normally throughout.

steps.text: Let the muscle go soft.
Tighten the thigh to press the back of your knee down (quad set) or squeeze your buttocks together (glute set).
Hold the squeeze about 5 seconds, breathing.
Let go fully, rest a couple of seconds, repeat.

cues.cue: Press the back of your knee down into the bed.
cues.why: This is the standard quad set; it switches the quads back on when swelling or pain inhibits them.

cues.cue: Watch the kneecap slide up as you tighten.
cues.why: A moving kneecap shows the quads are really contracting.

cues.cue: Squeeze your buttocks hard and hold 5 seconds.
cues.why: Regular 5-second glute squeezes improved hip extension strength as much as bridges in a training study.

cues.cue: Strong but pain-free effort.
cues.why: Isometric holds can ease tendon pain; pain during the hold is a sign to ease off.

families.breathing: Breathe normally throughout the hold; never hold your breath.

tempo.note: Tighten in 1 second, hold 5, relax 2; about 10 reps, a few times a day.

mistakes.name: Lifting the leg
mistakes.looks: The heel or whole leg lifts off the bed instead of the knee pressing down.
mistakes.fix: Keep the heel on the bed; push the back of the knee down.
mistakes.why: Lifting uses the hip flexors and turns it into a leg raise.

mistakes.name: Knee stays bent
mistakes.looks: The kneecap does not move and the knee never flattens.
mistakes.fix: Try the other leg first to feel it, then use a towel under the knee to push into.
mistakes.why: The quads are inhibited; feeling the good side helps switch them on.

mistakes.name: Back arches
mistakes.looks: During a glute set the lower back lifts off the floor or arches in standing.
mistakes.fix: Keep your ribs down and squeeze only the buttocks.
mistakes.why: The back muscles take over from the glutes.

safety: After surgery follow your surgeon's or physio's plan; these are usually safe from day one.
Stop if the squeeze causes sharp pain.

variants.change: Standing glute squeeze: stand tall and squeeze, no movement.
Lying glute set on your back, legs straight or knees bent.
Towel under the knee: press down into it; inner-range version straightens the knee and lifts the heel.

easier: quad set with the leg supported

subtypes.name: Lying glute set
subtypes.change: On your back, legs straight; squeeze the buttocks together, the hips may rise a few millimetres.

subtypes.name: Standing glute squeeze
subtypes.change: Stand tall, squeeze the buttocks, knees soft; no movement.

motion.basis: Default is a right-leg quad set sitting propped on the elbows/backrest with legs straight (trunk -60, hips 60 estimated). Hold time and reps from fhft-knee; inhibition rationale from rice2010. Glute set from lehecka2019 (5-second maximal squeezes). Joint changes during a set are a few degrees and are exaggerated slightly for the animation.

families.name: Neck strengthening
families.pattern: The head moves (or holds) against resistance: nodding down (flexion), tipping back (extension), ear to shoulder (side bend), plus chin tucks for the deep neck flexors.
setup: Sit tall with your back supported, or lie on a bench with your head just off the end.
Shoulders down and still; only the head moves.
Start with your hand or a light band as resistance.

steps.text: Move the head slowly through a comfortable range: chin down, head back, or ear toward shoulder.
Pause briefly at the end of the range.
Return slowly to neutral.

cues.cue: Lead with a small chin tuck, like a nod.
cues.why: The deep neck flexors control the head nod; they are often weak and late in people with neck pain.

cues.cue: Shoulders stay still; only the head moves.
cues.why: Shrugging hands the work to the upper traps.

cues.cue: Start light and progress slowly.
cues.why: Progressive neck training reduced pain and disability in women with chronic neck pain.

cues.cue: Smooth, pain-free range; no fast jerks.
cues.why: Head-harness training increased neck strength and muscle size when done in a controlled range.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you push, in as you return. Don't hold your breath.

tempo.note: Move in about 2 s, return in 3. Isometric holds 5-10 s.

mistakes.name: Chin pokes forward
mistakes.looks: The chin juts forward instead of nodding.
mistakes.fix: Tuck the chin first, then move.
mistakes.why: The upper neck extends and the deep flexors switch off.

mistakes.name: Shrugging
mistakes.looks: Shoulders rise toward the ears.
mistakes.fix: Shoulders down and back; lighter load.
mistakes.why: The upper traps take over.

mistakes.name: Jerky, end-range swings
mistakes.looks: The head flings into full extension or flexion.
mistakes.fix: Slow down and stop short of the end.
mistakes.why: Fast end-range loading strains the neck.

safety: Arm pain, tingling, numbness, dizziness or headache with neck movement: stop and see a clinician.
After a neck injury, get cleared before loaded neck work.
Neck stretches belong to stretching; this family is for strength and control.

variants.change: External load (plate, harness, cable, machine): for athletes and strength goals.
Hold still against your hand or a band: safest way to start.
Ear toward shoulder: side flexors.
Lying: gravity is the load; face down trains extensors, face up trains flexors.
Rotation: turn the head side to side against resistance.

subtypes.name: Chin tuck
subtypes.change: Glide the head straight back and nod slightly, making a double chin; hold, then relax.

subtypes.name: Lying neck flexion
subtypes.change: On your back, head off the bench end; curl the chin toward the chest.

subtypes.name: Lying or prone neck extension
subtypes.change: Face down, head off the bench end; lift the head back until level or slightly higher.

subtypes.name: Neck side flexion
subtypes.change: Ear toward shoulder against a band, harness or hand; the convention has no neck side-bend key, so the rig needs one (about 30-40 degrees, estimate).

motion.basis: Default is seated flexion then extension. Working range kept short of normal end range (about 50 flexion and 60-70 extension in healthy adults, swinkels2014, approximate). Side flexion and rotation have no convention key. Angles estimated.

families.name: Nordic hamstring curl
families.pattern: Eccentric knee flexion: kneeling with the ankles held, the body lowers forward as one straight line while the hamstrings brake the fall.
setup: Kneel on a pad; a partner, bar or strap holds your ankles.
Body straight from knees to head, hips locked, arms ready in front of the chest.
Squeeze glutes and brace before you start.

steps.text: Lean forward slowly from the knees, keeping hips straight.
Resist as long as you can as the hamstrings start to give way.
Catch yourself with your hands, chest near the floor.
Push off lightly with the hands and curl back up with the hamstrings.

cues.cue: Hips straight: knees, hips and shoulders in a line.
cues.why: With neutral hips the long head of biceps femoris works hard near full knee extension; bending at the hips changes the exercise.

cues.cue: Fall as slowly as you can, 3-5 seconds.
cues.why: The value is in the slow eccentric braking.

cues.cue: Try to push the break point lower each week.
cues.why: The angle where you lose control marks how strong the hamstrings are eccentrically.

cues.cue: Few sets, done regularly.
cues.why: Programmes including the Nordic cut hamstring injuries by about half.

families.breathing: Breathe in at the top, slow steady breath out while lowering.

tempo.note: As slow as you can on the way down.

mistakes.name: Hips bend
mistakes.looks: The buttocks push back and the chest drops while the thighs stay upright.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze glutes; think of a plank falling forward.
mistakes.why: Bending at the hips shortens the lever and shifts work from the biceps femoris.

mistakes.name: Fast drop
mistakes.looks: You lower a little, then fall to the floor.
mistakes.fix: Use a band or a slope for help so you can control the whole range.
mistakes.why: Little eccentric work after the break point.

mistakes.name: Low back arches
mistakes.looks: The belly sags toward the floor during the descent.
mistakes.fix: Brace your abs as for a plank.
mistakes.why: The trunk is not stiff, so the line breaks.

safety: Expect strong soreness the first weeks; start with 1-2 sets of 3-5.
Recent hamstring strain: wait until cleared and pain-free.

variants.change: Band from above pulls the chest up: lower further under control.
On a glute-ham bench: start horizontal and curl up with the knees, hips straight.
One leg: similar torque and muscle activity per leg.
Hips bent 90°: higher knee torque, more semitendinosus at a longer length.

harder: full nordic curl with no hands

subtypes.name: Glute-ham raise
subtypes.change: Thighs on the pad of a glute-ham bench; from a horizontal body, curl up until upright, hips straight.

metrics.label: Break point (knee bend)
metrics.good: lower is stronger; about 55-60 is common

motion.basis: Rigid-body lowering: trunk = 90 - knee flexion with hips at 0. sconce2021 reports break-point angles of about 120-126°, which we read as the thigh-to-shank angle (so about 55-60° of knee flexion); this reading is our interpretation. Catch pose and arm angles are estimates.

families.name: Overhead press
families.pattern: Vertical push: the weight goes from the shoulders to straight arms overhead while the shoulder blades rotate up.
setup: Stand with feet hip width, bar on the front of your shoulders.
Hands just outside the shoulders, wrists stacked over the elbows, forearms vertical.
Squeeze glutes and brace, ribs down: no big lean back.

steps.text: Start with the bar at your collarbones, elbows slightly in front of the bar.
Move your head back a little and press the bar straight up past your face.
Finish with arms straight, bar over your mid-foot, head through between the arms.
Bring the bar back down the same line to the collarbones.

cues.cue: Ribs down, glutes tight: stand tall, do not lean back.
cues.why: Standing presses need trunk stiffness; the spine moves about 12-15° during the press and more without bracing.

cues.cue: Bar in front of your face, finish over the back of your head.
cues.why: Pressing in front avoids the end-range externally rotated position linked to shoulder instability.

cues.cue: Let them rotate up; at lockout reach tall.
cues.why: At full arm elevation the shoulder blade rotates up about 50° and tilts back; that clears room for the rotator cuff.

cues.cue: Elbows a little in front of the bar, forearms vertical.
cues.why: Vertical forearms push the load straight up through the arm.

cues.cue: Bar low in the palm, wrists only slightly bent.
cues.why: Bent-back wrists move the bar behind the forearm and strain the wrist.

families.breathing: Breathe in and brace at the shoulders, breathe out after lockout.

tempo.note: Press in about 1 s, lower in 2 s.

mistakes.name: Leaning back
mistakes.looks: The lower back arches and the chest points up as you press.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze glutes, ribs down; use less weight.
mistakes.why: It turns the press into an incline press and loads the lower back.

mistakes.name: Bar stays in front
mistakes.looks: At the top the bar is in front of the head, arms angled forward.
mistakes.fix: Push your head through once the bar passes your forehead.
mistakes.why: The load sits forward of the shoulder and the arms never reach full elevation.

mistakes.name: Elbows flare behind the bar
mistakes.looks: Elbows point straight out to the sides at the start, bar drifts forward.
mistakes.fix: Bring elbows slightly forward, forearms vertical.
mistakes.why: It puts the shoulder near the high-five position with the load behind it.

mistakes.name: Wrists bent back
mistakes.looks: Knuckles point back, bar sits on the fingers.
mistakes.fix: Bar low in the palm over the forearm.
mistakes.why: The bar's weight bends the wrist instead of stacking on the forearm.

safety: Behind-the-neck pressing needs full shoulder external rotation; press in front if you lack it.
Shoulder pain overhead: use a landmine press or a neutral-grip dumbbell press.
Lower-back pain: sit with back support or kneel.

variants.change: Seated: less trunk demand and more 1RM; deltoid activity a bit lower than standing.
Dumbbells: deltoid activity about 7-15% higher than barbell but about 7% less weight.
Behind the neck: needs full external rotation and a straight upper back.
Palms facing each other, elbows forward: often easier on the shoulder.
Kneeling: the trunk has to resist leaning back.
Sitting on the floor legs straight: no leg or back help, strict torso.
Kettlebell bottom up: grip and rotator cuff work much harder; light weight.
One side: resist leaning to the side.
Curl first, then press from the shoulder.

subtypes.name: Arnold press
subtypes.change: Start with palms facing you in front of the shoulders, open the elbows to the sides and turn the palms forward as you press.

subtypes.name: Landmine press
subtypes.change: One end of a bar in the floor; press the other end up and forward on a diagonal, often half-kneeling. Arm finishes about 120-135° raised, so it is kinder to stiff shoulders.

subtypes.name: Pike push-up
subtypes.change: Hands on the floor, hips high in an upside-down V, lower the top of your head toward the floor in front of the hands.

subtypes.name: Handstand and handstand push-up
subtypes.change: Upside down on your hands, body in one line, usually against a wall. Push tall through the shoulders; balance is kept mostly at the wrists. Handstand push-ups lower the head to the floor or between benches.

subtypes.name: Seated press
subtypes.change: Sitting with back support, hips and knees about 90°: same arm keyframes as the standing press.

subtypes.name: Dumbbell press
subtypes.change: Dumbbells start at ear height, elbows about 30° in front of the body line; press up and slightly in. Same arm keyframes.

subtypes.name: Cuban press
subtypes.change: Upright row to elbow height, rotate the forearms up to vertical, then press: light weight, a rotator cuff drill.

motion.basis: Scapular upward rotation at full elevation (about 46-50°, posterior tilt about 30°, glenohumeral to scapular ratio 1.7-2:1) from mcclure2001 and ludewig2009, scaled to arm angle at each keyframe. Spine movement of 12-15° from mckean2015. Rack, mid-press and lockout shoulder and elbow angles, shoulder rotation (forearm vertical at the rack gives about 60° external rotation) and the inverted subtypes are estimates from the bar path; no study measured them directly. Handstand balance mostly at the wrists from mcdonald2025.

families.name: Paddling and rowing on water
families.pattern: A pull through the water driven by the legs and trunk; the arms mostly connect the body to the blade.
setup: Wear a buoyancy aid (PFD) and check wind, current and water temperature.
Kayak and canoe: sit tall, feet braced; grip the shaft a little wider than your shoulders.
SUP: feet hip width either side of the handle, knees soft, eyes on the horizon.
Rowing: feet strapped, handle in the fingers, start with arms only, then add body and legs.

steps.text: Reach forward from the hips with long arms and put the blade fully in.
Push with the legs first (or the foot brace in a kayak).
Open the trunk (rowing) or rotate it (kayak, SUP) while the arms stay long.
Arms finish the stroke near the ribs or hip; take the blade out cleanly.
Arms away, body forward, then slide or reach for the next catch.

cues.cue: Legs, then body, then arms; reverse on the way back.
cues.why: The legs give most rowing power; arms-first pulling wastes it and tires the arms.

cues.cue: Hinge from the hips with a long spine at the catch.
cues.why: The lower back is the most injured area in rowing; deep slumped flexion at the catch adds strain.

cues.cue: Kayak and SUP: rotate the trunk; the bottom arm stays fairly straight.
cues.why: Trunk, pelvis and leg motion drive kayak power; arm-only strokes overload the shoulder.

cues.cue: Keep the top hand at or below eye level and in front of you.
cues.why: A high, wide top hand puts the shoulder at the end range where dislocations happen in kayaking.

cues.cue: Plant the whole blade, pull it to your hip or feet, then lift it out.
cues.why: Strokes past the hip lift water and twist the trunk with little speed.

cues.cue: Loose grip; push the top hand, pull the bottom.
cues.why: A tight grip tires the forearms and wrists, a common overuse site.

families.breathing: Breathe out on the pull, in on the recovery; at higher rates breathe twice per stroke.

tempo.note: Rowing: drive about 1 part, recovery 2 parts; 18-24 strokes per minute steady. Kayak about 50-70 strokes per minute (both sides). SUP 30-40 per minute.

mistakes.name: Pulling with the arms
mistakes.looks: The elbows bend as soon as the blade goes in; legs and trunk stay still.
mistakes.fix: Keep the arms long until the legs (rowing) or trunk rotation (kayak) has done its part.
mistakes.why: Small arm muscles do the work of big ones; power drops and elbows and shoulders tire.

mistakes.name: Slumped catch
mistakes.looks: The back rounds and the head drops as you reach forward.
mistakes.fix: Sit tall on the sit bones and hinge from the hips; reach only as far as your back stays long.
mistakes.why: Large lumbar flexion under load goes with low back pain in rowers.

mistakes.name: Top hand too high
mistakes.looks: The top hand goes above the head or far behind it (bracing or steep strokes).
mistakes.fix: Top hand at eye height; on support strokes keep elbows low and close.
mistakes.why: Overhead, rotated arm positions are where kayak shoulder dislocations occur.

mistakes.name: SUP: bent at the waist, legs straight
mistakes.looks: Knees locked and the back bends to reach the water.
mistakes.fix: Soft knees, hinge at the hips, let the legs help lower the blade.
mistakes.why: It loads the lower back and makes balance harder.

safety: Always wear a buoyancy aid; dress for the water temperature, not the air.
Learn a capsize or wet exit in calm water with help before going out alone.
Rowing rib pain that is sharp with deep breaths: stop and get checked (rib stress fracture).
Low back pain: shorten sessions, lower the stroke rate and check your catch.

variants.change: Rowing or canoeing for pleasure, general. MET 3.5 (Compendium 18070).
Crew or sculling, competition. MET 12.0 (Compendium 18080).
Kayaking, moderate effort. MET 5.0 (Compendium 18100).
Kayaking, competition. MET 13.5 (Compendium 18104).
Whitewater rafting, kayaking or canoeing. MET 5.0 (Compendium 18370).
Canoeing 2.0-3.9 mph, light effort. MET 2.8 (Compendium 18040).
Canoeing 4.0-5.9 mph, moderate effort. MET 5.8 (Compendium 18050).
Canoeing, rowing or kayaking, faster than 6 mph, vigorous. MET 12.5 (Compendium 18060).
Stand-up paddle boarding, general. MET 6.5 (Compendium 18224).
SUP at 10-19 strokes/min. MET 2.8 (Compendium 18225).
SUP at 30-39 strokes/min. MET 5.0 (Compendium 18227).
SUP at 40-49 strokes/min. MET 9.8 (Compendium 18228).
Indoor rowing machine is the row-erg family, not this one.

subtypes.name: Rowing on water
subtypes.change: Sliding seat: legs, body, arms on the drive; arms, body, legs on the recovery. Sweep rowers add a little trunk rotation toward the oar.

subtypes.name: Kayaking
subtypes.change: Seated with knees slightly bent and braced; push the foot brace on the stroke side, rotate the trunk, top hand pushes at eye level.

subtypes.name: Stand-up paddle
subtypes.change: Standing, knees soft, hinge at the hips; top hand over the bottom hand when the blade is in; stroke to your feet, switch sides every few strokes.

subtypes.name: Canoe
subtypes.change: Seated or kneeling, single blade; same reach-plant-pull as SUP; the stern paddler ends each stroke with a J (thumb turns down) to steer.

keyframes.phase: Exit with a J (thumb turns down)

metrics.label: Elbow bend early in the drive

motion.basis: Default clip is a rowing stroke. Catch lumbar flexion and posterior pelvic tilt pattern from mcgregor2002; trunk angles, drive/recovery ratio and limb angles from soper2004 descriptions and our estimates. Kayak and SUP keyframes are estimates; the rig has no trunk axial-rotation key, so trunk rotation (a main contributor in bjerkefors2018) is described in text, not keyed.

families.name: Pallof press
families.pattern: Anti-rotation: a cable or band pulls sideways while you press it straight out in front, and the trunk refuses to turn.
setup: Stand side-on to the anchor, about a step away, handle at chest height.
Hold the handle at your breastbone with both hands, feet hip width, knees soft.
Step out until the band is tight; square your hips and chest forward.

steps.text: Press the handle straight out from your chest without letting it pull you around.
Hold the arms straight for 2-5 s; breathe.
Bring the handle back to your chest slowly. Finish the set, then face the other way.

cues.cue: Chest and hips stay square; the hands stay on the midline.
cues.why: Resisting a turning force trains the obliques and deep trunk to stiffen the spine against rotation.

cues.cue: Press straight out, not toward the anchor.
cues.why: The force arm is longest with arms straight, so the press is the hardest point.

cues.cue: Narrow your stance or go standing to make it harder.
cues.why: Standing instead of kneeling and a smaller base raised the balance demand; an unstable surface raised it most.

cues.cue: Ribs down, glutes lightly on.
cues.why: A modest brace stiffens the trunk without breath holding.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you press, keep breathing during the hold.

tempo.note: Press in 2 s, hold 2-5 s, return in 2 s.

mistakes.name: Turning toward the anchor
mistakes.looks: Shoulders and hips twist toward the cable as you press.
mistakes.fix: Lighter load; keep the hands on your midline.
mistakes.why: The trunk is losing the anti-rotation fight.

mistakes.name: Leaning away
mistakes.looks: The body tilts away from the anchor to fight the pull.
mistakes.fix: Stand tall, weight even on both feet.
mistakes.why: Leaning replaces trunk work with body weight.

mistakes.name: Ribs flare, back arches
mistakes.looks: The low back arches as the arms go out.
mistakes.fix: Ribs down, slight glute squeeze.
mistakes.why: It turns into a shoulder press.

safety: Low back pain: anti-rotation work is often well tolerated; start kneeling with a light band.
Shoulder pain: keep the press below shoulder height.

variants.change: Kneeling: lower centre of mass and less balance demand.
Narrow split stance: harder balance.
Press overhead instead of forward.
Hold the press while squatting, stepping, bridging or doing a dead bug.
Anti-rotation chop: arms move high to low while the trunk stays square.

subtypes.name: Half-kneeling Pallof press
subtypes.change: Inside knee down, outside foot forward.

subtypes.name: Lying Pallof press or anti-rotation dead bug
subtypes.change: On your back (or in a bridge) pressing the handle to the ceiling against the side pull.

motion.basis: Anchor is on the subject's right. Angles are estimates from the technique; the convention has no trunk-rotation key, so a rotation fault is shown with hip rotation and arm drift. Difficulty ranking from juanrecio2025.

families.name: Pilates mat
families.pattern: Controlled trunk curls, rolls, leg reaches and extensions on a mat, done slowly with the breath while the deep abdominals hold the pelvis steady.
setup: Lie on your back on a mat, knees bent, feet flat, arms by your sides.
Find a neutral pelvis: hip bones and pubic bone level.
Draw your lower belly gently in toward the spine before you move.

steps.text: Lie long, legs together, arms reaching overhead.
Breathe in, lift the arms and head; breathe out and peel the spine off the mat one bone at a time.
Fold over your legs, belly scooped, reaching past your toes.
Breathe in and roll back down slowly, one bone at a time, until the head returns.

cues.cue: Draw your lower belly in and up before each move.
cues.why: Hollowing turns on the transversus abdominis and internal oblique most selectively.

cues.cue: Keep the pelvis still while the legs move.
cues.why: Bracing reduced unwanted pelvic rotation in leg-pull work.

cues.cue: Roll one bone at a time; no jerks or swings.
cues.why: Control, precision and flow are core Pilates principles; momentum takes the work off the trunk.

cues.cue: Chin a fist from the chest, eyes to your knees.
cues.why: Keeps the neck long while the trunk curls; a tense neck often means the abs have let go.

cues.cue: Breathe out on the effort, in to prepare.
cues.why: Breathing is the Pilates principle used most consistently in research and rehab programmes.

families.breathing: Breathe in to prepare, out as you curl, reach or press. Hundred: in for 5 pumps, out for 5.

tempo.note: Slow and even, about 3 s each way; 5-10 reps of each exercise.

mistakes.name: Low back peels off the mat
mistakes.looks: When the legs reach long, the low back arches up off the mat.
mistakes.fix: Raise the legs higher or bend the knees until the back stays down.
mistakes.why: The legs out-lever the abs; the load moves to the lower back.

mistakes.name: Throws up with momentum
mistakes.looks: Arms swing and the feet lift as you jerk up in the roll up or teaser.
mistakes.fix: Slow down; bend the knees or hold the backs of the thighs.
mistakes.why: Momentum skips the controlled curl that trains the trunk.

mistakes.name: Neck strain
mistakes.looks: Chin jams to the chest or the hands pull the head.
mistakes.fix: Fist space under the chin, lift from the breastbone.
mistakes.why: The neck flexors tire long before the abs.

safety: Low back pain: Pilates helps pain and function about as much as other exercise; start with bent-knee versions.
Osteoporosis: skip rolling-on-the-spine moves (rolling like a ball, rollover, jackknife, seal) and loaded forward flexion.
Neck pain: keep the head down for the hundred and stretches.
Pregnancy after the first trimester: avoid long work lying flat on the back.

variants.change: Knees bent: shorter lever, easier for the abs.
Side kicks from kneeling on one knee with one hand down: more balance work, less range.
Hands or forearms support the trunk: easier.

subtypes.name: Hundred
subtypes.change: Head and shoulders curled up, legs raised to about 45°, straight arms pump up and down a few cm; 10 breaths of 10 pumps.

subtypes.name: Rolling like a ball, rocker, seal
subtypes.change: Balanced in a tight ball (or legs open holding the ankles), roll back to the shoulder blades and up again; never onto the neck.

subtypes.name: Rollover, jackknife, corkscrew
subtypes.change: Lying face up, legs lift over the head until parallel to the floor, then roll down with control. Jackknife shoots the legs to the ceiling; corkscrew circles them.

subtypes.name: Single leg stretch, scissors
subtypes.change: Head and shoulders up; one knee hugs in while the other leg reaches out at about 45°, switch each breath. Straight-leg version scissors two straight legs.

subtypes.name: Double leg stretch
subtypes.change: Curled up hugging both knees; breathe in and reach arms overhead and legs out long, breathe out and circle the arms back to hug.

subtypes.name: Criss-cross, bicycle
subtypes.change: Curled up, hands behind the head; rotate one elbow toward the opposite knee as that leg bends in. Chest lift is the plain curl; neck pull rolls all the way up and down.

subtypes.name: Single leg circle
subtypes.match: single leg circle|lying single leg circle
subtypes.change: Lying face up, one leg to the ceiling draws small circles; the pelvis does not rock.

subtypes.name: Spine stretch forward, saw, spine twist
subtypes.change: Sit tall, legs straight and wider than the hips. Spine stretch curls forward; saw twists and reaches the hand past the opposite little toe; spine twist turns without folding.

subtypes.name: Swan and prone kicks
subtypes.change: Lying face down; press the chest up with long legs (swan). Kicks bend one or both knees toward the glutes while the chest stays lifted.

subtypes.name: Teaser
subtypes.change: From lying, roll up into a V balance: legs at about 45°, arms reaching parallel to the legs, then roll down.

subtypes.name: Shoulder bridge
subtypes.change: Lying face up, feet flat; roll the hips up one bone at a time, lift and lower one straight leg, roll down. Rolling bridge is the roll only.

subtypes.name: Side kick series
subtypes.match: side kick|leg lift side|side lying leg circle|leg circle kick
subtypes.change: Lying on your side, body in a line, top leg lifts, swings forward and back, or circles while the trunk stays still. Kneeling version: one knee and one hand down.

subtypes.name: Side bend, mermaid, side twist
subtypes.change: Side plank on one straight arm, hips lifted into an arch; mermaid is a seated side stretch with the knees bent to one side. Body lies on the side in this rig (trunk shown upright).

subtypes.name: Leg pull front and back
subtypes.change: Front plank (leg pull front) or reverse plank (leg pull back) while one leg lifts and lowers; hips stay level. Hip twist circles both legs from a seated lean back on the hands.

motion.basis: Default keyframes are the roll up. No published joint-angle data for most classic mat exercises; all angles are estimates from the standard repertoire. Muscle emphasis from EMG and ultrasound work (jung2022, queiroz2010, tsartsapakis2023). Subtypes are listed most specific first; the first match wins. trunkRot (+ toward the right) is an extra key not yet in the README convention.

families.name: Pilates reformer
families.pattern: Pilates moves on a sliding carriage pulled back by springs: you push or pull the carriage away with control and resist the springs on the way back.
setup: Set the springs before you get on; ask an instructor for your first sessions.
Footwork: lie face up, head on the headrest, shoulders against the shoulder blocks.
Feet on the footbar hip width, knees bent, pelvis neutral.

steps.text: Breathe out and straighten your legs, pushing the carriage away in 2 counts.
Legs long but not locked; pelvis still on the carriage.
Breathe in and resist the springs as the carriage slides back in 3 counts; don't let it crash.

cues.cue: Control the return; the carriage never bangs the stopper.
cues.why: The return is eccentric work against the springs; letting go loses it and jolts the joints.

cues.cue: Pelvis and trunk stay still while the legs or arms move.
cues.why: Heavier springs gave more trunk and pelvis stability and more gluteus medius, oblique and multifidus work in side splits.

cues.cue: Heavier spring for stability, lighter spring for range and control.
cues.why: Lighter springs gave a larger, more even hip range but more trunk shift.

cues.cue: Knees track over the second toe; stop just short of locking.
cues.why: Same lower-limb alignment rules as squats and leg presses.

cues.cue: Out on the push, in on the return.
cues.why: Breath timing is the most used Pilates principle in research programmes.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you push the carriage away, in as it returns.

tempo.note: Push in about 2 s, return in about 3 s; 8-12 reps.

mistakes.name: Carriage crashes back
mistakes.looks: The carriage snaps home and hits the stopper.
mistakes.fix: Slow the return to 3 counts; lighten the spring if needed.
mistakes.why: Loses the eccentric work and jolts the joints.

mistakes.name: Pelvis rocks or tilts
mistakes.looks: The hips lift, tuck or shift side to side as the legs push.
mistakes.fix: Brace lightly, heavier spring, smaller range.
mistakes.why: The trunk is not holding; load moves to the low back.

mistakes.name: Knees snap straight
mistakes.looks: At full push the knees lock back hard.
mistakes.fix: Stop with the knees long but soft.
mistakes.why: Hyperextension loads the back of the knee.

safety: Get on and off only when the carriage is locked in at the stopper.
Standing work (side splits, standing lunges) needs light springs and an instructor until confident.
Osteoporosis: avoid loaded forward flexion like long spine and rolling moves.

variants.change: Feet on the bar on the balls of the feet: more calf work, ankles held high.
Heels on the bar: more glutes and hamstrings, feet flexed.
Legs straight, heels lower under the bar and rise: ankle only.

subtypes.name: Calf raises
subtypes.change: Legs straight on the footbar; lower the heels below the bar and rise onto the toes.

subtypes.name: Hundred
subtypes.change: Holding the straps, head and shoulders up, legs at 45°; straight arms pump by the sides against the straps.

subtypes.name: Frog, leg circles, long spine
subtypes.change: Feet in the straps: legs press out from a frog (heels together, knees wide) or draw circles; long spine rolls the hips over and down.

subtypes.name: Pelvic lift
subtypes.change: Feet on the bar, roll the hips up into a bridge, then press the carriage out and in from the bridge.

subtypes.name: Side split, Russian split and squat
subtypes.change: Standing with one foot on the platform and one on the carriage: push the carriage out into a wide straddle (side split) or a split stance, then pull it back with the inner thighs.

subtypes.name: Arm work (circles, chest expansion, overhead)
subtypes.change: Kneeling or lying, hands in the straps; pull the straps down past the hips (chest expansion), draw circles, or press overhead while the trunk stays still.

motion.basis: Default is footwork (lying leg press). Few kinematic studies exist; lee2023 (side splits, heavy vs light springs) informs trunk and spring cues. Angles are estimates from the standard repertoire. Members are few (14), so subtypes group them by body position.

families.name: Plank
families.pattern: Anti-extension hold: face down on forearms (or hands) and toes, the body stays one straight line while the trunk resists sagging.
setup: Forearms on the floor, elbows under your shoulders.
Legs straight, on your toes, feet hip width.
Squeeze your glutes, brace your belly, head in line with your back.

steps.text: Hold one straight line from head to heels and breathe steadily. Stop when the line breaks.

cues.cue: One straight line, head to heels.
cues.why: The prone bridge is an anti-extension hold; a neutral line lets the abdominals carry the load.

cues.cue: Tuck the tailbone slightly and squeeze your glutes.
cues.why: A posterior pelvic tilt with glutes on, elbows reaching forward (long lever), raised abdominal activity well above a standard plank.

cues.cue: Elbows under the shoulders; push the floor away.
cues.why: Pushing through the forearms keeps the shoulder blades set and spreads load to the serratus.

cues.cue: Keep breathing behind the brace.
cues.why: A moderate brace is enough to stiffen the trunk; you should still be able to breathe.

cues.cue: Quality over time: short sets with a perfect line.
cues.why: Endurance holds are timed only while form holds; once the line breaks, the test (and the set) is over.

families.breathing: Breathe slowly and evenly; do not hold your breath.

tempo.note: Hold 10-30 s, rest, repeat. Add time only while the line stays straight.

mistakes.name: Hips sag
mistakes.looks: The low back arches and the hips drop toward the floor.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze glutes, tuck the tailbone, brace.
mistakes.why: The spine hangs into extension instead of being held.

mistakes.name: Hips too high
mistakes.looks: The body makes a tent with the hips highest.
mistakes.fix: Lower the hips until shoulders, hips and heels line up.
mistakes.why: Piking unloads the abdominals.

mistakes.name: Head drops
mistakes.looks: The head hangs and the chin points down.
mistakes.fix: Look at the floor just ahead of your hands.
mistakes.why: It breaks the line and rounds the upper back.

safety: Shoulder pain: plank on the hands from a bench (incline) or on the knees.
High blood pressure: keep breathing; use short holds.

variants.change: Knees down: shorter lever, easier.
Hands on a bench or wall: easier.
Unstable support raises abdominal activity.
Lifting a limb removes a support: the trunk must also resist rotation; keep hips level.

variants.when: walk|up and down|walk up|to push up|dynamic
variants.change: Moving between forearms and hands: keep hips still while the arms move.
Plate on the back: harder; keep the same line.

subtypes.name: High plank and shoulder taps
subtypes.match: on hands|push.?up position|shoulder tap|tap|walk|up and down|to push|knee tap|hit the ball|pass through|pull
subtypes.change: On straight arms, hands under shoulders; for taps lift one hand to the opposite shoulder without the hips rocking.

subtypes.name: Hollow hold and rock
subtypes.change: On your back, low back pressed down, shoulders and straight legs just off the floor, arms by the ears.

subtypes.name: Reverse plank
subtypes.change: Face up on hands or forearms and heels, hips lifted level with shoulders and ankles.

subtypes.name: Bear plank
subtypes.change: On hands and toes with knees bent 90 degrees and hovering a few centimetres off the floor.

motion.basis: Body line and elbow under shoulder from the standard prone bridge (ekstrom2007); trunk 84 because shoulders sit a forearm's height above the toes (estimate). Dynamic and hollow subtype angles are estimates.

families.name: Pull-up
families.pattern: Vertical pull: hanging from a bar, the arms pull the body up until the chin passes the bar, shoulder blades pulling down and back.
setup: Hands on the bar a little wider than your shoulders, palms away (palms toward you for a chin-up).
Hang with arms straight, legs together, ribs down.
Before you bend your arms, pull your shoulders down away from your ears.

steps.text: Start from straight arms, body still.
Pull your shoulder blades down and slightly back; you rise a few centimetres with straight arms.
Drive your elbows down toward your ribs until your chin clears the bar.
Chest toward the bar, shoulders down, no chin poke.
Lower under control all the way to straight arms.

cues.cue: Shoulders down and back before the arms bend.
cues.why: The lower trapezius fires first and starts the pull; it is more active in the pull-up than the chin-up.

cues.cue: Drive your elbows down to your back pockets.
cues.why: The lats are the main mover (over 100% MVIC in testing) and finish the pull with the biceps.

cues.cue: Hands just outside your shoulders; avoid very wide or behind-the-neck pulls.
cues.why: Wide and palms-toward pulls showed shoulder positions linked with impingement risk; shoulder-width front pulls are safer.

cues.cue: Ribs down, legs together, no swing.
cues.why: The trunk muscles work to keep the body still; swinging turns it into a different, kipping skill.

cues.cue: Straight arms at the bottom, chin over the bar at the top.
cues.why: Full elbow range is about 90-100° in a strict rep; partial reps cut the work done.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you pull up, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Pull in about 1 second, short pause, lower in 2 to 3.

mistakes.name: Shoulders shrug up
mistakes.looks: Shoulders ride up to the ears and the neck disappears at the top.
mistakes.fix: Pull your shoulders down first and keep them down.
mistakes.why: Pulling with elevated shoulder blades reduces space under the acromion at high arm angles.

mistakes.name: Half reps
mistakes.looks: Arms never straighten at the bottom, or the chin never reaches the bar.
mistakes.fix: Lower to straight arms each rep; use a band if you cannot finish.
mistakes.why: Strict reps move the elbow through about 90-100°; short reps skip the hardest part.

mistakes.name: Kipping and swinging
mistakes.looks: Knees drive up and the hips swing to throw the body to the bar.
mistakes.fix: Legs together, glutes tight, slow down; use a band or negatives if needed.
mistakes.why: Momentum shifts load away from the back muscles and adds sudden stress on the shoulder.

mistakes.name: Chin reaches
mistakes.looks: The head pokes forward and up to get the chin over the bar.
mistakes.fix: Keep a long neck and bring your chest to the bar.
mistakes.why: Reaching with the neck fakes the last few centimetres and strains the neck.

safety: Shoulder pain: use a shoulder-width or neutral grip and avoid behind-the-neck pulls.
Elbow pain: try a neutral grip or rings so the hands can turn.
Drop off with bent knees; do not let go from a high hang onto straight legs.

variants.change: Palms toward you: more biceps and chest; less lower trapezius; elbow range a little larger (about 100°).
Palms facing: overall muscle activity similar; slightly less mid trapezius than the pronated grip.
Hands about 2x shoulder width: shorter range and shoulder positions linked with more impingement risk.
Behind the neck: forces the shoulder into end-range external rotation; best avoided.
Belt or vest load; same form.
One arm does most of the work; shoulders stay level as long as you can.
Rope grip: much harder on the forearms and grip.
Rings let the hands turn; the bar path can curve.
Legs held straight out in front at 90°: adds hip flexor and abdominal work.
Ring muscle-up needs more biceps, forearm and upper-trapezius work than the bar version; learn it on the bar first.

subtypes.name: Assisted pull-up
subtypes.change: Feet on a box or floor, knee on a pad, or a band under the feet takes part of the body weight. Same arm and shoulder-blade path.

subtypes.name: Negative and hold
subtypes.match: negative|eccentric|isometric|hold|top pull up hold|half pull|top half
subtypes.change: Jump or step to the top position, then hold or lower slowly for 3-5 seconds.

subtypes.name: Dead hang
subtypes.change: Hold the bottom position for time. Passive hang: shoulders relax up. Active hang: shoulders pulled down with straight arms.

subtypes.name: Muscle-up
subtypes.change: Explosive pull to the lower chest, wrists turn over the bar or rings, then press up like a dip to straight arms. Learn on a bar before rings.

subtypes.name: Rope climb
subtypes.change: Hand over hand up a rope (feet can clamp the rope) or along monkey bars; each pull is a one-arm pull-up path with the other arm reaching up.

metrics.label: Elbow bend
metrics.good: 0-15 at the bottom, 100-120 at the top

metrics.label: Chin height
metrics.good: chin above the bar at the top

metrics.label: Shoulders down
metrics.good: below 0 from the Set phase on

motion.basis: Elbow range (about 93-100°) and the lower-trapezius-first timing from youdas2010; scapular pattern (upward rotation near 45° with arms overhead, falling to about 10° at the top; depression and retraction during the pull) from prinold2016 and escamilla2009, values rounded by us. Trunk, hip and shoulder angles estimated from video convention.

families.name: Pullover
families.pattern: Straight-arm shoulder extension: the arms swing from overhead down to the hips or chest with the elbows nearly fixed.
setup: Lie face up on a bench, head supported, feet flat on the floor.
Hold one dumbbell with both hands over your chest, elbows slightly bent.
Ribs down and lower back gently on the bench.

steps.text: Weight over your chest, arms nearly straight.
Keeping the elbow bend fixed, lower the weight in an arc behind your head until your arms are beside your ears.
Stop where you feel a stretch under the arms, ribs still down.
Pull the weight back over your chest along the same arc.

cues.cue: Fix a soft elbow bend; do not bend and press.
cues.why: The moment arm of the load at the shoulder sets which muscle works; bending the elbows shortens it and turns it into a triceps press.

cues.cue: Ribs down, lower back stays on the bench.
cues.why: Arching the back fakes shoulder range; the arms can only reach about as far as your shoulder flexion allows.

cues.cue: Lower until your arms are beside your ears, not further.
cues.why: Above about 150-170° of arm elevation the shoulder runs out of range and the load moves to the joint.

cues.cue: For chest, lie across the bench; for lats, use a cable straight-arm pulldown.
cues.why: The free-weight pullover worked the pectoralis more than the latissimus.

families.breathing: Breathe in as the weight goes back, out as you pull it over.

tempo.note: Slow arc both ways; short pause in the stretch.

mistakes.name: Back arches
mistakes.looks: The lower back lifts off the bench and the ribs flare as the weight goes overhead.
mistakes.fix: Shorten the range and keep your ribs pulled down.
mistakes.why: The spine is bending to finish range the shoulder does not have.

mistakes.name: Elbows bend and press
mistakes.looks: The elbows bend a lot behind the head, then straighten as the weight comes up.
mistakes.fix: Keep the same small elbow bend for the whole arc.
