mistakes.why: It turns the pullover into a triceps extension and changes the muscles worked.

mistakes.name: Too deep
mistakes.looks: The weight drops below the bench line and the shoulders feel pinched.
mistakes.fix: Stop when your arms are beside your ears.
mistakes.why: Loading the end of shoulder range strains the joint capsule and rotator cuff.

safety: Shoulder pain or instability: keep the range short, or use a cable straight-arm pulldown.
Hold the dumbbell by the inside of the top plate with both palms; check it is secure.

variants.change: Elbows bent about 60-90°: shorter lever, more weight, more triceps.
Elbows near straight: longer lever, lighter weight.
Head lower than hips: the hardest part moves later in the arc.
Shoulders on a ball, hips up in a bridge: adds glute and trunk work.
Hold the stretched position for time.
Pullover then press: bend the elbows at the chest and press the bar up.

subtypes.name: Straight-arm pulldown
subtypes.change: Standing at a high cable, hips hinged slightly; arms nearly straight sweep from overhead down to the thighs. Lats work most at the end.

motion.basis: Muscle emphasis from marchetti2011; scapular upward rotation with arm elevation (about 45-55° at full elevation) from escamilla2009 and ludewig2009, scaled by us to the arm angle. Bench and leg positions are convention; elbow angle estimated.

families.name: Punches and boxing
families.pattern: Strike from a guard: the push starts in the feet and hips, the trunk turns, and the fist travels last, then snaps back to guard.
setup: Stance (right-handed): left foot forward, feet a little wider than your hips, back heel slightly raised.
Knees soft, weight even between the feet.
Guard: fists by your cheeks, elbows in front of your ribs, chin tucked.

steps.text: Relax in your stance with your hands up and chin down.
Push off the floor and turn your hips and shoulders as your fist goes straight out, turning palm down.
Hit with the first two knuckles, wrist straight, arm just short of locked.
Bring the fist straight back to your face along the same line.

cues.cue: Other hand stays at your chin.
cues.why: Dropping the non-punching hand is the most coached fault: it leaves the head open.

cues.cue: Punch from the floor: turn the back foot and hip.
cues.why: Lower body drive and trunk rotation add much of the speed and force of straight punches and hooks.

cues.cue: Snap out, snap back; do not lock the elbow.
cues.why: Elbow extension speed peaks just before impact; locking out hard strains the joint.

cues.cue: Wrist straight, fist tight at impact.
cues.why: A bent wrist on a bag is a common cause of wrist injury.

cues.cue: Chin tucked, eyes on the target.
cues.why: Protects the jaw and keeps balance.

families.breathing: Short, sharp breath out through the nose or mouth with each punch.

tempo.note: Rounds: commonly 2-3 minutes on, 1 minute rest.

mistakes.name: Guard drops
mistakes.looks: The non-punching hand falls toward the chest or waist.
mistakes.fix: Touch your cheek with the guard glove on every punch.
mistakes.why: Leaves you open and unbalances the stance.

mistakes.name: Elbow flares (chicken wing)
mistakes.looks: The elbow lifts out to the side before a straight punch.
mistakes.fix: Elbow down and in, fist travels in a straight line.
mistakes.why: It telegraphs the punch and slows it.

mistakes.name: Arm-only punch
mistakes.looks: Feet flat and hips square while the arm reaches.
mistakes.fix: Turn the back heel out and rotate the hip with the cross.
mistakes.why: Little force reaches the fist without the legs and trunk.

mistakes.name: Over-reaching
mistakes.looks: Head and chest lean past the front knee.
mistakes.fix: Step closer; nose stays behind the front toes.
mistakes.why: You lose balance and power.

safety: Wrap your hands and wear bag gloves for bag work.
Start bag work gently; full-power punches on a bag stress wrists and knuckles.
Shoulder pain: shorter rounds and less snap on full extension.

variants.change: Heavy bag work: about 5.8 MET (15110). At 60, 120, 180 punches a minute: about 7.0, 8.5, 10.8 MET.
Kickboxing class: about 7.3 MET (15457).
Shadow boxing or a simulated round: about 9.3 MET (15125).
Pad work with a partner: oxygen use is close to sparring (sparring about 7.8 MET, 15120).
Band or cable from behind adds resistance to the push; slower, strength-focused.
Seated: only the arms and trunk turn; low-impact cardio.
Punches combined with another move; keep the guard rules.
Defence drill: forearms and gloves cover the head, no strike.

subtypes.name: Cross
subtypes.change: Rear hand straight punch: back heel turns out, hips and shoulders rotate fully.

subtypes.name: Hook
subtypes.change: Elbow lifts to shoulder height, arm bent about 90°, fist swings across on a horizontal arc as the trunk turns.

subtypes.name: Uppercut
subtypes.change: Dip the knees a little, then drive up: the bent arm rises on a vertical arc, palm facing you.

subtypes.name: Block and guard
subtypes.change: Hold a tight guard; forearms lift to cover the head, small knee dips.

easier: shadow boxing at an easy pace
harder: bag rounds at 120-180 punches a minute

metrics.label: Elbow out to the side on straight punches
Trunk turn on cross and hook

motion.basis: Default loop is a left jab (orthodox stance, left-side keys). Punch types and speeds from piorkowski2011 and whiting1988; trunk and lower-body contributions from dinu2020 and lowerlimb2025; phases from lenetsky2020. Joint angles are estimates. METs from the 2024 Compendium (herrmann2024) and bag VO2 data in arseneau2011.

families.name: Push-up
families.pattern: Horizontal push: the body stays one straight plank while the arms bend and straighten.
setup: Hands under your shoulders, a little wider, fingers forward.
Legs straight, feet together or hip width, on your toes.
Squeeze your glutes and brace: head, hips and heels in one line.

steps.text: Bend your elbows and lower your chest between your hands, elbows about 45° from your sides.
Stop with your chest a fist's height from the floor.
Push the floor away until your arms are straight, the body rising as one piece.
At the top, keep pushing so your shoulder blades spread around your ribs.

cues.cue: One straight line from head to heels.
cues.why: The abdominals give most of the stiffness that stops the lower back sagging.

cues.cue: Under your shoulders, fingers forward.
cues.why: Hands turned in or placed forward raise the load on the elbow.

cues.cue: About 45° from your sides, like an arrow, not a T.
cues.why: Arms above about 60° from the body limit how the shoulder blade can rotate and tilt.

cues.cue: Chest to a fist's height from the floor.
cues.why: Full range trains the whole movement; most test standards ask for a 90° elbow.

cues.cue: Push the floor away at the top, shoulders away from your ears.
cues.why: The push-up plus trains the serratus anterior and lowers upper-trapezius dominance.

families.breathing: Breathe in on the way down, out as you push up.

tempo.note: Lower for about 2 seconds, press in 1 to 2.

mistakes.name: Hips sag
mistakes.looks: The lower back arches and the hips drop below the line.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze your glutes, ribs down, body like a plank.
mistakes.why: The trunk muscles are not holding the spine; regress to an incline until you can hold the line.

mistakes.name: Elbows flare out
mistakes.looks: Upper arms point straight out to the sides, like a T.
mistakes.fix: Elbows about 45° from your sides.
mistakes.why: Wide elbows move the load onto the front of the shoulder.

mistakes.name: Head drops
mistakes.looks: The head hangs and the chin reaches for the floor first.
mistakes.fix: Look at the floor just ahead of your hands.
mistakes.why: It breaks the straight line and lets the shoulders round.

safety: Shoulder pain: keep elbows tucked below 60° and shorten the range.
Wrist pain: use fists or handles to keep the wrist straight; muscle activity stays the same.
Elbow pain: avoid turning the hands in and very narrow hands.

variants.change: Hands raised: about 41% body weight at 61 cm, 55% at 30 cm. Same arm keyframes, body tilted to the bench angle.
Knees down: about 49-62% body weight.
Feet raised: about 70-74% body weight; more upper chest and front delt.
Hands narrow: more triceps and more load on the elbow.
Hands wide: more chest, more load moves to the shoulder.

subtypes.name: Knee push-up
subtypes.change: Knees on the floor about 90°, hips straight, same arms.

subtypes.name: Incline push-up
subtypes.change: Whole body tilted up to the bench or wall, same arms.

subtypes.name: Pike push-up
subtypes.change: Hips high, trunk near vertical, head goes toward the floor: an overhead press pattern.

motion.basis: Elbow flexion, elbow flare and scapular angles from suprak2013 and lunden2010; trunk (90 = horizontal, here 75-86 because the hands are higher than the feet) and shoulder flexion estimated from the body line. Baked rig: Body/anatomy/rig_za.py.

families.name: Racket sports
families.pattern: Short bursts: split step, move to the ball, set the feet, swing from the legs and trunk through the arm, recover to the middle.
setup: Court shoes for your surface: they grip side-to-side and support the ankle.
Grip: hold the racket or paddle relaxed, like a handshake.
Warm up 5-10 minutes: easy rallies, side shuffles, a few lunges.
Squash and badminton: wear eye protection if your club advises it.

steps.text: Small hop as your opponent hits, landing on the balls of your feet, knees bent.

steps.phase: Turn and take the racket back
steps.text: Turn your shoulders and hips sideways as you move; racket goes back early.

steps.phase: Contact in front of the body
steps.text: Step in, push from the legs, rotate the trunk and meet the ball in front of you.
Let the swing finish over the opposite shoulder, then recover to the middle.

cues.cue: Split step every time your opponent hits.
cues.why: Skilled players time a split step with the opponent's contact so they can push off in any direction.

cues.cue: Swing from the legs and trunk; the arm finishes the chain.
cues.why: Most stroke energy comes from the legs and trunk; an arm-only swing loads the shoulder and elbow.

cues.cue: Backhand: wrist firm and slightly back at contact, not bending forward.
cues.why: Novices who hit with a flexing wrist load the forearm extensors, the classic route to tennis elbow.

cues.cue: Lunge with the knee over the toes, heel first, then push straight back.
cues.why: The lead knee and ankle take large braking forces in badminton and squash lunges.

cues.cue: Hit in front of your body, not beside or behind it.
cues.why: Late contact forces the arm and wrist to rescue the shot.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you hit; recover your breath between points.

tempo.note: Rallies last a few seconds with short rests; one loop = one shot from ready to recovery.

mistakes.name: Flat-footed
mistakes.looks: Standing tall on the heels, no split step, reaching for the ball.
mistakes.fix: Knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet, split step on the opponent's hit.
mistakes.why: You arrive late and stretch with the arm.

mistakes.name: Wrist-led backhand
mistakes.looks: The wrist bends forward at contact and the elbow leads.
mistakes.fix: Lead with the shoulder, wrist firm; try a two-handed backhand.
mistakes.why: Repeated forearm extensor strain causes tennis elbow.

mistakes.name: Knee caves in the lunge
mistakes.looks: The front knee drops inward or far past the toes.
mistakes.fix: Point the foot to the ball and keep the knee in line with it.
mistakes.why: It twists the knee under high braking load.

mistakes.name: Arm-only swing
mistakes.looks: Feet and shoulders stay facing the net while the arm swings.
mistakes.fix: Turn sideways early and rotate through the shot.
mistakes.why: Shoulder and elbow do the work the legs and trunk should do.

safety: Pickleball: many injuries are falls, sprains and strains, mostly in older players; do not backpedal for lobs, turn and move sideways.
Sudden calf or heel pain on a push-off (Achilles): stop at once.
Elbow pain on the outside: check grip size, strings and backhand technique.
Squash: stay out of your opponent's swing; let a point go rather than run into them.

variants.change: Tennis, general, moderate. MET 6.8 (Compendium 15675).
Tennis, singles. MET 8.0 (Compendium 15690).
Tennis, doubles. MET 4.5 (Compendium 15685).
Tennis, general, competitive. MET 8.0 (Compendium 15676).
Tennis, hitting balls, non-game. MET 5.0 (Compendium 15695).
No pickleball code in the 2024 Compendium; closest is paddleball, casual (competitive 10.0, code 15490). MET 6.0 (Compendium 15500).
Badminton, social singles and doubles. MET 5.5 (Compendium 15030).
Badminton, competitive (match play 9.0, code 15025). MET 7.0 (Compendium 15020).
Squash, general. MET 7.3 (Compendium 15652).
Squash (Taylor code). MET 12.0 (Compendium 15650).
Racquetball, general (competitive 10.0, code 15520). MET 7.0 (Compendium 15530).
Table tennis. MET 4.0 (Compendium 15660).

subtypes.name: Tennis
subtypes.change: Forehand groundstroke shown: split step, unit turn, contact in front at waist height, finish over the shoulder.

keyframes.phase: Turn and take the racket back
Contact in front of the body

subtypes.name: Pickleball
subtypes.change: Low ready stance at the kitchen line, paddle in front; short, shoulder-led dinks and blocks with little wrist.

subtypes.name: Badminton
subtypes.change: Forward lunge to the net shown: long reach with the racket leg, heel first, racket up in front, push back to base.

keyframes.phase: Lunge: right foot reaches, heel first
Hit with the racket in front

subtypes.name: Squash
subtypes.change: Lunge to the front corner shown: racket up early, short compact swing, back to the T after each shot.

keyframes.phase: Turn and take the racket back
Contact in front of the body

motion.basis: Movement pattern from dines2015 (kinetic chain), filipcic2017 (split step) and kuntze2010 (lunges). All joint angles are our estimates for a right-handed player; the rig has no trunk axial-rotation key, so shoulder turn is a readout.

families.name: Rear delt fly
families.pattern: Horizontal abduction: with the elbows nearly straight, the arms sweep out to the sides and back while the shoulder blades squeeze together.
setup: Hold light dumbbells, hinge at the hips until your chest is nearly parallel to the floor.
Back flat, knees soft, neck long.
Let the arms hang under your shoulders, palms facing each other, elbows slightly bent.

steps.text: Arms hang straight down under your chest.
Sweep the arms out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with the back of the hands.
Stop with the arms level with your back, shoulder blades pulled together.
Lower slowly along the same arc.

cues.cue: Soft, fixed elbow bend; arms move as one long lever.
cues.why: Keeping the elbow still makes it a single-joint shoulder move; the reverse fly works the rear delt more than rows or pulldowns.

cues.cue: Arms out to the sides at shoulder line, not back toward the hips.
cues.why: Horizontal abduction near 90-100° of arm raise gives the highest rear delt and middle trapezius activity.

cues.cue: Finish by squeezing the shoulder blades together, shoulders away from your ears.
cues.why: Prone horizontal abduction with external rotation is one of the best exercises for mid and lower trapezius with low upper-trap use.

cues.cue: Thumbs up or forward for the cuff; palms down to bias the rear delt.
cues.why: Palm-up grips raised infraspinatus and lower trapezius; palm-down raised rear delt and upper trapezius.

cues.cue: Flat back, chest still.
cues.why: Bobbing the trunk throws the weight and loads the lower back.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you raise, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Raise in 1 second, pause, lower in 2.

mistakes.name: Turns into a row
mistakes.looks: The elbows bend a lot and drive back toward the hips.
mistakes.fix: Lighter weights; keep the elbows nearly straight and move the arms out, not back.
mistakes.why: Bending the elbows shortens the lever and shifts work to the lats and arms.

mistakes.name: Shrugging
mistakes.looks: Shoulders lift toward the ears and the neck tenses.
mistakes.fix: Shoulders down first, then sweep.
mistakes.why: Upper trapezius takes over; the aim is mid trapezius and rear delt.

mistakes.name: Swinging the trunk
mistakes.looks: The chest rises with each rep to throw the weights up.
mistakes.fix: Support your chest on an incline bench or use less weight.
mistakes.why: Momentum replaces the rear-shoulder work.

safety: Low-back pain: do the fly chest-down on an incline bench or seated at a reverse fly machine.
Shoulder pain: lower the arm line toward 45-70° from the body.

variants.change: Rear-delt row: elbows bend about 90° and pull wide at shoulder height; heavier than the fly.
Arms move diagonally at 45°: between a fly and a high row.
One arm at a time, free hand on a bench.
Palms forward or up: more infraspinatus and lower trapezius.
Cable: tension stays on even when the arms hang.

subtypes.name: Rear-delt row
subtypes.match: delt row|rear delt row|delt horizontal row
subtypes.change: Elbows bend to about 90° and pull out wide at shoulder height; hands finish beside the chest.

subtypes.name: Prone Y, T and incline raise
subtypes.change: Lying face down on a bench or floor; T: arms out to the sides, thumbs up. Y: arms raised overhead at about 120-135° in line with the lower trapezius.

subtypes.name: Reverse fly machine and standing cable
subtypes.match: lever|machine|seated reverse fly|peck|standing.*reverse fly|cross-over|cable standing|cable 45|cable one arm reverse|seated rear lateral|pull apart|pullapart|bed sheet|towel
subtypes.change: Seated or standing tall, arms forward at shoulder height; sweep the arms out to the sides.

metrics.label: Arm height
metrics.good: 75-95 at the top (level with the back)

motion.basis: Top position matches the prone horizontal abduction tested in reinold2004, ekstrom2003 and cools2007 (arm near 90-100°); hand effects from fukunaga2022. Scapular retraction path and upward rotation (about 15-20° at 85-95° of arm raise) estimated from ludewig2009 rhythm. Trunk angle and elbow bend are coaching convention.

families.name: Rowing machine
families.pattern: Seated full-body pull: legs push, the body swings back from the hips, then the arms pull, and the return goes in reverse order.
setup: Strap your feet so the strap crosses the widest part of the foot.
Damper at 3-5: higher feels heavier but is not a better workout.
Hold the handle with a loose overhand grip, wrists flat.

steps.text: At the front: shins near vertical, arms long, body tipped forward from the hips (about 1 o'clock).
Push the footplate away with your legs. Arms stay straight and the back keeps its angle.
Legs flat, lean back to about 11 o'clock, pull the handle to your lower ribs.
Straighten your arms first, then tip your body forward from the hips.
Once the handle passes your knees, bend them and slide forward slowly to the catch.

cues.cue: Legs, body, arms. Then arms, body, legs.
cues.why: The legs make most of the power; arms pulling early lose it and the handle path breaks.

cues.cue: Hinge at the hips, chest proud, do not slump at the catch.
cues.why: Lumbar flexion at the catch is about 15° in elite rowers and it grows with fatigue, which is linked to back pain.

cues.cue: Drive fast, return slow: about 1 count out, 2 counts back.
cues.why: Rushing the slide makes you arrive at the catch in a poor position and wastes energy.

cues.cue: Stop the slide when the shins are vertical.
cues.why: Going further cramps the hips and lets the back round.

cues.cue: Shoulders low, elbows draw back past the ribs.
cues.why: Shrugging tires the neck and adds nothing to the stroke.

families.breathing: Out on the drive, in on the recovery. At high rates add a quick breath at the finish.

tempo.note: Drive about 1/3 of the stroke, recovery 2/3. Steady rowing 18-24 strokes a minute.

mistakes.name: Arms bend early
mistakes.looks: The elbows bend before the legs are flat.
mistakes.fix: Arms long like ropes until the handle passes your knees.
mistakes.why: The small arm muscles take the load the legs should carry.

mistakes.name: Back rounds at the catch
mistakes.looks: The lower back slumps and the head drops as you reach forward.
mistakes.fix: Tip forward from the hips with a long spine; reach less if you must.
mistakes.why: Rounding grows as you tire and puts the load on the lower back.

mistakes.name: Rushed slide
mistakes.looks: You shoot back up the slide as fast as you drove.
mistakes.fix: Count 1 on the drive, 1-2 on the way back.
mistakes.why: It raises effort, shortens the stroke and makes the next catch weak.

mistakes.name: Leaning too far back
mistakes.looks: Shoulders well behind the hips at the finish.
mistakes.fix: Stop at 11 o'clock, about 30° back.
mistakes.why: Extra lean adds little length and strains the back and abs.

safety: Lower-back pain: shorten the reach at the catch and keep the damper low.
Rib pain in heavy training can be a stress fracture; stop and get it checked.

variants.change: Under 100 W: about 5.0 MET (02071).
About 7.5 MET (02072).
About 11.0 MET (02073).
200 W or more: about 14.0 MET (02074).

metrics.label: Body angle
metrics.good: 20 to 30 forward at catch, 20 to 35 back at finish

motion.basis: Lumbar flexion at the catch (about 15°) from fohanno2015; the clock-face trunk angles (±25-30°) and 1:2 rhythm are Concept2 coaching convention. Hip, knee, ankle and arm angles are estimates from the seat and handle geometry.

families.name: Row
families.pattern: Horizontal pull: the hands pull a load toward the torso while the shoulder blades squeeze back, the trunk held still.
setup: Bar over the middle of your feet, feet hip width, knees soft.
Hinge at the hips until your chest leans well forward, back flat, neck long.
Let your arms hang straight under your shoulders, grip just wider than shoulder width.

steps.text: Start with arms long and shoulder blades slightly spread, back flat.
Squeeze your shoulder blades back first, then drive your elbows back toward your hips.
Touch the bar to your lower ribs or belly, chest still, and hold for a moment.
Straighten your arms under control and let the shoulder blades glide forward again.

cues.cue: Flat back, hips hinged, trunk does not move.
cues.why: The bent-over row gives the highest lower-back load of common rows; a still, braced trunk keeps that load safe.

cues.cue: Start each pull by squeezing your shoulder blades together.
cues.why: Rowing is one of the core exercises for the mid trapezius and rhomboids, which pull the shoulder blades back.

cues.cue: Drive your elbows back toward your hips, not your hands up.
cues.why: Thinking about the back, not the arms, raises lat activity and lowers rear-delt takeover.

cues.cue: Shoulders down, away from your ears.
cues.why: Shrugging shifts work to the upper trapezius instead of the mid and lower trapezius.

cues.cue: Arms fully long at the bottom, bar to your belly at the top.
cues.why: Letting the shoulder blades move through their range trains both the pull and the reach; fixing them only changes where the muscles work.

families.breathing: Breathe in and brace before you pull, breathe out as you lower or at the top.

tempo.note: Pull in about 1 second, hold the squeeze, lower in 2.

mistakes.name: Back rounds
mistakes.looks: The lower back curves and the chest drops toward the floor as you pull.
mistakes.fix: Brace, push your hips back and keep your chest proud; use less weight.
mistakes.why: A flexed lower spine under a hanging load raises spine compression; the bent-over row already has the highest load of the rows tested.

mistakes.name: Body heaves
mistakes.looks: The trunk swings up with each rep to throw the bar back.
mistakes.fix: Keep your chest angle fixed; if you need to swing, the weight is too heavy.
mistakes.why: Momentum moves the work from the back to the hips and loads the lower back with each jerk.

mistakes.name: Shoulders shrug
mistakes.looks: Shoulders ride up toward the ears at the top instead of squeezing back.
mistakes.fix: Pull your shoulder blades back and down, elbows toward your hips.
mistakes.why: Upper-trapezius dominance is the imbalance scapular training aims to avoid.

mistakes.name: Arms-only pull
mistakes.looks: The elbows bend but the shoulder blades never move; the bar stops short of the body.
mistakes.fix: Lead with your shoulder blades, then finish with the arms.
mistakes.why: Without scapular retraction the mid trapezius and rhomboids do little; seated rows give their highest activity when the blades move.

safety: Low-back pain: use a chest-supported or inverted row; the inverted row had the lowest spine load.
Shoulder pain: use a neutral grip and keep the elbows below shoulder height.
One-arm rows twist the trunk: start light if your back is sensitive.

variants.change: Palms up: elbows stay closer to the body, more biceps and lower lats.
Wide grip: elbows flare toward 60-75°, more rear delt and upper back.
Trunk near horizontal (about 80-90°), bar returns to the floor each rep.
One arm: free hand on a bench; the trunk must resist twisting, more oblique activity.
Palms facing: forearm 0, elbows close to the sides.
Pull line higher, toward the chest: elbows near 70-90° from the body, more rear delt and mid traps.
Band: load rises toward the end of the pull; control the return.

subtypes.name: Chest-supported row
subtypes.match: chest support|incline.*row|prone.*row|lying.*row|seal row|head supported|on rack|lying t bar|lying banded
subtypes.change: Chest on an incline bench or pad, legs and back passive; same arm and shoulder-blade path as the bent-over row.

subtypes.name: Inverted row
subtypes.match: inverted|suspen|suspended|ring.*row|towel row|bodyweight.*row|doorway|bed sheet|under table|between.*chairs|pulse row|parallel bars
subtypes.change: Hang under a bar or straps, body straight and face up, heels on the floor; pull the chest to the hands.

subtypes.name: Renegade row
subtypes.change: High plank on two dumbbells, feet wide; row one dumbbell while the hips stay square to the floor.

subtypes.name: Shoulder-blade squeeze
subtypes.change: Arms stay mostly still; only the shoulder blades pull back and glide forward. Small range, slow.

subtypes.name: Seated row
subtypes.match: seated|sitting|low row|high row|upper row|elevated row|standing.*row|kneeling|floor.*row|kayak|split stance|push pull|lever (alternating|narrow|one arm seated|row|seated|unilateral|low|one arm low|pronated|reverse grip high|reverse grip vertical|one arm lateral)
subtypes.change: Sitting tall with feet braced, trunk upright; arms reach forward and pull to the belly.

motion.basis: Shoulder-blade path (protraction at the reach, full retraction at the squeeze) from moseley1992, lehman2004 and padovan2025; upward rotation values estimated from humeral elevation using scapulohumeral rhythm data (ludewig2009). Trunk and hip angles for the bent-over row are coaching convention (nsca2016); fenwick2009 measured lumbar flexion only. Arm angles estimated.

families.name: Running
families.pattern: Gait with a flight phase: you land under your body, spring off one foot and float before the other foot lands.
setup: Shoes that feel comfortable; no need to match a 'foot type'.
Start with 5-10 minutes of easy jogging or brisk walking.
Stand tall, eyes ahead about 20-30 m, shoulders loose.

steps.text: Land with your foot close under your hips, knee softly bent.
Let the knee and ankle bend a little to soak up the landing.
Push the ground back and away; the hip extends behind you.
Float, then land the other foot under you, arms swinging opposite.
Same soft load on the left; right heel comes up toward your seat.
Push off left while the right knee swings forward, not up.

cues.cue: Land under you, not out in front.
cues.why: Landing with the foot and shin far ahead of the hips raises braking force and the load at the hip and knee.

cues.cue: Quick, light steps: if you overstride, add 5-10% steps per minute.
cues.why: A 5-10% higher step rate at the same speed shortens the stride and lowers knee and hip loading.

cues.cue: Tall, with a slight lean from the ankles, not the waist.
cues.why: Trunk lean changes how the hip and knee share the work; a big waist bend loads the hip and back.

cues.cue: Run forward, not up: keep the bounce small.
cues.why: Less vertical oscillation and less braking go with better running economy.

cues.cue: Elbows about 90°, hands swing by your hips, not across your chest.
cues.why: Arm swing balances the rotation of the legs; crossing arms twist the trunk.

cues.cue: Most runs easy: you can still talk in full sentences.
cues.why: Build weekly time slowly; sudden jumps in load are a common route to running injury.

families.breathing: Breathe through mouth and nose in an even rhythm; on easy runs you should be able to talk.

tempo.note: One loop = two steps. Easy running is usually 155-175 steps per minute; faster running raises it.

mistakes.name: Overstriding
mistakes.looks: The foot lands far ahead of the body with a nearly straight knee and a hard heel.
mistakes.fix: Shorter, quicker steps; land with your foot under your knee.
mistakes.why: It works like a brake each step and raises loading at the hip and knee.

mistakes.name: Bent at the waist
mistakes.looks: Hips sit back and the chest folds forward.
mistakes.fix: Stand tall, hips under you, lean from the ankles.
mistakes.why: Folding at the hips shortens hip extension and loads the back.

mistakes.name: Too much bounce
mistakes.looks: The head rises and drops a lot each step.
mistakes.fix: Think 'forward', quicker steps, push back not up.
mistakes.why: Energy spent going up is wasted and each landing is harder.

mistakes.name: Arms swing across
mistakes.looks: Hands cross the middle of the chest and the shoulders twist.
mistakes.fix: Swing the hands forward and back past your hips.
mistakes.why: It adds trunk rotation that the legs must then correct.

safety: New runners: mix running and walking and add no more than about 10% time per week.
Sharp pain in a bone (shin, foot) that gets worse with each run: stop and get it checked.
Knee pain at the front: try a 5-10% higher step rate and shorter runs.
Heat: drink, slow down and stop if dizzy.

variants.change: Jogging, general, self-selected pace. MET 7.5 (Compendium 12020).
Running 5.0-5.2 mph (12 min/mile, 7:27 min/km). MET 8.5 (Compendium 12030).
Running 6.0-6.3 mph (10 min/mile, 6:13 min/km). MET 9.3 (Compendium 12050).
Running 7 mph (8.5 min/mile). MET 11.0 (Compendium 12070).
Running 8 mph (7.5 min/mile). MET 12.0 (Compendium 12090).
Running 9 mph (6.5 min/mile). MET 13.0 (Compendium 12110).
Running 10 mph (6 min/mile). MET 14.8 (Compendium 12120).
Cross-country / trail running. MET 9.3 (Compendium 12140).
Hilly terrain, about 100 m up and down. MET 16.0 (Compendium 12350).
Jogging in place. MET 4.8 (Compendium 12025).
Running 5.0-5.9 mph with a 1-3 kg backpack. MET 8.5 (Compendium 12508).
Skipping, 5.5-6.0 mph. MET 11.5 (Compendium 12600).
Marathon racing. MET 13.3 (Compendium 12200).
Hard repeats: 12-14 mph efforts are 18.5-23.0 MET while moving (12132-12135); the session average is lower because of rests. MET 18.5 (Compendium 12132).
Running backwards: shorter steps, land on the forefoot, look over your shoulder; use a flat, clear path.

subtypes.name: Sprint intervals
subtypes.change: Big arm drive, high knee recovery, foot strikes under the hips on the forefoot; trunk upright at top speed.

subtypes.name: Jog in place
subtypes.change: No travel: land on the balls of the feet, knees lift in front, heels may touch lightly.

subtypes.name: Trail run
subtypes.change: Shorter steps, more knee bend, eyes 3-5 m ahead; on steep climbs power-hike; on descents lean slightly forward, quick light steps.

subtypes.name: Road run
subtypes.change: Default gait on a flat, firm surface.

motion.basis: Sagittal joint ranges for jogging from novacheck1998 (knee about 20° at contact, 40-45° in stance, about 100° in swing; hip about 30° flexed at contact to 10-15° extended at toe-off). Timing at 166 steps/min and arm angles are our estimates. Trunk lean from folland2017 range.

families.name: Shoulder rotation
families.pattern: Rotation of the upper arm: with the elbow bent about 90° and the upper arm still, the forearm swings out (external rotation) or in (internal rotation) like a door on a hinge.
setup: Stand side-on to a band or cable set at elbow height.
Elbow bent 90°, upper arm by your side; a small rolled towel between elbow and ribs helps.
Stand tall, shoulder blade gently back and down.

steps.text: Start with the hand in front of your belly.
Turn the forearm out, away from your body, keeping the elbow at your side.
Stop when the forearm points forward-out at about 45-60°, or before your shoulder blade or trunk moves.
Let the hand come back in slowly.

cues.cue: Keep the elbow touching your side or the towel.
cues.why: If the elbow drifts, the deltoid joins in and the rotator cuff does less.

cues.cue: For the most cuff work, lie on your side with the top arm doing the rotation.
cues.why: Side-lying external rotation gave the highest infraspinatus (62% MVIC) and teres minor (67%) activity.

cues.cue: Shoulder blade back and down, not pinched hard; no shrug.
cues.why: Side-lying external rotation is one of the exercises with the best trapezius balance (low upper trap).

cues.cue: Rotate the arm, not your body.
cues.why: Turning the trunk fakes range and takes load off the cuff.

cues.cue: Light load, slow, many reps.
cues.why: The cuff's main job is to steady and centre the ball of the shoulder; it does not need heavy loads to work.

families.breathing: Breathe normally; out as you rotate out.

tempo.note: Rotate out in about 2 seconds, hold, return in 3.

mistakes.name: Elbow lifts away
mistakes.looks: The elbow swings out from the side as the hand rotates.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze a towel between your elbow and ribs.
mistakes.why: Abducting the arm brings in the deltoid and supraspinatus instead of the external rotators.

mistakes.name: Trunk turns
mistakes.looks: The chest rotates away to move the band further.
mistakes.fix: Face forward; stop the rotation where your body would start to turn.
mistakes.why: The range comes from the spine, not the shoulder.

mistakes.name: Shoulder hikes or rolls forward
mistakes.looks: The shoulder rises or rolls forward as the arm turns.
mistakes.fix: Lighter band; shoulder blade gently back and down first.
mistakes.why: Upper-trapezius overuse and a tipped shoulder blade reduce the space for the cuff.

safety: After shoulder surgery or dislocation, follow your clinician's range limits; 90/90 rotation stresses the front of the shoulder.
Stop if you feel sharp pain or catching; a mild muscle burn is normal.
Rotation tests and mobility drills are for checking range, not for loading.

variants.change: Internal rotation: band from the outside, hand moves in toward the belly; works subscapularis and chest.
Isometric: press into a wall or towel without moving; good early in rehab.
Arm 30-45° out to the side and slightly forward (scapular plane): a comfortable middle position.
Rotation then press: rotate out at 90/90, then press the hand overhead.
A stick or the other hand moves the arm: mobility or a range test, not a strength set.

subtypes.name: Side-lying external rotation
subtypes.match: side lying|lying.*external|bench supported|lying shoulder|on a bench
subtypes.change: Lie on your side, top elbow bent 90° and resting on the ribs, towel under it; lift the weight by rotating the forearm up. The whole body is rolled 90° onto its side.

subtypes.name: 90/90 rotation
subtypes.change: Upper arm out to the side at shoulder height, elbow bent 90°; the forearm rotates from pointing forward up to vertical (and down for internal rotation).

subtypes.name: Internal rotation
subtypes.change: Band or cable from the outside; the hand moves from out to the side in toward the belly, elbow by the side.

easier: isometric external rotation against a wall

motion.basis: Exercise positions (0° with towel, side-lying, 90° abduction, scapular plane) from reinold2004; scapular balance from cools2007. Rotation end ranges are typical active ranges set by us (estimate); scapular retraction during external rotation is small and estimated; upward rotation at 90° abduction (about 20-25°) from ludewig2009 rhythm.

families.name: Shrug
families.pattern: Shoulder blade elevation: arms hang straight while the shoulders lift straight up toward the ears and lower.
setup: Stand tall, weights at your sides or bar in front of the thighs.
Arms straight and relaxed, grip just outside the hips.
Chin level, neck long, brace your trunk.

steps.text: Lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Hold for a second at the top.
Lower slowly until the shoulders are fully down and stretched.

cues.cue: Straight up and straight down, no rolling.
cues.why: The upper trap and levator lift the shoulder blade; rolling adds no work and strains the shoulder.

cues.cue: Arms stay straight, do not bend the elbows.
cues.why: Bending the elbows turns it into a row or curl.

cues.cue: Try arms slightly out to the sides (about 30°).
cues.why: Shrugging with the arms abducted 30° raised upper, middle and lower trapezius and serratus activity versus arms at the sides.

cues.cue: Chin level, do not push the head forward.
cues.why: A jutting head loads the neck instead of the traps.

cues.cue: Full range: stretch at the bottom, ears at the top.
cues.why: The shrug is the highest upper-trapezius exercise when done through full range.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you lift, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Lift in 1 s, hold 1 s, lower in 2 s.

mistakes.name: Rolling the shoulders
mistakes.looks: Shoulders circle forward or back at the top.
mistakes.fix: Straight up and down only.
mistakes.why: It adds no muscle work and can irritate the shoulder.

mistakes.name: Head pokes forward
mistakes.looks: The chin juts out as you lift.
mistakes.fix: Keep your chin tucked and level.
mistakes.why: Loads the neck joints and turns the move into a neck strain.

mistakes.name: Elbows bend
mistakes.looks: Elbows bend and the weight is pulled up with the arms.
mistakes.fix: Relax the arms, use straps if grip fails.
mistakes.why: The biceps and deltoids help and the traps do less.

mistakes.name: Tiny range
mistakes.looks: Shoulders barely move with a very heavy load.
mistakes.fix: Use a weight you can lift to your ears.
mistakes.why: The trap gets most of its work through full elevation.

safety: Neck pain: lighter weight, slower reps, chin level.
Heavy loads: use straps and keep the back straight when picking up the weight.

variants.change: Bar behind the thighs: shoulders slightly back, a bit more mid-trap.
On a bench: no leg help, different angle of pull.
Trap bar: handles at your sides, neutral grip.
Arms wider: more upward rotation; more lower trapezius and serratus.
Power shrug: small hip and knee dip then a fast shrug, like the top of a clean.
Gripless machine: pads on the shoulders, grip does not limit you.
One side: do not lean away.

subtypes.name: Overhead shrug
subtypes.change: Arms locked overhead (or upside down on the hands): push up tall to lift the shoulders toward the ears, then let them sink.

subtypes.name: Scapular retraction
subtypes.change: Seated or lying, arms straight in front: pull the shoulder blades together, then let them spread; arms do not bend.

motion.basis: Muscle roles from ekstrom2003 (shrug gives the highest upper-trapezius activity) and pizzari2014 (shrug at 30° abduction recruits the upward rotators). Scapular elevation values are on the app's -1..+1 scale and are estimates; a small upward rotation with elevation is an estimate. No kinematic study of the loaded shrug was found.

families.name: Side bend
families.pattern: Lateral flexion: the trunk bends sideways and back up against a load, or curls sideways on the floor (side crunch, heel touches). Windmills add a hip hinge.
setup: Stand tall, feet hip width, a dumbbell in one hand at your side.
Other hand on your hip or behind your head.
Knees soft, hips square.

steps.text: Bend sideways toward the weight, sliding it down the outside of your thigh.
Stop at a comfortable stretch, no twisting or leaning forward.
Pull yourself back to upright with the opposite side, then a little past.

cues.cue: Bend straight sideways, like between two panes of glass.
cues.why: Pure side bending targets the obliques and quadratus lumborum; mixing in twist or forward bend changes the load.

cues.cue: Moderate range, smooth and controlled.
cues.why: End-range lateral bending raises the load on spine tissues.

cues.cue: One weight only; the other hand is free.
cues.why: Weights in both hands cancel each other out.

cues.cue: Hips stay still; the movement is above the belt.
cues.why: Shifting the hips sideways hides the trunk bend.

families.breathing: Breathe in as you bend, out as you come up.

tempo.note: About 2 s down and 2 s up.

mistakes.name: Twisting or leaning forward
mistakes.looks: The shoulders rotate or the chest drops forward as you bend.
mistakes.fix: Keep your chest facing forward.
mistakes.why: It turns the bend into a loaded twist or flexion.

mistakes.name: Hips slide sideways
mistakes.looks: The hips push out away from the weight while the trunk stays straight.
mistakes.fix: Keep the hips over the feet.
mistakes.why: The trunk barely bends.

mistakes.name: Jerking up
mistakes.looks: Fast bounce out of the bottom.
mistakes.fix: Slow down; pause briefly at the bottom.
mistakes.why: Momentum loads the spine at end range.

safety: Low back pain: try a side plank first; it trains the same muscles with less spine load.
Windmills: only with good hip hinge and shoulder mobility; keep the arm vertical and eyes on the weight.

variants.change: Side-lying on a 45 degree bench: the trunk lowers and lifts sideways against gravity.
Lying on the floor: a small sideways curl of the ribs toward the hip.
Weight overhead, hips push sideways and hinge down: also a hip-hinge and shoulder-stability drill.
Arm overhead: longer lever, harder.
Seated side crunch machine.

subtypes.name: Side crunch and heel touches
subtypes.change: Lying on your back with knees bent (heel touches) or on your side; reach one hand toward the same-side heel with a small sideways curl.

subtypes.name: Windmill
subtypes.change: Weight locked overhead in the right hand, feet angled left; push the hips right and hinge down until the left hand reaches the left foot.

motion.basis: Default is the standing dumbbell side bend, weight in the right hand. The convention has no trunk side-bend key: the rig needs one (about 25-30 degrees at the bottom, estimate); here only the arms, scapula and hips show the change. All angles estimated.

families.name: Side plank
families.pattern: Anti-lateral-flexion hold: on one forearm and the side of the feet, the body stays straight while the bottom-side trunk muscles stop the hips dropping.
setup: Lie on your side, elbow under your shoulder, forearm flat.
Legs straight, top foot in front of or on top of the bottom foot.
Top hand on your hip or reaching up.

steps.text: Lift your hips until your body is one straight line from head to feet, and hold. Switch sides.

cues.cue: Hips high: one straight line from head to feet.
cues.why: The side bridge challenges quadratus lumborum and the obliques with low spine load.

cues.cue: Elbow right under the shoulder.
cues.why: A stacked arm keeps the shoulder stable and comfortable.

cues.cue: Push the hips slightly forward, glutes squeezed.
cues.why: Hips drifting back turn it into a pike; glute med works hard in this hold.

cues.cue: Chest faces forward, don't roll toward the floor.
cues.why: Rolling shifts load off the side muscles.

families.breathing: Breathe steadily; keep a light brace.

tempo.note: Hold 10-30 s each side. In healthy adults side hold time was about 99% of the flexor test in men and 79% in women.

mistakes.name: Hips sag
mistakes.looks: The hips sink toward the floor and the body bends sideways.
mistakes.fix: Lift the bottom hip up to the line.
mistakes.why: The side muscles have let go.

mistakes.name: Hips push back
mistakes.looks: The hips sit back behind the shoulders and feet.
mistakes.fix: Push your hips forward, glutes on.
mistakes.why: Hip flexion shortens the lever and takes load off the obliques.

mistakes.name: Sinking into the shoulder
mistakes.looks: The bottom shoulder rises toward the ear.
mistakes.fix: Push the floor away with the forearm.
mistakes.why: Hanging on the shoulder strains it.

safety: Shoulder pain: start with a bent-knee side plank or with the hand on a bench.
Keep both sides balanced; big side-to-side differences are worth working on.

variants.change: Knees bent, weight on the bottom knee: easier.
Forearm on a bench: easier.
On the hand with a straight arm: higher, more shoulder work.
Top leg lifts: a very high gluteus medius exercise.
Top foot on a bench, bottom leg free (Copenhagen): heavy adductor work.
Load in the top hand or a row: adds rotation demand.
Moving the top elbow or arm while holding the hips up.

subtypes.name: Bent-knee side plank
subtypes.change: Knees bent about 90 degrees; hips lift from the knee.

subtypes.name: Side plank with leg lift
subtypes.change: Top leg lifts about 30 degrees and lowers while the hips stay high.

motion.basis: Body lies on its right side (rig rolls the whole body 90 degrees); joint angles are relative to the body. Hip sag is shown as bottom-hip adduction because the convention has no trunk side-bend key. Angles are estimates; hold-time ratios from mcgill1999.

families.name: Single-leg Romanian deadlift
families.pattern: One-leg hip hinge: the trunk tips forward and the free leg swings back as one line while the standing hip bends.
setup: Stand on one foot, knee soft, weight over the middle of the foot.
Hold the weight in the hand opposite the standing leg, arm long.
Hips level and facing the floor, like headlights pointing down.

steps.text: Push your hips back and tip forward; the free leg rises behind you in line with your back.
Stop when your trunk is near level or your back starts to round.
Drive the standing heel into the floor and bring the hips through to stand tall.

cues.cue: Keep both hip bones level, pointing at the floor.
cues.why: Resisting the hip opening is what loads the gluteus medius; it is among the top exercises for it.

cues.cue: Head to back heel in one straight line.
cues.why: The leg moving with the trunk keeps the movement at the standing hip and the spine still.

cues.cue: Soft knee, fixed angle; do not squat down.
cues.why: The work stays on the hip extensors and hamstrings.

cues.cue: Weight in the hand opposite the standing leg.
cues.why: Contralateral loading raised glute and back activity in a loaded single-leg RDL.

cues.cue: Grip the floor with the whole foot.
cues.why: Balance limits the load; a stable foot lets the hip do the work.

families.breathing: Breathe in as you hinge down, out as you stand up.

tempo.note: Slow down; balance is easier with control.

mistakes.name: Hips open up
mistakes.looks: The free-leg hip rotates up toward the ceiling and the toes turn out.
mistakes.fix: Point the back toes at the floor; keep hips level.
mistakes.why: It turns the hinge into a twist and takes load off the glutes.

mistakes.name: Back rounds
mistakes.looks: You reach the weight to the floor by curling the spine.
mistakes.fix: Stop higher; reach with the hips, not the hands.
mistakes.why: Range should come from the hip, not the lower back.

mistakes.name: Standing knee bends deep
mistakes.looks: The standing knee bends a lot and the hips drop instead of going back.
mistakes.fix: Lock in a soft knee and push the hips back.
mistakes.why: It turns the hinge into a squat and moves the work to the quads.

safety: Use a wall, rack or kickstand stance until balance is steady.
Hamstring strain history: keep the range short and build slowly.

variants.change: Back toes stay on the floor for balance; most weight on the front leg.
Support or a guided bar: easier balance, more load possible.
At the top, drive the free knee up to hip height.
Pass the weight hand to hand at the top or under the leg.
Weight on the same side as the standing leg: less balance and glute medius challenge.
Hold the bottom position for time.

harder: single-leg RDL on an unstable surface

subtypes.name: Kickstand RDL
subtypes.change: Back foot stays down on its toes, a half step behind.

subtypes.name: Single-leg RDL with knee drive
subtypes.change: Ends each rep with the free knee driven up to hip height.

motion.basis: Right leg stands; left (L keys) is the free leg. No study in the set reports full joint angles; values are estimates from the hinge geometry (back leg in line with trunk, so hipFlexL about 0 to -5). Muscle findings from diamant2021, mo2023 and collings2023.

families.name: Single-leg squat
families.pattern: One-leg squat: the standing hip, knee and ankle bend while the free leg is held off the floor.
setup: Stand on one leg, foot straight ahead, the other foot just off the floor in front.
Arms forward for balance, or hold a support.
Pick a box or bench behind you to sit to until you have the full range.

steps.text: Stand tall on one leg, hips level.
Sit back and down, knee over your middle toes, free leg reaching forward.
Go as low as you can control, from a 60° knee bend up to a full pistol.
Drive through your whole foot back to standing without leaning to the side.

cues.cue: Knee stays over your middle toes.
cues.why: Poor single-leg squatters showed weaker, later-firing hip abductors and more knee drift inward.

cues.cue: Hips level: do not let the free side drop.
cues.why: A dropping pelvis is the other sign of weak glute medius; the single-leg squat trains it well.

cues.cue: Lean forward as a unit, chest over the knee.
cues.why: A forward lean balances the free leg and brings the glutes into the lift.

cues.cue: Heel down, weight over the middle of the foot.
cues.why: Deep single-leg squats need about 35-40° of ankle bend; raise the heel slightly if you lack it.

cues.cue: Use a box and lower it over time.
cues.why: Depth you can control matters more than depth.

families.breathing: Breathe in on the way down, out as you stand.

tempo.note: Lower slowly, about 3 seconds; control is the point.

mistakes.name: Knee caves in
mistakes.looks: The knee falls inside the big toe as you go down.
mistakes.fix: Push the knee out over your little toe; shorten the range.
mistakes.why: Weak or late hip abductors; the main failure in the single-leg squat test.

mistakes.name: Hip drops
mistakes.looks: The free-leg side of the pelvis sinks and the trunk leans over the standing leg.
mistakes.fix: Keep your belt line level; squeeze the side of your standing hip.
mistakes.why: The glute medius is not holding the pelvis.

mistakes.name: Heel lifts
mistakes.looks: The standing heel rises and you tip forward at the bottom.
mistakes.fix: Stop higher, or put a small plate under the heel.
mistakes.why: Not enough ankle bend for the depth.

mistakes.name: Back rounds and falls back
mistakes.looks: At the bottom the lower back curls and you roll back onto the floor.
mistakes.fix: Reach your arms forward, use a counterweight, or sit to a box.
mistakes.why: The body's weight is behind the foot; rounding is the spine giving the missing range.

safety: Knee pain: stay in the range above the pain, often a 45-60° knee bend.
Balance: hold a rail, a strap or a doorway until you can control the descent.

variants.change: Hold a strap or support: less load, easier balance.
Sit to a box to set the depth.
Stand on a box with the free leg hanging down: full depth without the leg hitting the floor.
Weight held in front acts as a counterweight; easier to stay balanced.
Jump from the bottom and land on the same leg, soft knee.
Unstable surface: much harder balance, lighter range.

subtypes.name: Pistol squat
subtypes.change: Full depth, free leg straight out in front, held level.

subtypes.name: Shrimp squat
subtypes.change: Free knee bent behind you, hand holding that foot; lower until the back knee touches the floor.

subtypes.name: Single-leg wall sit
subtypes.change: Back on the wall, one foot on the floor with thigh level, other leg held straight out. Tracking: hold.

metrics.label: Knee inside the foot line (front view)

motion.basis: Standing leg is the right. Default is a single-leg squat to about 90° knee bend (clinical tests use 45-60°, crossley2011, ugalde2015). Pistol bottom angles estimated from the needed knee, hip and ankle range; not measured in these sources.

families.name: Ski erg
families.pattern: Standing double-pole pull: arms pull the handles down while the body hinges at the hips and knees, then you rise and reach back up.
setup: Stand a foot from the machine, feet hip width.
Damper 3-6. Grip the handles with relaxed hands.
Start tall, arms reaching up and a little forward, elbows soft.

steps.text: Tall, on the balls of your feet, hands above your head.
Drive the handles down with your arms and lats as your hips hinge back and knees soften.
Hands pass your hips and slightly behind, chest over your thighs, back flat.
Let the arms float up as you stand tall again; reset before the next pull.

cues.cue: Hinge, do not squat: hips back, knees only a little bent.
cues.why: Body weight through a hip hinge gives most of the force; in skiers, a deeper body crunch with small hip and elbow angles went with more pole force.

cues.cue: Elbows stay bent and high as you start the pull, then press down.
cues.why: Fixing the elbow angle early lets the lats and trunk move the handles, not just the triceps.

cues.cue: Flat back at the bottom, eyes a little ahead.
cues.why: A rounded back under load strains the lower back.

cues.cue: Pull fast, rise relaxed.
cues.why: The return is recovery time; rushing it raises effort without more speed.

families.breathing: Out on the pull, in as you rise.

tempo.note: About 1/3 pull, 2/3 return. Steady 30-40 pulls a minute.

mistakes.name: Squatting the pull
mistakes.looks: Knees bend deep and the hips drop straight down.
mistakes.fix: Push the hips back, knees soft.
mistakes.why: Squatting uses the legs inefficiently and shortens the pull.

mistakes.name: Arms only
mistakes.looks: You stand tall and pull with the arms.
mistakes.fix: Let your body weight fall into the handles as you hinge.
mistakes.why: It wastes the large trunk and hip muscles; power drops.

mistakes.name: Back rounds
mistakes.looks: The spine curls forward at the bottom.
mistakes.fix: Chest proud, hinge at the hips.
mistakes.why: Load goes into the lower back.

safety: Lower-back pain: hinge less and stay taller.

variants.change: General ski machine: about 6.8 MET (02080).
Double poling slow to moderate: about 10.5 MET (02082).
Fast to maximum: about 18.0 MET (02084).

motion.basis: Pattern from double-poling data (holmberg2005: joint minima near peak pole force); all angles are estimates for a fitness user on a SkiErg, not measured on the machine.

families.name: Sled push, drag and pull
families.pattern: Loaded locomotion: the legs drive the ground back in short powerful steps while the trunk leans into a weighted sled.
setup: Load the sled so you can keep moving without stopping; check the surface.
Hands on the poles, arms nearly straight, body leaning about 45°.
Head in line with the spine, one foot back ready to drive.

steps.text: Drive the back leg into the ground and push it long behind you.
Bring the other knee through low and fast; keep the lean.
Plant the foot under your hips, on the ball of the foot, and drive again.

cues.cue: Lean in with a straight line from head to back heel.
cues.why: A strong forward lean lets you push harder; pushing force grows with body lean.

cues.cue: Short, quick, powerful steps.
cues.why: Faster sled efforts come from longer strides, quicker steps and shorter ground contact.

cues.cue: Push through the balls of the feet, heels up.
cues.why: Heavier sleds raise calf and quad demand.

cues.cue: Light sled for speed, heavy sled for strength.
cues.why: Heavier loads change sprint posture more: more trunk lean, more hip and knee bend, longer contacts.

cues.cue: Brace; do not let the hips sag or the back round.
cues.why: The trunk passes the leg drive into the sled.

families.breathing: Short rhythmic breaths with the steps; brace on each drive.

tempo.note: Work in bouts of about 10-30 m or 10-30 s with full rest for power, shorter rests for conditioning.

mistakes.name: Standing too upright
mistakes.looks: Shoulders above the hips, arms bent, short pushes from the arms.
mistakes.fix: Lean in about 45°, arms long, push from the legs.
mistakes.why: Less of the leg drive goes into the sled.

mistakes.name: Hips sag or back rounds
mistakes.looks: The hips drop or the spine curves between the hands and feet.
mistakes.fix: Brace like a plank; lighter sled.
mistakes.why: Force leaks out through the trunk.

mistakes.name: Tiny shuffling steps
mistakes.looks: Feet barely leave the ground and land in front of the hips.
mistakes.fix: Drive each leg back until it is straight.
mistakes.why: Slower sleds have shorter strides and longer contact times.

safety: Check the floor and the path are clear.
Heavy sleds: stop when form breaks rather than grinding.

variants.change: Hands on the poles, forward lean; high poles are easier, low poles harder.
Facing the sled, straps in hands, walk backward: knees stay bent, mostly quads.
Harness or straps behind, walk or run forward: more hip extensors and hamstrings.
Stand still and pull the sled toward you hand over hand on a rope: upper back, lats and grip.
Burpee between pushes for conditioning.

subtypes.name: Backward drag
subtypes.change: Facing the sled, leaning back, stepping backward.

subtypes.name: Forward drag
subtypes.change: Harness or straps behind you, leaning forward, walking or running away from the sled.

subtypes.name: Rope pull
subtypes.change: Standing still in an athletic stance, pulling the rope hand over hand.

metrics.label: Stride
metrics.good: longer at the same step rate

motion.basis: Two-step cycle, right leg leading at t=0. lockie2003 and martinezserrano2021 show more trunk lean and joint flexion with heavier sleds and keogh2010sled a more horizontal trunk than sprinting; sanjaya2014 found 30° best for static pushing. The 45° lean and leg angles are estimates. MET: the 2024 Compendium has no sled entry; 02050 (vigorous resistance training, 6.0) is a stand-in.

families.name: Snatch
families.pattern: One explosive pull takes the weight from the floor or hang straight to locked arms overhead, while you drop under it.
setup: Wide grip: the bar sits in your hip crease when you stand with straight arms.
Feet hip width, bar over the middle of your feet, hook grip.
Hips a little lower than for a clean, chest up, back flat, arms straight.

steps.text: Push the floor away; keep the bar close and your back angle the same to the knee.
Knees move back under the bar as it slides into your hip crease.
Jump hard and shrug, arms long, bar brushing your hips.
Pull yourself under with high elbows, then punch your arms straight.
Catch with locked arms over the back of your head in a quarter squat (or full squat).
Stand with the bar overhead, then lower it to your hips and the floor.

cues.cue: Arms long until you have jumped.
cues.why: The legs and hips make the bar speed; early arm bend slows it.

cues.cue: Bar close to your body the whole way.
cues.why: A bar that loops forward is a common cause of missed snatches.

cues.cue: Lock out hard as you land, armpits forward.
cues.why: A soft or late lockout lets the bar crash and strains the elbows.

cues.cue: Bar over the back of your head and your mid-foot.
cues.why: Bar in front of the head pulls you forward out of balance.

cues.cue: Land with feet flat and knees out.
cues.why: Heels down and knees tracking the toes give a stable base under the bar.

families.breathing: Breathe in and brace before you pull, hold it through the catch, breathe out once you stand.

tempo.note: The lift is under a second; lower under control and reset each rep.

mistakes.name: Arms pull early
mistakes.looks: Elbows bend before the hips reach the bar.
mistakes.fix: Ropes for arms until you jump.
mistakes.why: It slows the bar and pulls it forward.

mistakes.name: Bar swings out
mistakes.looks: The bar bangs off the hips and travels away in front of you.
mistakes.fix: Keep the bar brushing your thighs; knees back under it, not hips forward into it.
mistakes.why: The more the bar drifts forward, the more likely the miss.

mistakes.name: Pressing out
mistakes.looks: Arms are bent when the bar lands, then you push it up.
mistakes.fix: Punch up as you go under, locked on landing.
mistakes.why: Bent elbows under load stress the elbow and fail the lift.

mistakes.name: Bar in front of your head
mistakes.looks: Arms reach forward in the catch and you stumble forward.
mistakes.fix: Push your head through the window between your arms.
mistakes.why: The bar is outside your base of support.

safety: Needs full overhead mobility; if you cannot hold an overhead squat with an empty bar, train that first.
If you miss behind, push the bar away and step forward; use bumper plates.
Shoulder pain: use power or hang versions and lighter loads.

variants.change: Catch above parallel.
Start standing, slide the bar to the knee, then extend.
Bar starts on blocks; no lowering phase.
No re-bend of the legs: the arms turn the bar over and press to lockout.
Bar starts behind the neck; dip and drop into an overhead squat. Trains the catch only.
One weight in one hand, between the feet; same hinge and jump, punch to lockout.
Swing-style: hike, hip snap, the bell travels close and the hand punches through so the bell lands softly on the forearm. Ground forces are higher than in the swing.

subtypes.name: Kettlebell snatch
subtypes.change: One bell swings between the legs, the hip snap floats it up close to the body, and the hand punches through to lockout.

subtypes.name: Snatch balance
subtypes.change: Bar on the back, wide grip: short dip, then drive yourself down into an overhead squat.

subtypes.name: One-arm snatch
subtypes.change: Dumbbell or bar in one hand between the feet; free arm out for balance, same hinge, jump and punch.

subtypes.name: Squat snatch
subtypes.change: Catch in a deep overhead squat (split stance for split snatch), then stand.

harder: snatch from the floor at heavier loads

metrics.label: Bar distance in front of the hips at contact (cm)
Arm angle overhead
metrics.good: 160-180 (bar over the back of the head)

motion.basis: Phase structure (first pull, knee re-bend in the transition, second pull, turnover, catch) and bar path from gourgoulis2000. Joint angles are estimates from coaching texts and typical lifter positions, not measured values. Kettlebell subtype from lake2014a and mcgill2012 descriptions; angles estimated.

families.name: Squat
families.pattern: Knee-dominant squat: hips, knees and ankles bend together on two feet, then drive up to standing.
setup: Feet about shoulder width, toes turned out a little (about 15-30°).
Bar on your upper back (or weight held at your chest), elbows under it.
Big breath into your belly and brace before each rep.

steps.text: Stand tall, weight over the middle of your feet.
Bend hips and knees together, knees moving out over your toes.
Sit down until your hip crease is level with or just below your knees, back still flat.
Push the floor away with your whole foot; hips and chest rise at the same rate.

cues.cue: Knees track over your toes, not inward.
cues.why: Knees caving in is the most common fault and puts sideways stress on the knee.

cues.cue: Whole foot down: heel, big toe, little toe.
cues.why: Stiff ankles make the heels rise and the knees cave; raise your heels on plates if needed.

cues.cue: Brace and keep your back flat to the bottom.
cues.why: A braced, neutral spine handles the load; rounding at the bottom raises stress on the lower back.

cues.cue: Thighs to parallel or below, if your back stays flat.
cues.why: Full squats grew the glutes and adductors more than half squats, and do not raise knee risk with good form.

cues.cue: Let your knees pass your toes if your heels stay down.
cues.why: Holding the knees back cut knee load a little but raised hip load and forward lean a lot.

cues.cue: Pick the width and toe-out that lets you sit deep.
cues.why: Wider stances and more toe-out shift load toward the hips; both are fine choices.

families.breathing: Breathe in and brace at the top, hold it on the way down, breathe out past the hardest part on the way up.

tempo.note: Lower under control in about 2 seconds, stand up in 1.

mistakes.name: Knees cave in
mistakes.looks: The knees move inside the line of the feet, often on the way up.
mistakes.fix: Push your knees out over your little toes; lighten the load.
mistakes.why: Weak or late hip abductors let the thigh roll in, which stresses the knee.

mistakes.name: Heels lift
mistakes.looks: The heels come off the floor and weight shifts to the toes.
mistakes.fix: Sit back a little more, or squat with your heels on small plates.
mistakes.why: Limited ankle bend; it pushes the bar forward and the knees inward.

mistakes.name: Lower back rounds at the bottom
mistakes.looks: The pelvis tucks under and the lower back curls at the deepest point.
mistakes.fix: Stop just above the depth where your back starts to round, and brace harder.
mistakes.why: Rounding under load moves stress from the muscles to the discs and ligaments.

mistakes.name: Hips shoot up first
mistakes.looks: On the way up the hips rise but the chest stays down, turning the squat into a bend-over.
mistakes.fix: Lead with your chest; hips and shoulders rise together.
mistakes.why: It moves the work off the quads onto the lower back.

safety: Use safety pins or spotter arms set just below your bottom position with a barbell.
Knee pain: shorten the depth to a box and keep the shins more upright.
Back pain: try a goblet or front squat, which keep the trunk more upright.
High blood pressure: avoid long breath holds; breathe out on each rep.

variants.change: Weight in front: trunk more upright (about 20-30° at the bottom), similar muscle work, less compressive load on the knee.
Bar lower on the back: more trunk lean and more hip load.
Bar high on the traps: trunk more upright, deeper knees.
Sit to a box or pins: shins more vertical, depth set by the box.
Wide stance, toes out 30-45°: more hip and adductor load, trunk more upright.
Feet hip width or closer: more knee bend, harder on ankle mobility.
Partial range: knees bent only about 45-90°.
Heels on a wedge: knees travel further forward, more quads, easier for stiff ankles.
Pause 2 seconds at the bottom, staying braced.
Bar on a fixed path: feet can go a little in front; balance is not trained.
Bands or chains make the top harder; same keyframes.
Stand on plates for extra depth.
Squat then press the weight overhead as you stand (thruster).

subtypes.name: Wall sit
subtypes.match: sit \(wall\)|wall sit|wall squat|wall slide|ball wall|on the wall|stability ball wall
subtypes.change: Back flat on the wall, feet forward, thighs level, held still. Tracking: hold. Repeated wall-sit holds of about 2 minutes lowered resting blood pressure in a home training study.

subtypes.name: Front or goblet squat
subtypes.change: Weight held at the chest or front of the shoulders; trunk stays more upright. A front squat is more upright than a back squat with similar muscle work and less knee compression; a low-bar back squat leans the most.

subtypes.name: Sumo squat
subtypes.change: Feet wide, toes out, weight hangs between the legs; knees push out hard.

subtypes.name: Overhead squat
subtypes.change: Arms locked overhead, wide grip if using a bar; needs an upright trunk and mobile shoulders.

subtypes.name: Box squat
subtypes.change: Sit back to a box at about knee height, touch without relaxing, stand up; shins stay near vertical.

metrics.label: Knee inside the foot line (front view)
Trunk lean
metrics.good: 20-30 front squat, 35-50 back squat at the bottom

motion.basis: Depth ranges from schoenfeld2010, hartmann2013 and kubo2019; trunk lean by bar position from glassbrook2017 and gullett2009; stance and toe-out from lorenzetti2018. Exact keyframe angles are estimates for an average adult high-bar squat to just below parallel. Arm angles estimated for a back-squat grip.

families.name: Stair climbing
families.pattern: Stepping gait up a flight of stairs, one step at a time: each leg lifts the body one riser.
setup: Stand at the bottom of the flight, tall, eyes two or three steps ahead.
Rest a hand lightly on the rail if there is one.

steps.text: Place the whole foot on the next step, toes near the riser, heel on the tread.
Push down through the middle of the foot and heel and straighten the front leg to rise.
Lift the back foot clearly over the edge and place it two steps up.

cues.cue: Stand tall, lean a little from the hips; look two or three steps ahead.
cues.why: A small forward lean shifts work to the hips and lowers the load on the knee.

cues.cue: Whole foot on the step.
cues.why: A full foot gives a bigger base and stops the calf doing all the lifting; the foot cannot slip off the edge.

cues.cue: Push up through the front leg, not off the back toes.
cues.why: The knee and hip extensors of the leading leg lift the body in the pull-up phase.

cues.cue: Knee over your second toe.
cues.why: A knee that falls in raises patellofemoral stress.

cues.cue: Steady pace, breathe in for two steps and out for two.
cues.why: 80-100 steps a minute keeps steady cardio work.

families.breathing: Rhythmic: in for two steps, out for two.

mistakes.name: Knee caves in
mistakes.looks: The knee drops inside the line from hip to foot while the foot is on the step.
mistakes.fix: Keep the knee over your second toe.
mistakes.why: Hip adduction and internal rotation load the kneecap unevenly; a little more forward lean reduced it.

mistakes.name: Only toes on the step
mistakes.looks: The ball of the foot sits on the edge and the heel hangs.
mistakes.fix: Put the whole foot on the step, toes near the next riser.
mistakes.why: Smaller base, the calf does the lifting, and the foot can slip.

mistakes.name: Head down, hunched
mistakes.looks: Folded at the trunk, eyes on the feet.
mistakes.fix: Chest up, look two or three steps ahead.
mistakes.why: Folding further hides the stairs ahead and closes the chest.

safety: Use the rail on steep or unfamiliar stairs.
Going down is mostly eccentric and loads the kneecap more: go slower and use the rail.

variants.change: Slow pace: MET 4.5 (Compendium 17131).
Fast, one step at a time: MET 9.3 (17134).
Two steps at a time: hip 51° and knee 52° range against 30° and 41°; MET 7.5 (17136). Needs its own clip.
Stair machine: HealthKit stairClimbing; the stairs move, same cues; do not lean on the rails.
Going down: own clip and cues, slower, whole foot, rail.

motion.basis: Joint ranges from physiopedia-stairs (after McFadyen and Winter 1988) and protopapadaki2007; exact timing and the baked clip are ours (Body/anatomy/climb_za.py, 90 steps/min, 175 mm rise, 280 mm going).

families.name: Cycling
families.pattern: Seated pedalling: legs push the pedals round in a circle while the trunk stays still. Covers indoor bikes and riding outdoors.
setup: Saddle height: at the bottom of the stroke the knee is bent about 25-30°.
Saddle level, at about hip height when you stand beside the bike.
Balls of the feet over the pedal axles, straps or clips snug.

steps.text: Knee at its highest; start pushing forward over the top.
Press down through the ball of the foot from 1 to 5 o'clock.
Knee slightly bent, never locked; sweep the foot back.
Lift the knee back up toward the bar, the other leg pushing.

cues.cue: Saddle high enough for a 25-30° knee bend at the bottom.
cues.why: A low saddle raises kneecap compression; too high makes the hips rock.

cues.cue: Knees point straight ahead over the feet.
cues.why: Knees caving in or out move load to the sides of the knee.

cues.cue: Still hips, relaxed shoulders, soft elbows.
cues.why: Rocking on the saddle means the saddle is too high or the resistance too low.

cues.cue: Steady 80-100 rpm; add resistance rather than grinding slow.
cues.why: Moderate cadence with resistance spreads the work and is easier on the knees.

families.breathing: Steady breathing; on hard climbs breathe deeper, not faster.

tempo.note: Cadence 80-100 rpm for most rides; 60-80 for heavy climbs.

mistakes.name: Saddle too low
mistakes.looks: The knee stays very bent at the bottom and comes up high.
mistakes.fix: Raise the saddle until the knee bends 25-30° at the bottom.
mistakes.why: It raises patellofemoral load and front-of-knee pain.

mistakes.name: Saddle too high
mistakes.looks: Leg locks straight and the hips rock side to side.
mistakes.fix: Lower the saddle until the knee stays soft at the bottom.
mistakes.why: It overstretches the back of the knee and chafes the saddle.

mistakes.name: Knees cave in
mistakes.looks: Knees drift toward the top tube on the push.
mistakes.fix: Push straight down, knee over the second toe.
mistakes.why: Side load on the knee.

safety: Knee pain at the front: check saddle height first.
Back pain: raise the handlebars.
Outdoors: wear a helmet and use lights in low light.

variants.change: Spin class: 9.0 MET (01270). Out of the saddle on climbs: trunk more upright, knees ahead of the pedals.
Arm ergometer: 2.0-3.5 MET at 15-45 W (02116-02118).
Outdoors under 10 mph, leisure: 4.0 MET (01010).
16-19 mph racing: 12.0 MET (01050); over 20 mph not drafting: 16.8 MET (01060).
Mountain biking uphill, vigorous: 14.0 MET (01003).
Mountain bike racing: 16.0 MET (01004).
E-bike with light support: 6.0 MET (01084); high support: 4.0 MET (01088).

subtypes.name: Upright bike
subtypes.change: Default keyframes. Assault/air bikes add pushing and pulling handles that move opposite the legs.

subtypes.name: Recumbent bike
subtypes.change: Seat with back rest; trunk leans back about 30° and the hips stay less flexed.

subtypes.name: Spin class standing climb
subtypes.change: Out of the saddle, body over the pedals.

subtypes.name: Arm ergometer
subtypes.change: Seated still; the hands crank in a circle, opposite each other.

subtypes.name: Road cycling
subtypes.change: Outdoors on a road bike: trunk lower (about 45° on the hoods), same leg circle. Look ahead, not at the front wheel.

subtypes.name: Mountain biking
subtypes.change: Off-road: more time standing on the pedals with knees and elbows bent to soak up bumps; trunk 30-45° forward.

motion.basis: Knee 25-30° at bottom and the about 75° knee, 45° hip and 20° ankle ranges from bini2011; hip and trunk values are estimates for an upright bike.

families.name: Step-up
families.pattern: Single-leg climb: one foot on a box drives the body up to standing, then lowers under control.
setup: Box about knee height or lower, so your thigh is level or less on the box.
Place your whole working foot on the box, heel included.
Stand tall, weights at your sides or bar on your back.

steps.text: Lean slightly forward over the front foot, weight on its heel.
Push through the box foot to stand up; the back foot just follows.
Stand tall on the box, hip and knee straight, the other foot beside it or knee raised.
Lower the free foot back to the floor slowly, controlled by the box leg.

cues.cue: Lift yourself with the top leg, not a bounce off the floor.
cues.why: Pushing off the back foot takes most of the work away from the box leg.

cues.cue: Box knee in line with your middle toes.
cues.why: The knee drifting inward is a common single-leg fault linked to weak side-hip muscles.

cues.cue: Lean your chest a little over the box foot.
cues.why: A slight forward lean brings the hips into the lift; all step-up versions train the glutes and hamstrings well.

cues.cue: Whole foot on the box, push through the heel.
cues.why: Toes only shift the load to the knee and calf and costs balance.

cues.cue: Come down slowly, about 2 seconds.
cues.why: The lowering half trains control of the knee and hip.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you step up, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Step up in about 1 second, lower in 2.

mistakes.name: Push off the back foot
mistakes.looks: The floor foot springs up on its toes and does the lifting.
mistakes.fix: Lift your back toes up before you drive, or lower the box.
mistakes.why: The trailing leg steals the work from the box leg.

mistakes.name: Box knee caves in
mistakes.looks: The working knee drifts inward as you stand up.
mistakes.fix: Push the knee out over your little toes; use a lower box.
mistakes.why: Weak hip abductors let the thigh roll in under load.

mistakes.name: Heel hangs off or lifts
mistakes.looks: Only the front of the foot is on the box; the heel rises as you drive.
mistakes.fix: Put the whole foot on the box and drive through the heel.
mistakes.why: Load goes to the knee and calf, and balance suffers.

safety: Use a stable box that cannot slide or tip.
Knee pain: lower the box so the knee bends less than 90° at the start.
Balance: start with bodyweight and hold a rail.

variants.change: Higher box: more hip bend at the start and more glutes.
Box beside you: step up sideways, more side-hip work.
Cross the far leg over to the box.
Lean further forward and drive through the heel for more glutes.
At the top drive the free knee up or step back into a lunge.
Bar on the back or front rack: watch balance and box height.
Arm movement added at the top; keep the stance leg still.

subtypes.name: Lateral step-up
subtypes.change: Stand beside the box and step up sideways; the free leg stays out to the side.

subtypes.name: Step-down (Peterson, Poliquin, Patrick)
subtypes.change: Stand on the box and slowly tap the other heel to the floor in front or to the side, then stand up; knee travels far forward (heel raised in the Peterson and Poliquin versions).

metrics.label: Box knee bend at the start
Box knee inside the foot line (front view)
Push from the floor foot (ankle point, degrees)

motion.basis: Right leg on the box, left leg on the floor. Box knee and hip angles set for a box at about knee height (estimate); muscle emphasis from simenz2012 and muyor2020. Other angles estimated from the movement.

families.name: Calf stretch
families.pattern: Static hold: the shin moves forward over a flat foot, lengthening the calf and Achilles. Knee straight hits the gastrocnemius; knee bent hits the soleus.
setup: Face a wall, hands on it at chest height.
Step one foot back, heel flat, toes pointing straight at the wall.
Front knee bent, back knee straight.

steps.text: Lean the hips toward the wall until you feel the back calf pull.
