mistakes.name: Forcing the twist
mistakes.looks: You yank yourself round with the arms, hips swinging with you.
mistakes.fix: Hips still, twist with your breath, go less far.
mistakes.why: Rotation piles into the low back.

mistakes.name: Sinking or crunching the low back
mistakes.looks: In back bends the low back hinges sharply while the upper back stays flat.
mistakes.fix: Lift the chest up and forward; keep glutes relaxed, go lower.
mistakes.why: One spot in the low back takes all the bend.

mistakes.name: Bouncing
mistakes.looks: You bob in and out of the stretch instead of holding still.
mistakes.fix: Ease in slowly, then stay still and let it relax.
mistakes.why: Bouncing triggers the muscle to tighten back and can strain it.

mistakes.name: Holding your breath
mistakes.looks: You tense up: shoulders creep up, jaw tight, breath held.
mistakes.fix: Breathe slowly; let each breath out take you a little deeper.
mistakes.why: Tension fights the stretch; relaxed breathing lets the muscle let go.

safety: Back pain that shoots down a leg: skip deep rounding and twisting; see a clinician.
Early in the morning the spine is stiffer: go easy on deep rounding right after waking.
Osteoporosis: avoid loaded rounding and forced twists.

variants.change: On a chair: same move with the hips on the seat, feet flat; easier to keep the pelvis still.
Over a ball: face up arches the back, face down rounds it. Keep the feet wide for balance.
Contract-relax: push gently against the stretch for 3-6 s, relax, then ease deeper. Similar range gains to static holds; also best after training.
A partner moves the limb. Go slowly and say when you feel a mild pull; the partner holds there, never pushes into pain.
Moving version: controlled swings through the range, 8-12 reps. Better before training than long holds.

subtypes.name: Cat stretch (round)
subtypes.change: On hands and knees, round the whole back up, head down.

subtypes.name: Cow stretch (arch)
subtypes.change: On hands and knees, let the belly drop and lift the chest and gaze.

subtypes.name: Side bend stretch
subtypes.change: Standing or seated tall, one arm overhead; bend sideways over the other hip, no leaning forward.

keyframes.note: trunk side-bent 25° to the right (no joint key yet; proposed trunkRot/trunkSide)

subtypes.name: Seated twist
subtypes.change: Sit tall, turn the chest toward one side, hand behind you; hips stay square.

keyframes.note: trunk twisted 40° (chest turns right) (no joint key yet; proposed trunkRot/trunkSide)

subtypes.name: Stability ball back stretch
subtypes.change: Lie back over a ball, feet wide, arms overhead, and let the spine curve over it.

subtypes.name: Lying twist
subtypes.change: On your back, knees bent, arms out; let the knees fall to one side, shoulders down.

keyframes.note: trunk twisted 40° (chest turns right) (no joint key yet; proposed trunkRot/trunkSide)

subtypes.name: Back extension stretch
subtypes.match: prone|cobra|abdominal|stomach|lean back|backbend|backward|thoracic bridge|lumbar\) extension|lower trunk flexor|t spine press
subtypes.change: Face down, hands under the shoulders; press the chest up, hips down (or lean back standing, hands on hips).

subtypes.name: Kneeling thoracic rotation
subtypes.change: On hands and knees, hand behind the head or reaching under; turn the chest up to the ceiling.

keyframes.note: trunk twisted 45° (chest turns right) (no joint key yet; proposed trunkRot/trunkSide)

subtypes.name: Standing twist
subtypes.change: Stand tall, feet planted; turn the chest to one side, hips facing forward.

keyframes.note: trunk twisted 40° (chest turns right) (no joint key yet; proposed trunkRot/trunkSide)

subtypes.name: Seated forward bend
subtypes.match: bent over back|seated lower|sitting lower trunk|cross legged|spine stretch|standing back stretch
subtypes.change: Sit with the feet flat, then fold forward and let the back round, arms hanging.

subtypes.name: Upper back stretch
subtypes.change: Hold a post or clasp your hands in front, push the arms forward and round the upper back.

subtypes.name: Knees to chest
subtypes.change: On your back, hug both knees toward the chest; let the low back round onto the floor.

metrics.label: Movement during hold
metrics.good: < 3° once you are in the stretch

motion.basis: Cat-camel cycles from mcgill2001; dose from garber2011, bandy1994, thomas2018. Twist and side bend have no joint key yet: keyframes carry them in note; mistakes and metrics use proposed keys trunkRot (+ = chest turns right) and trunkSide (+ = bend right). All angles are estimates.

families.name: Wrist and forearm stretch
families.pattern: Static hold: the wrist bends back or forward with the elbow straight, lengthening the forearm flexors or extensors.
setup: Stand or sit tall, shoulders down.
Reach one arm straight forward at shoulder height, palm up.
Other hand holds the fingers of the reaching hand.

steps.text: Straighten the elbow fully, then gently pull the fingers down and back.
Stay still 15-30 s. Feel it along the inside of the forearm. Turn the palm down and bend the wrist for the outside.
Come out slowly, then switch sides.

cues.cue: Elbow straight.
cues.why: The forearm muscles cross the elbow; bending it slackens them.

cues.cue: Pull slowly with the other hand, no yanking.
cues.why: Slow, steady holds of 30-45 s are what tendon programs use.

cues.cue: Shoulders down and relaxed.
cues.why: Shrugging adds neck tension and does not help the stretch.

cues.cue: Ease in to a mild pull, never pain.
cues.why: Gentle stretches still gain range; stretching into pain did not help and can irritate the muscle.

cues.cue: Hold 15-30 s, 2-4 times, about 60 s in total per side.
cues.why: 30 s holds gave the same gains as 60 s; aim for at least 5 min per muscle each week, most days.

families.breathing: Breathe slowly and normally. Ease a little deeper as you breathe out.

tempo.note: Ease in for about 3 s, hold 15-30 s, ease out. Repeat 2-4 times each side.

mistakes.name: Elbow bent
mistakes.looks: The reaching arm bends as you pull on the fingers.
mistakes.fix: Lock the elbow out softly first, then pull less hard.
mistakes.why: The stretch on the forearm muscles is lost.

mistakes.name: Pulling too hard
mistakes.looks: You crank the hand back fast to the end of range.
mistakes.fix: Ease in to a mild pull and hold.
mistakes.why: Wrist ligaments and tendons are small and irritate easily.

mistakes.name: Holding your breath
mistakes.looks: You tense up: shoulders creep up, jaw tight, breath held.
mistakes.fix: Breathe slowly; let each breath out take you a little deeper.
mistakes.why: Tension fights the stretch; relaxed breathing lets the muscle let go.

safety: Tingling or numbness in the fingers: ease off, a nerve is being pulled.
Tennis or golfer's elbow: keep it mild; pain should not linger after.

variants.change: Hands on the floor or a wall, fingers pointing back: body weight gives the stretch, lean only a little.
Fingers or thumb pulled back one at a time: smaller, more local stretch.
Contract-relax: push gently against the stretch for 3-6 s, relax, then ease deeper. Similar range gains to static holds; also best after training.
A partner moves the limb. Go slowly and say when you feel a mild pull; the partner holds there, never pushes into pain.
Moving version: controlled swings through the range, 8-12 reps. Better before training than long holds.

subtypes.name: Kneeling wrist stretch
subtypes.change: On hands and knees, turn the hands so the fingers point to your knees; lean back slowly.

subtypes.name: Wrist extensor stretch
subtypes.change: Arm forward, palm down; bend the wrist so the fingers point down and press gently on the back of the hand.

subtypes.name: Finger and thumb stretch
subtypes.change: Pull one finger or the thumb gently back, or spread the fingers wide; elbow straight.

subtypes.name: Forearm rotation stretch
subtypes.change: Elbow straight or bent at your side; turn the palm fully up or down and help gently with the other hand.

metrics.label: Movement during hold
metrics.good: < 3° once you are in the stretch

motion.basis: Hold time from stasinopoulos2005 and garber2011. Wrist ranges are estimates from typical end range (about 70° each way); finger and deviation positions have no joint key, so wristExt and forearm stand in. Little direct research on these stretches.

families.name: Strongman events
families.pattern: Odd-object lifting and moving: heavy, awkward loads are lifted, flipped, pressed, thrown or pulled with the whole body as one stiff linkage.
setup: Learn each event with light implements and a coach before going heavy.
Clear the area, use tacky or chalk as the event allows, and plan where the object goes.
Brace hard before every lift: belly, glutes and grip.

steps.text: Stone: straddle it, hinge over, hands spread under the sides, arms wrapped round.
Pull it off the floor and roll it up onto your thighs as you sit back.
Re-grip high, hug it to your chest, drop the hips under it.
Drive the hips through hard and extend up and over the bar or onto the platform.

cues.cue: Hips first, then back.
cues.why: In the stone lift the hip extensors need to fire before the back extensors.

cues.cue: Brace like a block for carries and the yoke.
cues.why: Huge trunk co-contraction stiffens the spine and makes up for hip abductor strength in the yoke walk.

cues.cue: Use the lap: the second pull is a front squat with a hug.
cues.why: The stone lift shares its patterns with the RDL and the front squat; train those.

cues.cue: Tire flip: chest on the tire, push forward and up; arms straight, palms up.
cues.why: A fast second pull separates fast and slow flips; pulling with bent arms risks the biceps tendon.

cues.cue: Log press: elbows high on the clean, then dip and drive.
cues.why: A log is harder to drive than a barbell, and a thicker log is harder still.

families.breathing: Big breath and brace before each lift; on long events breathe at the top or between steps.

tempo.note: Events are timed or for max reps; train with 30-60 s efforts and 2-4 min rest.

mistakes.name: Lifting the stone with straight legs
mistakes.looks: The stone is hauled up with the back, no lap, legs barely bent.
mistakes.fix: Lap the stone, re-grip, then extend from the hips.
mistakes.why: The stone forces a rounded back; without the legs the back takes even more load.

mistakes.name: Curling the tire
mistakes.looks: The elbows bend and the arms pull the tire up.
mistakes.fix: Arms straight; drive with the legs and chest into the tire.
mistakes.why: A heavy curl with palms up is a known way to rupture the distal biceps.

mistakes.name: Hips too high on the tire
mistakes.looks: Legs nearly straight at the start, back rounded like a stiff-leg deadlift.
mistakes.fix: Get low: chest on the tire, hips near knee height.
mistakes.why: Puts the whole lift on the back and slows the second pull.

mistakes.name: Yoke sways
mistakes.looks: The yoke rocks side to side or the steps get long and slow.
mistakes.fix: Short fast steps, brace hard, eyes ahead.
mistakes.why: The hips cannot hold the frontal load without a stiff trunk.

safety: These are high-load events; the yoke gave the highest spine loads of all tested events.
Distal biceps: keep the arms straight in tire flips and stone lifts.
Train under supervision, on a safe surface, and stop sets before technique fails.

variants.change: Pick a bag or stone and load it to the shoulder or onto a platform; same lap-and-extend pattern.
Static hold: arms out to the sides or in front for time.
Lift and push one end of a long object up and over, walking hand over hand.
Push a lever arm on the shoulder around a circle: a loaded walk.
Seated tug of war on a stick: grip and back.
Pressing events: like the log press with a thick bar, lever or block.

subtypes.name: Atlas stone
subtypes.change: Default event: grip, lap, second pull, over the bar.

subtypes.name: Tire flip
subtypes.change: Deep start with chest on the tire, palms up; drive forward, knee the tire, flip the hands and push it over.

subtypes.name: Yoke walk
subtypes.change: Frame across the upper back; short fast steps over a set distance.

subtypes.name: Log press
subtypes.change: Clean the log to the chest, dip and drive it overhead.

subtypes.name: Keg toss / weight for height
subtypes.change: Swing the implement between the legs, then extend hard and throw it up and back over the head.

subtypes.name: Truck pull
subtypes.change: Harness on, rope in hand, very low lean, drive with short powerful steps. Arm-over-arm: pull the rope hand over hand instead.

subtypes.name: Static hold
subtypes.change: Hold the load with arms out for time.

motion.basis: Atlas stone default. Phase order and which joints peak in each phase from hindle2021stone (max hip flexion at the first pull, max knee flexion at the second pull); exact angles are estimates. Yoke gait shape from hindle2021yoke (hip flexed and knee near straight at heel strike, short strides); tire flip phases from keogh2010tire; others are estimates. Lumbar flexion in the stone lift is shown because mcgill2009 found a neutral spine impossible with the stone.

families.name: Swimming
families.pattern: Lying long in the water, the arms pull you forward in turn or together while the legs kick to keep the hips high.
setup: Goggles on and snug; cap if your hair is long.
Push off the wall in a long streamline: arms by your ears, hands stacked.
Lap pools: swim on the right of the lane, pass at the wall.
Open water: never alone, bright cap, know your exit points.

steps.text: Hand enters in front of the shoulder, fingertips first, and reaches forward.
Bend the elbow so the forearm faces back, elbow higher than the hand, and pull under your body.
Push the water back past your hip while the body rolls to the other side.
Lift the elbow out first and swing the relaxed hand forward close to the water.

cues.cue: Head down, eyes to the floor, hips at the surface.
cues.why: Drag is the main brake in swimming; a lifted head drops the hips and legs.

cues.cue: Roll the body with each stroke, both sides, to breathe.
cues.why: Too little roll on the breathing side and one-sided breathing were tied to shoulder impingement.

cues.cue: Enter in line with your shoulder, never across your head.
cues.why: Crossing the midline at entry pinches the rotator cuff under the shoulder roof.

cues.cue: High elbow catch: forearm vertical early, elbow above the hand.
cues.why: A dropped elbow pushes water down instead of back and loads the front of the shoulder.

cues.cue: Kick from the hips, small and fast, toes pointed.
cues.why: The kick mainly keeps the legs up; big knee-driven kicks add drag.

cues.cue: Breathe out under water all the time, turn to breathe in.
cues.why: Holding air makes you rush and lift your head to breathe.

families.breathing: Exhale steadily through nose and mouth under water; turn the head with the body roll to inhale. Freestyle: every 2-3 strokes, both sides if you can.

tempo.note: One loop = one full arm cycle (both arms). Easy freestyle is about 30-45 cycles per minute.

mistakes.name: Head up, hips sink
mistakes.looks: Eyes forward, chin up, legs angled down in the water.
mistakes.fix: Look at the floor, press your chest down slightly.
mistakes.why: The body tilts and frontal drag rises sharply.

mistakes.name: Hand crosses the midline
mistakes.looks: The hand enters in front of the head or across the centre line.
mistakes.fix: Enter wide, in front of the same shoulder.
mistakes.why: It pinches the shoulder and makes the hips snake sideways.

mistakes.name: Swimming flat
mistakes.looks: Shoulders stay level; the head lifts or twists to breathe.
mistakes.fix: Roll about 40-50° to each side, head turns with the body.
mistakes.why: Low roll on the breathing side went with shoulder impingement.

mistakes.name: Dropped elbow
mistakes.looks: The arm pulls straight and the elbow sinks below the hand.
mistakes.fix: Bend the elbow early, like reaching over a barrel.
mistakes.why: Less push back and more stress on the front of the shoulder.

safety: Shoulder pain: shorten sessions, breathe both sides, mix in backstroke, check hand entry.
Breaststroke knee pain on the inside: narrow the kick and warm up gradually.
Open water: swim with others, near shore, with a bright cap or buoy; cold water below 15 °C needs a gradual entry.
Never practise breath-holding swims alone (risk of blackout).

variants.change: Freestyle laps, slow, recreational. MET 5.8 (Compendium 18240).
Crawl at about 50 yd/min, vigorous. MET 8.0 (Compendium 18290).
Freestyle laps, fast, vigorous. MET 9.8 (Compendium 18230).
Breaststroke, recreational (training or racing 10.3, code 18260). MET 5.3 (Compendium 18265).
Backstroke, recreational (training or racing 9.5, code 18250). MET 4.8 (Compendium 18255).
Butterfly, general. MET 13.8 (Compendium 18270).
Swimming in a lake, ocean or river (5 km open-water race pace 10.5, code 18285). MET 6.0 (Compendium 18300).
Sidestroke, general. MET 7.0 (Compendium 18320).
Treading water, moderate. MET 3.5 (Compendium 18350).
Water aerobics, general (high intensity 7.5, code 18358). MET 5.5 (Compendium 18355).
Water jogging, vigorous. MET 9.8 (Compendium 18366).

subtypes.name: Breaststroke
subtypes.change: Pull, breathe, kick, glide. Arms sweep out and in under the chest; heels draw up to the seat, feet turn out, kick back and squeeze together. Keep the knees about hip width.

mistakes.name: Knees too wide
mistakes.looks: Knees spread far apart as the heels come up.
mistakes.fix: Knees about hip width; the feet go wider than the knees.
mistakes.why: A wide, forceful whip kick stresses the inner knee (breaststroker's knee).

subtypes.name: Backstroke
subtypes.change: On your back, head still and ears in the water, hips up. Straight-arm recovery over the shoulder, pinky enters first, bent-arm pull at your side; roll with each stroke.

keyframes.phase: Right bent-arm pull at the side

subtypes.name: Butterfly
subtypes.change: Both arms together, two dolphin kicks per stroke (one as the hands enter, one as they push). The body waves from the chest; breathe forward low, chin near the water.

subtypes.name: Open-water swim
subtypes.change: Freestyle with a sight every 6-10 strokes: lift only the eyes forward, then roll to breathe. Slightly higher stroke rate in chop; draft behind others if racing.

keyframes.phase: Sight: eyes lift, then breathe to the side

subtypes.name: Water aerobics
subtypes.change: Upright in chest-deep water: jog, jacks and kicks with the arms pushing and pulling water. The water slows impact; push harder for more effort.

keyframes.phase: Right knee up, arms push forward
Left knee up, arms push forward

subtypes.name: Freestyle
subtypes.change: Default stroke: alternating arms, flutter kick, side breathing.

motion.basis: Shoulder and hip roll magnitudes from psycharakis2008/psycharakis2011; arm keyframes, elbow bend mid-pull and kick angles are our estimates from standard coaching descriptions. The rig has no long-axis trunk roll key, so roll is a readout only. Trunk 88 = prone near horizontal; backstroke -85 = supine.

families.name: Team sports
families.pattern: Stop-and-go running with jumps, landings, cuts and kicks or shots, repeated over a game.
setup: Shoes for the surface: court shoes for basketball, studs or turf shoes for soccer.
Warm up 10-15 minutes with a structured routine (jogging, strength, landing and cutting drills).
Shin guards for soccer; consider an ankle brace if you have sprained it before.

steps.text: Bend hips and knees together, ball set above your shooting eye, elbow under the ball.

steps.phase: Jump and release at the top
steps.text: Drive up through the legs and release as you near the top, wrist snapping forward.
Land where you took off, on both feet, hips and knees bending, knees over toes.
Athletic stance: knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet.

cues.cue: On every landing and cut, knees stay over your toes, never caving in.
cues.why: Higher knee valgus angle and load on landing predicted ACL injury in a prospective study.

cues.cue: Land soft and quiet: hips and knees bend together.
cues.why: A simple 'land softly' instruction lowers impact force and increases knee bend.

cues.cue: Slow down with short steps before a sharp cut.
cues.why: Sharper cuts at higher speed raise knee loading; braking over the steps before the cut spreads it out.

cues.cue: Do a full injury-prevention warm-up (like FIFA 11+) before games.
cues.why: In youth female soccer a structured warm-up cut injuries by about a third and severe injuries by about half.

cues.cue: Soccer: plant beside the ball, knee over it, toes pointed on an instep drive.
cues.why: Plant-foot position and a firm, extended ankle at impact set ball speed and direction.

families.breathing: Breathe freely; use stoppages to slow your breathing.

tempo.note: Intermittent: sprints, jumps and cuts every few seconds with walking and jogging between. One loop = one move.

mistakes.name: Knees cave in
mistakes.looks: On landing or cutting the knee collapses inside the foot.
mistakes.fix: Push the knees out over the toes; strengthen the hips.
mistakes.why: This pattern predicted ACL injury.

mistakes.name: Stiff landing
mistakes.looks: Lands on straight legs, loud, upright trunk.
mistakes.fix: Land softly, bend hips and knees, chest over knees.
mistakes.why: Higher impact forces and less knee bend raise ACL and knee stress.

mistakes.name: Cutting at full speed
mistakes.looks: One big plant step at full speed, trunk leaning away from the new direction.
mistakes.fix: Brake over 2-3 short steps, lean into the cut.
mistakes.why: Late braking and sharp angles raise knee loads.

safety: A previous ankle sprain raises the risk of another; brace or tape and do balance training.
Landing is the most common way basketball ankle injuries happen, often on another player's foot.
Concussion signs after a head knock: stop playing for the day.
Build up game time gradually after a break.

variants.change: Basketball, general. MET 7.5 (Compendium 15055).
Basketball, game. MET 8.0 (Compendium 15040).
Basketball, shooting baskets. MET 5.0 (Compendium 15070).
Basketball, drills, practice. MET 9.3 (Compendium 15072).
Soccer, casual, general. MET 7.0 (Compendium 15610).
Soccer, competitive. MET 9.5 (Compendium 15605).
Futsal. MET 7.8 (Compendium 15195).
Walking football. MET 3.5 (Compendium 15615).
Volleyball, competitive in a gym (beach 8.0, code 15725). MET 6.0 (Compendium 15711).
Team handball. MET 8.0 (Compendium 15330).
Field hockey. MET 7.8 (Compendium 15350).
Ultimate frisbee. MET 8.0 (Compendium 15250).
Rugby union, competitive (touch 6.3, code 15562). MET 8.3 (Compendium 15560).

subtypes.name: Basketball
subtypes.change: Jump shot shown: dip, jump, release at the top, two-foot soft landing.

keyframes.phase: Jump and release at the top

subtypes.name: Soccer
subtypes.change: Instep kick shown: angled approach, plant beside the ball, knee over the ball, toes down, follow through.

keyframes.phase: Plant beside the ball, leg back
Strike: knee over the ball, toes down
Follow through and land on the kicking foot

subtypes.name: Change of direction
subtypes.change: Side-step cut used in all field and court sports: brake, plant the outside foot, push off.

keyframes.phase: Slow down: short steps, hips low
Plant outside foot, knee over toes
Push off into the new direction
Jump and release at the top

metrics.label: Knee inside the foot on landing

motion.basis: Landing and cutting risk factors from hewett2005, milner2012 and dossantos2018; kick from kellis2007. All joint angles are our estimates.

families.name: Treadmill
families.pattern: Running or walking gait on a moving belt: same stride as outdoors, with the belt setting the speed.
setup: Straddle the belt, start it slow, then step on.
Clip the safety key to your clothes.
Run in the middle of the belt, close enough to reach the console.

steps.text: Land softly with the foot close under your hips.
Knee and ankle bend to absorb, body tall over the foot.
Push off behind you; the other knee swings through.
Heel comes up under the hip and the leg reaches for the next step.

cues.cue: Short, quick steps; land under your hips.
cues.why: Raising step rate 5-10% cuts the load on the knee and hip.

cues.cue: Let go of the rails; arms swing at your sides.
cues.why: Holding the rails lowers the real effort and makes the console readings wrong.

cues.cue: Tall, eyes forward, slight lean from the ankles.
cues.why: Looking down at your feet rounds the upper back.

cues.cue: Set a 1% incline to feel like flat running outdoors.
cues.why: Treadmill running is close to overground running but with small changes in gait; a small incline offsets the missing air resistance.

families.breathing: Find a rhythm, such as in for 2-3 steps and out for 2-3.

tempo.note: Running cadence about 160-180 steps a minute; walking about 100-120.

mistakes.name: Holding the rails
mistakes.looks: Hands grip the front or side rails, often on an incline.
mistakes.fix: Lower the speed or incline until you can let go.
mistakes.why: The arms carry body weight; effort and calories are lower than the console shows.

mistakes.name: Over-striding
mistakes.looks: The heel lands far in front with a straight knee.
mistakes.fix: Shorter, quicker steps.
mistakes.why: It raises braking force and knee load.

mistakes.name: Running at the front edge
mistakes.looks: Toes near the motor cover, stride cut short.
mistakes.fix: Move back to the middle of the belt.
mistakes.why: High trip risk on the cover.

safety: Always clip the safety key.
Step to the side rails before stopping the belt; do not jump off a moving belt.

variants.change: Incline walk 6-10%, moderate to brisk: 7.0 MET (17035); 11-20%: 8.8 MET (17036). Trunk leans forward 5-10° more.
Backward walk 2.5 mph at +10%: 7.8 MET (17475).

subtypes.name: Backward walk
subtypes.change: Walking in reverse: toes land first, knee straightens as you push back.

subtypes.name: Incline walk
subtypes.change: Walking gait with trunk 8-10° more forward and more hip and ankle bend at contact.

subtypes.name: Treadmill walk
subtypes.change: Walking gait: one foot always down, heel strike, smaller knee bend.

subtypes.name: Treadmill run
subtypes.change: Default keyframes. Curved treadmills: belt moves only as you push, so you run a little more on the forefoot.

metrics.label: Foot ahead of hips at landing

motion.basis: Treadmill vs overground gait differences small (vanhooren2020); step rate effect from heiderscheit2011. Joint angles are typical textbook running and walking gait values, estimates.

families.name: Triceps extension
families.pattern: Elbow extension: the upper arm stays still while the forearm straightens against resistance.
setup: Pushdown: stand close to a high pulley, bar or rope at chest height.
Upper arms at your sides, elbows pinned to your ribs.
Slight forward lean, shoulders down, wrists straight.

steps.text: Straighten your elbows and push the handle down to your thighs.
Squeeze the triceps with arms fully straight.
Let the forearms rise until elbows are bent about 90-100°, upper arms still.

cues.cue: Elbows stay still, only the forearm moves.
cues.why: Moving the shoulder lets the lats and chest help and takes work off the triceps.

cues.cue: Mix in overhead extensions.
cues.why: Training with the arm overhead grew the triceps about 40% more than pushdowns (long head about 45% more) in 12 weeks.

cues.cue: Straighten fully every rep.
cues.why: Full range trains all three heads; with the arm down the long head does the most, with the arm raised 90° or more the medial head takes over.

cues.cue: Wrists straight, not curled.
cues.why: Bent wrists move effort to the forearm and strain the wrist.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you straighten, in as you bend.

tempo.note: Push in 1 s, return in 2 s.

mistakes.name: Elbows drift
mistakes.looks: Elbows move forward or out as you push.
mistakes.fix: Pin elbows to your sides; lighten the load.
mistakes.why: The shoulder joins in and the triceps get less work.

mistakes.name: Body weight pushes the bar
mistakes.looks: You lean over the bar and drop your body to move it.
mistakes.fix: Stand tall with a small lean only.
mistakes.why: Body weight moves the load instead of the triceps.

mistakes.name: Half reps
mistakes.looks: Elbows never fully straighten or never bend past 60°.
mistakes.fix: Full range: from about 100° bend to straight.
mistakes.why: Range is lost where the triceps work hardest and where they stretch.

safety: Elbow pain: use a rope or neutral grip and lighter loads; avoid fast lockouts.
Skull crushers: lower the bar behind the head, not onto the face; use a spotter or dumbbells when heavy.
Overhead extensions: keep ribs down so the back does not arch.

variants.change: Rope: neutral grip, spread the ends at the bottom.
Palms up: lighter loads, more wrist control.
Angled bar: easier on the wrists.
One arm: same path, brace the trunk.
On an incline or decline bench: shifts where in the range the load is hardest.
Tate press: dumbbells lower to the chest with elbows out, then press up by extending the elbows.

subtypes.name: Overhead extension
subtypes.match: overhead|french|behind neck|back of the head|high pulley|seated triceps|standing triceps|seated bench extension|bed sheet
subtypes.change: Arms overhead, elbows by your ears pointing up; lower the weight behind your head and straighten.

subtypes.name: Skull crusher / lying extension
subtypes.match: lying|skull|crusher|supine|across face|decline triceps|decline close grip|face press|tiger tail
subtypes.change: Lying on a bench, arms angled slightly back toward your head; bend only the elbows to bring the weight to your forehead or behind your head.

subtypes.name: Kickback
subtypes.change: Hinge forward with the upper arm along your side, parallel to the floor; straighten the elbow back.

subtypes.name: Bodyweight triceps extension
subtypes.change: Body leaning like a push-up with forearms on the floor, bar or straps; straighten the elbows to lift onto the hands. Harder the lower the body.

subtypes.name: Machine triceps extension
subtypes.change: Seated, upper arms on a pad in front, push the handles down or forward.

motion.basis: Default rig is the cable pushdown. Arm positions (arm by the side vs overhead) from maeo2023 and kholinne2018. All joint angles are estimates from the standard setups: upper arm still, elbow 100° to straight. Scapula is mostly still in pushdowns and kickbacks (slightly depressed or retracted); the overhead subtype uses the upward rotation of full arm elevation from mcclure2001.

families.name: Turkish get-up
families.pattern: Slow full-body sequence from lying to standing and back, one arm holding a weight straight up the whole time.
setup: Lie on your back, weight in your right hand, arm straight up over your shoulder.
Right knee bent, foot flat; left leg straight and out at about 45°, left arm out at 45°.
Wrist straight, eyes on the weight.

steps.text: Press the weight up and roll onto your left elbow, pushing with your right foot.
Push up from the elbow to your left hand; sit tall with the chest open.
Squeeze your glutes and lift your hips into a straight line.
Swing your left leg under you to kneel on the left knee.
Lift your hand off the floor, line up the back shin and come to a tall kneel.
Step up like a lunge to standing, weight still straight overhead. Then reverse every step.

cues.cue: Weight arm locked and vertical at every stage.
cues.why: The shoulder muscles work to hold the arm stable; a bent or drifting arm loses that and risks the shoulder.

cues.cue: Watch the weight until you kneel.
cues.why: It keeps the arm over the shoulder while the body moves under it.

cues.cue: Shoulder packed: down and away from your ear.
cues.why: A shrugged shoulder is less stable under a load held overhead.

cues.cue: Hips high in the bridge, glutes tight.
cues.why: Makes room for the leg sweep and trains hip extension.

cues.cue: Go slowly and pause at each stage.
cues.why: The value is control in every position, not speed.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you move into each new stage, breathe in during the short pause.

tempo.note: About 8-12 seconds up and the same down, pausing at each stage.

mistakes.name: Weight arm bends
mistakes.looks: The elbow softens and the weight sinks toward the face.
mistakes.fix: Lock the elbow; use a lighter weight or a shoe on the fist.
mistakes.why: Load shifts to the elbow and the weight can fall.

mistakes.name: Arm drifts off vertical
mistakes.looks: The weight leans forward or back instead of straight up.
mistakes.fix: Keep the knuckles to the ceiling, eyes on the weight.
mistakes.why: The further the weight drifts, the bigger the strain on the shoulder.

mistakes.name: Low bridge
mistakes.looks: The hips sag while the leg sweeps under.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze glutes and push the floor with the planted foot and hand.
mistakes.why: There is no room for the knee to pass and the lower back rounds.

mistakes.name: Shoulder shrugs up
mistakes.looks: The top shoulder rises to the ear.
mistakes.fix: Pull the shoulder down into its socket.
mistakes.why: The shoulder loses its stable base.

safety: Learn it with no weight (a shoe balanced on the fist), then a light bell.
Shoulder pain or poor overhead range: train the half get-up (to the hand) first.
Drop the weight to the side, never over yourself, if you lose control.

variants.change: Up to sitting on the hand or the high bridge, then back down.
Roll to the elbow and press up to the hand only.
Kettlebell held bell-up; grip and shoulder stability work much harder.
From the bridge, sweep into a low squat and stand, instead of the kneeling lunge.
No weight: hands behind the head; a kneel-to-stand pattern.

motion.basis: Stage order from ace2015 and the seven-stage description in shoulder-tgu2019. Joint angles are estimates of each stage position; trunk is measured from vertical so the lying stages are negative. Up phase only; the rig reverses the keyframes for the way down. Roll and trunk twist toward the posting hand are estimates.

families.name: Upright row
families.pattern: Vertical pull close to the body: elbows lift out and up to shoulder height while the hands stay near the trunk.
setup: Stand tall, bar in front of your thighs, overhand grip.
Hands about shoulder width or wider, not touching.
Brace, shoulders down, look straight ahead.

steps.text: Lift your elbows out and up, keeping the bar close to your body.
Stop when your elbows reach about shoulder height, bar around the lower chest.
Lower slowly to straight arms.

cues.cue: Elbows to shoulder height, not higher.
cues.why: The arm is turned in during this lift; above about 90° that pinches the rotator cuff under the shoulder bone.

cues.cue: Hands shoulder width or wider.
cues.why: Wider grips raise deltoid and trapezius activity and lower biceps work.

cues.cue: Lead with the elbows, elbows above the wrists.
cues.why: Pulling with the elbows keeps the load on the shoulders, not the forearms.

cues.cue: Bar close to your body the whole time.
cues.why: A bar drifting forward adds strain on the lower back and front shoulder.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you pull up, in as you lower.

tempo.note: Controlled; brief hold at the top.

mistakes.name: Elbows too high
mistakes.looks: Elbows go well above the shoulders and the bar reaches the chin.
mistakes.fix: Stop at shoulder height.
mistakes.why: Raising the turned-in arm past 90° is the impingement position.

mistakes.name: Hands too close
mistakes.looks: Hands touching in the middle of the bar.
mistakes.fix: Move hands to shoulder width or wider.
mistakes.why: More internal rotation and more biceps, less deltoid.

mistakes.name: Body swing
mistakes.looks: Hips drive and the trunk leans back to lift the bar.
mistakes.fix: Lighter weight, stand still.
mistakes.why: Momentum replaces shoulder work and loads the lower back.

safety: Shoulder pain or impingement history: stop lower than it hurts, or replace with a lateral raise.
Wrist pain: use a wider grip, dumbbells, cable rope or straps.

variants.change: Wide grip (about 2x shoulder width): most deltoid and trap, least biceps.
Dumbbells: each hand finds its own path, often easier on the wrists and shoulders.
Cable or band: steady tension.
One arm: keep the trunk square.
Lying cable row: on your back pulling from a low pulley toward the head; same arm path.

motion.basis: Elevation limit and the internally rotated arm from schoenfeld2011; grip effects from mcallister2013 (50%, 100% and 200% of shoulder width tested). Joint angles are estimates: internal rotation of about 50° at the top follows from the elbows above the hands with the arm at 80°; scapular upward rotation scaled from mcclure2001; scapular elevation at the top reflects the upper-trap work (estimate).

families.name: Walking
families.pattern: Gait with one foot always on the ground: heel lands, you roll over the foot and push off from the toes.
setup: Comfortable shoes with some grip; for hikes, ankle support if the trail is rough.
Stand tall, eyes ahead, shoulders relaxed and down.
Start at an easy pace for a few minutes, then pick it up.

steps.text: Land on the heel with the knee nearly straight, foot not far in front.
Roll onto the whole foot; the knee bends slightly to take your weight.
Your body passes over the foot, standing tall.
The left heel lands as the right heel lifts.
Push off the right toes; the knee bends and the foot swings through.
The right leg reaches forward to land again, arms swinging opposite.

cues.cue: For exercise, walk at 100+ steps per minute; 130 is vigorous.
cues.why: About 100 steps/min is a simple marker of moderate intensity (about 3 MET) in adults.

cues.cue: To go faster, take quicker steps, not longer ones.
cues.why: Reaching far ahead turns the heel strike into a brake; speed comes mostly from step rate and push-off.

cues.cue: Tall, head over shoulders, eyes ahead.
cues.why: Looking down drops the head forward and rounds the upper back.

cues.cue: Elbows bent, arms swing from the shoulder.
cues.why: Arm swing balances the legs and helps brisk pace; with poles it adds upper-body work.

cues.cue: Downhill: shorter steps, soft knees, use poles if you have them.
cues.why: Poles cut knee joint forces by roughly 12-25% walking downhill.

families.breathing: Breathe naturally. At a brisk pace you can talk but not sing.

tempo.note: One loop = two steps. Easy walking is about 90-100 steps per minute, brisk 110-130.

mistakes.name: Reaching too far
mistakes.looks: The front heel lands far ahead with a locked knee.
mistakes.fix: Shorter, quicker steps; push off with the back foot.
mistakes.why: Long reaches brake every step and load the shin and knee.

mistakes.name: Head down, slumped
mistakes.looks: Chin toward the chest, upper back rounded, eyes on the feet.
mistakes.fix: Eyes 10-20 m ahead, chest tall.
mistakes.why: The head drifts forward, especially with a pack or when tired.

mistakes.name: Leaning under a pack
mistakes.looks: With a pack, the trunk tips well forward from the hips.
mistakes.fix: Lighten the pack, load heavy items high and close, tighten the hip belt.
mistakes.why: Heavy loads push the trunk and head forward and raise back and foot stress.

safety: Rucking: start at about 10% of body weight and add load slowly; blisters and foot pain come first.
Hiking: carry water, check the weather and tell someone your route.
Balance problems: walk on even ground, use a pole or a rail.
Chest pain or unusual breathlessness: stop and seek help.

variants.change: Walking 2.5 mph (4 km/h), level. MET 3.0 (Compendium 17170).
Walking 2.8-3.4 mph, level. MET 3.8 (Compendium 17190).
Walking 3.5-3.9 mph (5.6-6.3 km/h), level. MET 4.8 (Compendium 17200).
Walking 4.0-4.4 mph. MET 5.5 (Compendium 17220).
Race walking. MET 6.5 (Compendium 17110).
Hiking at a normal pace through fields and hills, no load. MET 5.3 (Compendium 17082).
Hiking with a daypack. MET 7.8 (Compendium 17012).
Climbing hills, 6-10% grade, no load, moderate to brisk. MET 7.0 (Compendium 17035).
Climbing hills with a 21-40 lb (10-18 kg) load, 3-10% grade. MET 7.5 (Compendium 17050).
Nordic walking 3.6-4.4 mph, level. MET 5.3 (Compendium 17304).
Nordic walking 4.5-5.0 mph, level. MET 8.5 (Compendium 17305).
Walking backward 3.5 mph, level. MET 6.0 (Compendium 17320).
Marching, moderate speed. MET 4.5 (Compendium 17088).
Water walking, moderate effort. MET 4.8 (Compendium 18368).

subtypes.name: March in place
subtypes.change: No travel: lift each knee toward hip height, opposite arm forward.

subtypes.name: Nordic walking
subtypes.change: Long, straight-ish arm swing; plant each pole by the opposite heel, angled back, and push it past the hip.

subtypes.name: Ruck (weighted walk)
subtypes.change: Pack high and tight to the back; a little more trunk lean and knee bend; smaller arm swing.

subtypes.name: Hike
subtypes.change: Uphill: more hip and knee bend, slight lean from the ankles, whole foot down. Downhill: short steps, soft knees, poles.

subtypes.name: Walking
subtypes.change: Default level walking.

metrics.label: Trunk lean
metrics.good: 0-8 (up to 15 with a pack or uphill)

motion.basis: Sagittal hip, knee and ankle ranges from kadaba1990 normal-gait data (hip about 30° to -10°, knee about 15° in stance and 60° in swing, ankle about 10° up to 15° down). Keyframes at even 1/6 steps of the cycle and arm angles are our estimates; pack lean from attwells2006.

families.name: Woodchop and rotation
families.pattern: Trunk rotation: the arms carry a load across the body on a diagonal (chop, lift) or side to side (Russian twist, wipers) while the hips and trunk turn.
setup: Stand side-on to a high cable, feet a bit wider than hips, knees soft.
Grab the handle with both hands above your near shoulder, arms long.
Brace and stand tall.

steps.text: Pull the handle down and across to the opposite hip, turning your hips and shoulders together.
Finish with arms long by the far knee, back foot pivoting.
Let the handle travel back up the same line under control.

cues.cue: Turn from the hips; pivot the back foot.
cues.why: Sharing the turn with the hips keeps twisting load off the lumbar spine.

cues.cue: Tall spine: don't round forward as you twist.
cues.why: Twisting combined with bending forward raises the risk of disc injury.

cues.cue: Arms long, hands follow your chest.
cues.why: The trunk muscles make the turn; the arms just transmit it.

cues.cue: Control the return as much as the chop.
cues.why: Power and strength tests on the cable chop need steady technique to be repeatable.

families.breathing: Breathe out as you chop or twist, in as you return.

tempo.note: Chop in about 1 s, return in 2. Power versions move fast but stay controlled.

mistakes.name: Rounding while twisting
mistakes.looks: The back rounds forward as the arms come across.
mistakes.fix: Hinge at the hips and keep your chest up.
mistakes.why: Flexion plus twist is the riskiest spine load.

mistakes.name: Arms only
mistakes.looks: The hips and shoulders stay square while the arms swing across.
mistakes.fix: Turn your belt buckle with the handle.
mistakes.why: The trunk muscles are skipped and the shoulders take the load.

mistakes.name: Feet stuck
mistakes.looks: Both feet stay planted and the knees twist.
mistakes.fix: Pivot on the back foot as you turn.
mistakes.why: Rotation then twists the knees and low back.

safety: Disc problems or low back pain: avoid fast loaded twisting with a rounded back; use anti-rotation (Pallof) work first.
Russian twists: keep the chest up; turning the shoulders while rounded loads the discs.

variants.change: Low-to-high lift: the same path in reverse.
Kneeling: the hips cannot help, so the trunk does more.
Seated, leaning back about 45 degrees, rotating the load side to side.
Lying on your back, legs swing side to side.
Bar end in a landmine: arms trace an arc from hip to hip.
Seated rotation machine: hips fixed, trunk rotates against the pad.
Chop combined with a squat or lunge.

subtypes.name: Russian twist
subtypes.match: russian|seated twist|sitting|twist sit|twist crunch|knee to elbow|seated cross
subtypes.change: Seated, trunk leaning back, feet down or lifted; the load moves from hip to hip.

subtypes.name: Windshield wipers
subtypes.match: wiper|windshield|lying twist|leg twist|lower body rotation|hip lift
subtypes.change: On your back, arms out wide, legs up; lower both legs to one side and back.

subtypes.name: Standing twist and landmine
subtypes.match: standing twist|landmine|180|torso twist|cable twist|band twist|barbell|lever|machine|torso rotation|turn
subtypes.change: Standing or seated tall, the trunk turns side to side with the load held in front.

motion.basis: Default is the standing high-to-low cable chop, cable on the subject's right. The convention has no trunk-rotation key, so the turn is approximated with opposite hip rotations and arm angles; a rig needs a trunk rotation channel (about 30-45 degrees each way, estimate). All angles estimated.

families.name: Wrist and forearm
families.pattern: Small forearm moves: the wrist bends and straightens, the forearm turns, or the hand squeezes, while the elbow stays still.
setup: Sit with your forearms resting on your thighs or a bench, wrists just past the edge.
Hold a light bar or dumbbells, palms up for a wrist curl.
Elbows about 90°, forearms still on the support.

steps.text: Let the weight roll the hand back until the wrist is bent back as far as is comfortable.
Curl the wrist up as high as you can; only the hand moves.
Hold the top for a moment.
Lower slowly back to the stretch.

cues.cue: Forearms stay flat on the support; only the hands move.
cues.why: Keeping the elbow still isolates the wrist muscles instead of turning it into a curl.

cues.cue: Full, slow range, wrist bent back to curled up.
cues.why: Controlled lowering of the wrist extensors (the eccentric phase) helps tennis-elbow recovery.

cues.cue: For grip holds, keep the wrist slightly bent back, about 25-35°.
cues.why: Grip is strongest near 35° of wrist extension; a straight or bent-down wrist cuts grip to two thirds or less.

cues.cue: Use light weights and higher reps.
cues.why: The forearm muscles are small and the wrist lever is short; heavy loads strain the wrist and elbow tendons.

families.breathing: Breathe normally; out as you curl.

tempo.note: Curl in 1 second, lower in about 3.

mistakes.name: Forearms lift
mistakes.looks: The elbows and forearms come off the support to help move the weight.
mistakes.fix: Press your forearms down and use less weight.
mistakes.why: The arm muscles take over from the wrist muscles.

mistakes.name: Tiny range
mistakes.looks: The hand only flicks a few degrees up and down.
mistakes.fix: Lower to a full stretch each rep, then curl all the way up.
mistakes.why: Short, fast reps skip the slow lowering that loads the tendon in a useful way.

mistakes.name: Wrist bent down in grip holds
mistakes.looks: During a hold or squeeze the wrist bends down toward the palm.
mistakes.fix: Keep the knuckles slightly back, wrist bent back about 30°.
mistakes.why: Grip strength falls sharply when the wrist leaves its best position.

safety: Tennis elbow: start with slow lowering only, light load; mild pain that settles within a day is usually acceptable, sharp pain is not.
Wrist pain or recent wrist injury: reduce the range and load and get advice.

variants.change: Standing, bar held behind or in front of the thighs: same wrist motion, arms hang.
One hand at a time.
Thumbs up: the wrist moves side to side (radial deviation).
Finger curl: let the bar roll down to the fingertips, then close the hand.
Cable or band: tension stays on through the whole range.

subtypes.name: Reverse wrist curl
subtypes.change: Palms down (forearm 85); the back of the hand lifts up (wrist extension).

subtypes.name: Pronation and supination
subtypes.change: Forearm rests on a bench or the arm hangs, hand holds one end of a dumbbell or hammer; turn the palm down, then up.

subtypes.name: Grip and pinch hold
subtypes.change: Squeeze a gripper, pinch plates or hold a hang board; wrist slightly bent back.

subtypes.name: Wrist roller
subtypes.change: Arms straight forward at shoulder height; roll the rope up by turning the hands one after the other, then lower it slowly.

motion.basis: Best grip wrist angle (about 35° extension) from odriscoll1992; slow eccentric emphasis from tyler2010. Wrist ranges are typical active range (about 60° flexion, 50-60° extension) used by us as estimates; seated posture is convention. No kinematic study of these exercises was found.

families.name: Cross-country skiing and snowshoeing
families.pattern: Whole-body travel over snow: legs kick or push, poles add an arm push, and you glide or step between pushes.
setup: Classic skis need grip wax or skins for kick; skate skis are shorter and stiffer.
Pole length: classic about to the armpit, skate about to the chin or mouth.
Dress in layers you can open; you warm up fast.
Snowshoes: bindings snug, crampons under the ball of the foot; poles help on hills.

steps.phase: Right leg kicks, right pole plants
steps.text: Press the right ski down hard and kick back while the left ski glides forward.
Ride the left ski with your weight fully over it, knee soft, trunk leaning forward.

steps.phase: Left leg kicks, left pole plants
steps.text: Swap: kick on the left, plant the left pole by the right foot.
Ride the right ski, arms swinging opposite to the legs.

cues.cue: Commit your weight fully onto the gliding ski.
cues.why: A full weight shift sets the grip zone for the next kick; half-weighting slips and wastes energy.

cues.cue: Kick down and back from a bent knee, like a scooter push.
cues.why: A fast, short push from a flexed knee is how skilled skiers make propulsion uphill.

cues.cue: Double pole: fall onto the poles with your body weight, then push past the hips.
cues.why: Elite double poling uses trunk and hip flexion to load the poles, not just the arms.

cues.cue: Plant the pole angled back, by the opposite foot.
cues.why: A pole planted ahead and vertical pushes you up, not forward.

cues.cue: Snowshoes: slightly wider steps, lift the knee, land flat.
cues.why: Walking on snow costs more energy, more so in deep or unpacked snow, so a steady pace matters.

families.breathing: Breathe in rhythm with the stride; on double poling breathe out as you crunch onto the poles.

tempo.note: Diagonal stride about 45-60 cycles per minute; double poling 50-70 per minute; snowshoeing like brisk walking.

mistakes.name: Sitting back
mistakes.looks: Hips behind the feet, upright trunk, legs push forward instead of down.
mistakes.fix: Shins and trunk lean forward, hips over the front foot.
mistakes.why: Weight stays between the skis, so there is no grip and no glide.

mistakes.name: Double poling with arms only
mistakes.looks: The trunk stays upright and only the elbows bend and straighten.
mistakes.fix: Lead with the chest, crunch down onto the poles, then push.
mistakes.why: Body weight on the poles is the main power source; arms alone tire fast.

mistakes.name: Snowshoes too narrow
mistakes.looks: Feet step in a line and the shoe frames clip each other.
mistakes.fix: Walk a little wider than normal and lift the knees.
mistakes.why: Clipping frames trips you; falls cause many winter injuries.

safety: Falls are the main injury cause: learn to snowplough and to fall to the side on hills.
Thumb injuries: wear pole straps correctly and let go of the pole when you fall.
Cold: cover hands, face and ears; leave plenty of daylight.
Avalanche terrain: snowshoe only on known safe routes.

variants.change: Skiing, cross country, 2.5 mph, slow or light. MET 6.8 (Compendium 19080).
Skiing, cross country, 4.0-4.9 mph, moderate. MET 8.5 (Compendium 19090).
Skiing, cross country, 5.0-7.9 mph, vigorous. MET 11.3 (Compendium 19100).
Skiing, cross country, 8-12 mph, racing. MET 14.0 (Compendium 19110).
Skiing, cross-country, skating. MET 13.3 (Compendium 19135).
Cross country, hard snow, uphill, maximal. MET 15.5 (Compendium 19130).
Rollerskiing 13-16.9 km/h, flat. MET 6.8 (Compendium 19310).
Snowshoeing, moderate effort. MET 5.3 (Compendium 19190).
Snowshoeing, vigorous effort. MET 10.0 (Compendium 19192).
In-line skating 9 mph, recreational (11 mph 9.8, code 15592). MET 7.5 (Compendium 15591).

subtypes.name: Classic (diagonal stride)
subtypes.change: Skis in tracks; kick, glide, opposite arm and leg, like a long walking stride.

keyframes.phase: Right leg kicks, right pole plants
Left leg kicks, left pole plants

subtypes.name: Double poling
subtypes.change: Both poles together, legs mostly still; crunch onto the poles from the hips and rise again.

subtypes.name: Skate skiing
subtypes.change: Skis in a V; push each ski out to the side with a bent knee and glide on the other, poles together every one or two pushes.

keyframes.phase: Right ski lands, both poles plant

subtypes.name: Snowshoeing
subtypes.change: Walking gait with a slightly wider step and higher knee lift; land the whole shoe; uphill kick the toe in, downhill heels first, knees soft.

subtypes.name: In-line skating
subtypes.change: Same side push as skate skiing without poles: knees bent, push out to the side, recover the foot under the hip, arms swing.

keyframes.phase: Push right out to the side
Push left out to the side
Right leg kicks, right pole plants
Left leg kicks, left pole plants

metrics.label: Step width (snowshoe)
metrics.good: a little wider than the frames

motion.basis: Movement pattern from pellegrini2022 (diagonal stride) and holmberg2005/stoggl2016 (double poling: large trunk and hip flexion, elbow flexion then extension). All joint angles are our estimates from these descriptions; we did not have full-text angle tables. Skate and snowshoe keyframes are estimates.

families.name: Yoga pose
families.pattern: Static postures held for a few breaths, or linked with the breath into a flow such as the sun salutation.
setup: Use a non-slip mat on a flat floor, barefoot.
Start in the base position of the pose: standing, kneeling, seated, on hands and knees, or lying down.
Set your feet and hands first, then build the pose from the ground up.

steps.text: Move into the pose slowly, stop at a firm but easy stretch, and breathe steadily for 3-5 breaths.

cues.cue: Breathe slowly through your nose; if you cannot, back off.
cues.why: Forceful breathing and pushing past your limit are among the techniques most linked to yoga injuries.

cues.cue: Long spine first, depth second.
cues.why: Most yoga injuries are trunk sprains and strains; deep folds and backbends load the spine most.

cues.cue: In lunges and warriors, front knee over the ankle, pointing at your toes.
cues.why: Standing poses load the knee in the side-to-side plane; letting the knee drift in adds that load.

cues.cue: Press through the whole foot: big toe, little toe, heel.
cues.why: Every standing pose works the ankle; a stable foot base controls balance.

cues.cue: Bend your knees in folds and down dog if your back rounds.
cues.why: Soft knees let the hips tip forward so the stretch moves out of the lower back.

families.breathing: Slow nasal breaths. In many flows you breathe in as you open or lift, and out as you fold or twist.

tempo.note: Hold most poses for 3-5 slow breaths (about 20-40 s). In a flow, one movement per breath.

mistakes.name: Front knee falls in
mistakes.looks: In a lunge or warrior the front knee drifts inside the big toe.
mistakes.fix: Push the knee out over your little toes, keep the front heel down.
mistakes.why: It raises the side-to-side load on the knee.

mistakes.name: Low back dumps in backbends
mistakes.looks: In cobra or upward dog the bend is all in the lower back and the shoulders hunch up.
mistakes.fix: Lift through the chest, shoulders down and back, legs active.
mistakes.why: The lower back takes the bend that the upper back and hips should share.

mistakes.name: Back rounds in folds
mistakes.looks: In forward folds and down dog the back curves like a C and the hips stay tucked.
mistakes.fix: Bend your knees and tip from the hips, chest toward the thighs.
mistakes.why: Rounding moves the stretch from the hamstrings to the spine.

mistakes.name: Weight on the neck in inversions
mistakes.looks: In shoulder stand, plow or headstand the neck is crushed and the body sinks.
mistakes.fix: Weight on the shoulders and forearms, never turn your head; use a folded blanket or skip it.
mistakes.why: Headstand and shoulder stand are the poses most often reported in yoga injury cases.

safety: Beginners: skip headstand, full lotus and forceful breathing until taught in person.
Glaucoma, high blood pressure or eye surgery: avoid inversions (head below the heart for long).
Weak bones (osteoporosis): avoid deep forward folds and loaded twists.
Adults over 65 have the highest injury rate: use a wall or chair for balance poses.
Pregnancy: avoid lying on your belly and deep twists; ask your midwife.

variants.change: Prop shortens the reach; same shape with less range.
Same pose, different camera angle or hand position.

subtypes.name: Sun salutation
subtypes.change: A flow of 12 poses, one per breath: prayer, arms up, fold, lunge, down dog, eight-limb, cobra, down dog, lunge, fold, arms up, prayer.

subtypes.name: Twists
subtypes.change: Rotate the chest about 45° over a stable pelvis; lengthen on the in-breath, turn on the out-breath. trunkRot is rotation toward the right.

subtypes.name: Arm balances (crane, peacock)
subtypes.change: Weight on bent arms, knees on the backs of the upper arms, hips high.

subtypes.name: Shoulder stand, plow, headstand
subtypes.change: Legs over the body. Shoulder stand: trunk vertical upside down (trunk 180), hands support the back. Plow: hips bend so the toes reach the floor behind your head (hipFlex about 150). Headstand: forearms and crown down, neck neutral.

subtypes.name: Pigeon and hip openers
subtypes.change: Front shin across the mat, front hip turned out; back leg long behind. Cow face: knees stacked, hands clasp behind the back.

subtypes.name: Cat and cow
subtypes.match: cat pose|cat cow|bitilasana|cow yoga pose bitilasana|tiger
subtypes.change: On hands and knees; round (cat) on the out-breath, arch (cow) on the in-breath. Tiger adds one leg reaching back.

subtypes.name: Child's pose
subtypes.change: Sit back on your heels, chest toward the thighs, arms long in front. Puppy keeps the hips over the knees.

subtypes.name: Downward-facing dog
subtypes.change: Inverted V: hips high, arms in line with the trunk, heels toward the floor. Dolphin: forearms down. Three-leg: one leg lifts in line with the trunk.

subtypes.name: Cobra, sphinx, upward dog
subtypes.change: Lying face down, chest lifts on the hands; elbows stay bent in cobra, forearms down in sphinx, arms straight and thighs off the floor in upward dog.

subtypes.name: Locust and bow
subtypes.change: Face down; chest and legs lift together (locust), or hands hold the ankles and kick into them (bow, kneeFlex about 110). Crocodile rests flat with the forehead on the hands.

subtypes.name: Camel
subtypes.change: Kneeling, hips over the knees, chest lifts and the hands reach for the heels.

subtypes.name: Bridge and wheel
subtypes.change: Lying face up, feet flat; hips lift (bridge). Wheel: hands by the ears press the whole body up into an arch.

subtypes.name: Fish
subtypes.change: Lying face up on the forearms, chest lifted, crown of the head lightly on the floor.

subtypes.name: Warrior III, half moon
subtypes.change: Standing on the left leg, trunk and right leg level like a T. Half moon opens the hips and chest to the side.

subtypes.name: Tree and standing balances
subtypes.change: Stand on the left leg; right sole on the inner thigh or calf (never on the knee), knee out. Eagle wraps the legs and arms; dancer holds the back foot.

subtypes.name: Chair
subtypes.change: Feet together, sit back as if into a chair, arms up beside the ears.

subtypes.name: Warrior II, side angle
subtypes.match: warrior ii|warrior pose ii|virabhadrasana v\. 2|reverse warrior|side angle|parsvakonasana|straight angle
subtypes.change: Wide stance, front foot forward, back foot turned in; front knee bent over the ankle, hips and chest open to the side, arms out level. Side angle leans the trunk over the front thigh.

subtypes.name: Warrior I, lunges
subtypes.change: Long stance, hips square to the front; front knee over the ankle, back leg long, arms overhead. Low lunge puts the back knee down.

subtypes.name: Triangle, pyramid
subtypes.change: Legs straight and wide; the trunk tips to the side over the front leg (shown as trunk lean), arms in one vertical line. Pyramid folds forward over the front leg instead.

subtypes.name: Standing forward fold
subtypes.match: forward bend|uttanasana|hands to feet|hastasana|wide legged|prasarita|half bend|standing seal
subtypes.change: Fold from the hips, knees soft, head hangs. Half bend: flat back halfway up, hands on the shins.

subtypes.name: Garland squat
subtypes.change: Deep squat, heels down, knees wide, elbows press the knees out with the palms together.

subtypes.name: Boat
subtypes.change: Balance on the sit bones, trunk and legs make a V, arms forward. Half boat bends the knees.

subtypes.name: Plank and chaturanga
subtypes.change: Body in one line; chaturanga lowers until the elbows are bent about 90°, elbows by the ribs.

subtypes.name: Seated forward fold
subtypes.match: spread leg forward fold|upavista|seated wide angle|head to knee|janu
subtypes.change: Seated, legs long (or wide), fold from the hips toward the feet.

subtypes.name: Lotus and easy seats
subtypes.change: Tall seat for breathing. Cross-legged, lotus (feet on the thighs), butterfly (soles together), or kneeling on the heels (hero, thunderbolt: kneeFlex 160, no hip turn-out).

subtypes.name: Reclined and resting poses
subtypes.match: corpse|savasana|happy baby|pavanamuktasana|legs up the wall|reclining big toe
subtypes.change: Lying face up. Corpse: still and relaxed. Happy baby: knees to the armpits holding the feet. Legs up the wall: hips near the wall, legs vertical (hipFlex 90). Big toe pose: one straight leg raised with a strap.

subtypes.name: Mountain (standing)
subtypes.change: Stand tall, feet together or hip width, weight even, arms by the sides or overhead.

metrics.label: Head
metrics.good: in line with the spine; not loaded in inversions

motion.basis: Default keyframe is downward dog. Sun salutation hip, knee, ankle, elbow, wrist and spine angles from the 3-D motion capture of mullerpatan2019 (12 poses, timing from its pose durations); its knee in down dog (57°) and neck in cobra (-77°) were reduced to taught form, and shoulder flexion is estimated because that paper measured it differently. Standing-pose hip ranges checked against whissell2021 (triangle hip 90°) and the joint-moment profiles in wang2013, yu2012 and salem2013. All other pose angles are estimates from the classic shapes. Subtypes are listed most specific first; the first match wins. trunkRot (trunk rotation, + toward the right) is an extra key not yet in the README convention.
